chunks.content: 1 Introduction Mental health problems defined by symptomatology consistent with conditions such as Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) (Kessler and Bromet ), Anorexia Nervosa (AN) (Smink et al. ; Averous et al. ), Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) (Bandelow and Michaelis ; Penninx et al. ), Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD) (Stein et al. ), and Panic Disorder (PD) (De Jonge et al. ), present profound clinical challenges. They encompass distorted cognitions, emotional burdens, and sometimes life‐threatening consequences. The burden of these conditions extends across various domains, including high levels of morbidity and disability (Vigo et al. ), increased rates of mortality (Plana‐Ripoll et al. ; Krug et al. ), financial strain (Frankham et al. ), and significant disruptions to educational and occupational opportunities (McLeod and Fettes ). Understanding how individuals perceive and interpret their illnesses is crucial for managing these mental health conditions effectively. The Brief Illness Perception Questionnaire (BIPQ) (Broadbent et al. ) offers a concise psychometrically sound framework to capture individuals' perceptions of their mental health conditions. Rooted in the Self‐Regulatory Model (SRM) (Leventhal et al. , ; Baines and Wittkowski ), the BIPQ encapsulates key dimensions of illness perceptions (IPs): Identity, Cause, Timeline, Consequences, Controllability, Coherence and Emotional Representations. Although using a single item per dimension is less comprehensive than the 38‐item Illness Perception Questionnaire‐Revised (IPQ‐R; Moss‐Morris et al. ), the BIPQ's concise 8‐item format enables rapid assessment in clinical settings. Each dimension is rated on a 0–10 scale, providing an efficient way to capture patients' cognitive and emotional representations and guide targeted interventions (Broadbent et al. ). While the BIPQ has been extensively used to examine IPs in non‐psychiatric disorders (Broadbent et al. ), its application in mental health conditions remains limited. Research has mainly focused on its relationship with psychosocial adjustment and adherence to treatment in individuals with MDD (Averous et al. ; Broadbent et al. ; Vervoort et al. ; Glattacker et al. ; Spain et al. ), while neglecting other disorders that are frequently comorbid with MDD, such as anxiety disorders (Ter Meulen et al. ) and eating disorders (Hambleton et al. ). The current study addresses this gap by examining IPs in MDD, eating disorders, and anxiety disorders, enabling a broader understanding of IPs across highly comorbid and often overlapping mental health conditions. 1.1 Prior Studies on Illness Perceptions Across Mental Health Disorders 1.1.1 Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) The SRM has been validated as a reliable framework for understanding IPs in individuals with depression (Fortune et al. ), with findings in MDD indicating that, although these perceptions may not directly relate to symptom severity, they are strongly associated with treatment‐related behaviours. Accordingly, more negative illness views have been linked to lower help‐seeking, poorer treatment adherence, and reduced engagement with preferred interventions (Manber et al. ; Munson et al. ). However, the relationship between specific IP dimensions and depressive symptom severity remains underexplored, representing a notable gap in the literature. 1.1.2 Anorexia Nervosa In research involving individuals with AN, studies have consistently shown that IPs are closely linked to clinical eating disorder symptom severity. Early work found that people with AN often view their illness as chronic and distressing, with serious consequences, little sense of personal control, and low confidence in the effectiveness of treatment (Holliday et al. ; Stockford et al. ). These maladaptive perceptions, particularly viewing the condition as having a long timeline and being outside of one's control, are reliably linked to a greater eating disorder symptom severity (Stockford et al. ; Agüera et al. ). Highlighting the complexities of AN, some evidence reveals a potential paradox; when compared directly with other eating disorders (Bulimia Nervosa, Binge Eating Disorder [BED] and Other Specified Feeding or Eating Disorder [OSFED]), individuals with AN reported their condition as less chronic and with fewer negative consequences. This finding may reflect the poor insight or the ego‐syntonic nature of the condition, wherein the illness is deeply integrated into a person’s identity and sense of self (Agüera et al., ). Such complexities therefore underscore the need for nuanced assessment and tailored interventions that address both the cognitive representations of the illness and the unique motivational barriers to change in AN. 1.1.3 Anxiety Disorders Research exploring IPs within anxiety disorders reveals a complex landscape, highlighting not only key differences between conditions but also direct associations with clinical severity. When comparing across different anxiety conditions, individuals with symptoms of PD have been found to report lower personal and treatment control around their symptoms than those with SAD, a specific distinction that holds even when accounting for underlying anxiety sensitivity (Dias et al. ). In primary care settings for GAD, perceptions of severe consequences, low personal control, poor illness coherence, and biological causal beliefs have been linked to higher anxiety levels (Yap et al. ). In PD, El Amiri et al.

disorders reveals a complex landscape, highlighting not only key differences between conditions but also direct associations with clinical severity. When comparing across different anxiety conditions, individuals with symptoms of PD have been found to report lower personal and treatment control around their symptoms than those with SAD, a specific distinction that holds even when accounting for underlying anxiety sensitivity (Dias et al. ). In primary care settings for GAD, perceptions of severe consequences, low personal control, poor illness coherence, and biological causal beliefs have been linked to higher anxiety levels (Yap et al. ). In PD, El Amiri et al. ( ) examined the role of causal attributions in receiving cognitive behavioural therapy. They found that biological beliefs were associated with sex, illness duration and family history of psychiatric illness, while environmental beliefs were related to prior psychotherapy. Both types of beliefs predicted symptom severity 12 weeks after treatment. Together, these findings suggest that targeting specific IPs could be a promising avenue for improving treatment outcomes in anxiety disorders. 1.2 Addressing Literature Gaps Through a Transdiagnostic and Recovery‐Focused Lens Despite advances in understanding IPs, most existing research has been conducted in isolation for specific disorders, often with small sample sizes that limit robustness and generalisability. As a result, it remains unclear whether IPs differ meaningfully across mental health conditions. Moreover, confounding variables such as gender and age are rarely controlled for, potentially influencing findings. Adopting a transdiagnostic perspective can bridge the gap between research confined to diagnostic categories and the realities of clinical practice, where comorbidity is common (Dalgleish et al. ). Such an approach also facilitates the identification of shared and disorder‐specific processes, enabling more targeted, efficient, and personalised interventions. IPs in mental disorders are also relevant to the recovery model in psychiatry, which emphasises patient involvement, empowerment, and a holistic, person‐centred approach (Jacobson and Greenley ; Slade et al. ). By understanding patients' IPs, clinicians can tailor interventions that align with their perspectives, enhancing treatment adherence, satisfaction, and outcomes (Leamy et al. ). Integrating IPs into shared decision‐making fosters a sense of ownership and control—core principles of recovery (Anthony )—and supports not only clinical goals of symptom reduction and functional improvement, but also personal goals of living a fulfilling, meaningful life despite mental health challenges (Davidson et al. ; Leamy et al. ; Ramon et al. ). 1.3 The Current Study The present study focused on MDD, AN, GAD, SAD and PD, which are highly comorbid (McGrath et al. ) and share overlapping cognitive (Arango et al. ), emotional (Hogg et al. ), and neurobiological (Meyer‐Lindenberg and Tost ) risk factors. By assessing IPs concurrently across these conditions, the study enabled direct comparison of how different mental health disorders influence these perceptions, addressing limitations of prior research that examined disorders in isolation. Additional mental health diagnostic categories were not included due to practical constraints and to minimise participant burden, ensuring a focused and feasible scope. Understanding both shared and disorder‐specific IPs is particularly important given the diagnostic uncertainty, overlap, and comorbidity common in mental health (Aftab and Ryznar ). Accordingly, this study aimed to investigate the influence of IPs on clinical severity across MDD, AN, GAD, SAD and PD. By utilizing the well‐validated BIPQ, the study aimed to uncover how individuals perceive their illnesses across various IP dimensions and if these perceptions impacted their clinical presentations. Additionally, the study aimed to explore IPs cross‐diagnostically to identify commonalities and differences in IPs among individuals with different mental health disorders. It was hypothesised that: more negative IPs would be associated with increased clinical severity across MDD, AN, GAD, SAD, and PD (H1) and that IPs would show both shared features across disorders and disorder‐specific patterns (H2). 2 Methods 2.1 Participants A total of 774 participants were included, categorized into five diagnostic groups: MDD, AN, GAD, SAD and PD. Demographic information, self‐reported in nature, summarized in Table , revealed a predominantly female sample (86.7%), with participants ranging in age from 18 to 67 years. Significant differences were found in gender distribution, sexual orientation, education level, and ethnicity. While these differences were statistically significant, effect sizes were generally small, indicating that the magnitude of group‐level demographic variation was modest. The sample exhibited high levels of comorbidity, with significant overlap between diagnostic groups, as detailed in Table . Despite these variations, the overall sample offered a broad demographic range, facilitating an examination of IPs across diverse mental health presentations. 2.2 Data Sample The data was part of a larger research project, that collected data from 2019 to 2023, looking at transdiagnostic factors across several mental health conditions, multiple sclerosis, cancer, and endometriosis; the current study focused solely on the mental health disorders. Specifically, we assessed IPs in MDD, AN, GAD, SAD and PD. Other mental health disorders were assessed but excluded from the

Despite these variations, the overall sample offered a broad demographic range, facilitating an examination of IPs across diverse mental health presentations. 2.2 Data Sample The data was part of a larger research project, that collected data from 2019 to 2023, looking at transdiagnostic factors across several mental health conditions, multiple sclerosis, cancer, and endometriosis; the current study focused solely on the mental health disorders. Specifically, we assessed IPs in MDD, AN, GAD, SAD and PD. Other mental health disorders were assessed but excluded from the analyses due to small sample sizes, including BED ( n = 36), OSFED ( n = 26), Specific Phobia ( n = 27), Separation Anxiety Disorder ( n = 46), Agoraphobia ( n = 23), and Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder ( n = 43). Ethical approval was obtained from a University in Melbourne with an Ethics Committee HREC number: 1853137.6. Informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to their involvement for use of their data and publication. Participants received an e‐gift voucher for their participation. Data security was de‐identified and stored on university password protected serves. 2.3 Measures An online survey which included a number of validated measures were administered to all participants to assess various dimensions of IPs, symptom severity, and demographic and clinical information distributed through Qualtrics. For the present study the following measures were used: Brief Illness Perception Questionnaire (BIPQ) (Broadbent et al. ): An 8‐item measure assessing cognitive and emotional representations of illness, with items rated on an 11‐point scale from 0 to 10. Higher scores indicate more negative IPs. Centre for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES‐D) (Radloff ): A 20‐item measure assessing depressive symptoms experienced in the past week, scored from 0 (rarely or none of the time) to 3 (most or all of the time). Total scores range from 0 to 60, with higher scores indicating greater depressive symptoms. With a Cronbach's alpha value of α = 0.94 the reliability of the CES‐D was excellent. Eating Attitudes Test (EAT‐26) (Garner et al. ): A 26‐item self‐report measure assessing symptoms and concerns characteristic of eating disorders, scored from 0 (never) to 3 (always). Total scores range from 0 to 78, with higher scores indicating more severe ED symptoms. The Cronbach alpha value for the current sample for the EAT‐26 was excellent ( α = 0.92). Generalized Anxiety Disorder Assessment (GAD‐7) (Spitzer et al. ): A seven‐item self‐report measure assessing the severity of GAD symptoms, scored from 0 (not at all) to 3 (nearly every day). Total scores range from 0 to 21, with higher scores indicating greater severity. The Cronbach's alpha value for the GAD‐7 was good ( α = 0.88). Social Interaction Anxiety Scale (SIAS) (Mattick and Clarke ): A 20‐item measure assessing fear of social interactions, a measure of SAD, scored from 0 (not at all characteristic of me) to 4 (extremely characteristic of me). Total scores range from 0 to 80, with higher scores indicating greater social anxiety. The Cronbach alpha value for the current sample for the SIAS was excellent ( α = 0.93). Panic Disorder Severity Scale (PDSS) (Shear et al. ): A clinician‐administered scale with seven items rated on a five‐point scale, assessing the severity of symptoms. Higher scores indicate greater severity. With a Cronbach's alpha of value of α = 0.88 the reliability of the PDSS was considered good. 2.4 Procedure Participants were recruited through university networks, local health organizations, and affiliated mental health services. Interested individuals accessed the survey via a Qualtrics link, where they were provided with detailed study information, including the purpose, procedures, and confidentiality measures. Participants provided informed consent before proceeding. The survey was self‐administered online and asked participants to only identify illnesses that had been diagnosed by a mental health care clinician. Upon completion, responses were securely stored on password‐protected university servers. Data quality control measures included removing incomplete responses and duplicate entries. Following survey completion, participants received an electronic gift voucher as compensation for their time and contribution. 2.5 Statistical Analyses All data analysis was conducted using JASP 0.19.0 with significance set at p < 0.05 for all statistical models. Incomplete responses and duplicates excluded prior to analysis. This exclusion maintained the integrity of the dataset and ensured accurate interpretation of the results. A linear regression analysis was employed to assess our first aim, observing the relationship between IPs (BIPQ scores) and clinical severity (outcome measures i.e. MDD = CES‐D) for each disorder separately. A linear regression analysis was employed to assess our first aim, observing the relationship between IPs (BIPQ scores) and clinical severity (outcome measures i.e. MDD = CES‐D) for each disorder separately. The model included IPs as the predictor variable and clinical severity as the outcome variable. Age, gender, illness duration and body mass index (BMI, for the AN group only) were included as covariates to control for demographic influences. BMI was included in the AN analysis due to it being a diagnostic criterion of AN in the DSM‐5 (American Psychiatric Association ; Machado et al. ), and because starvation (a low BMI) impacts cognition (Spettigue et al. ). For our second aim, looking at the unique/shared IP dimensions across mental health conditions, a Kruskal‐Wallis test was conducted to compare the BIPQ subscales across the five diagnostic groups (MDD, AN, GAD, SAD and PD). Kruskal‐Wallis was chosen due to deviations from normality detected by the Shapiro‐Wilk test in all mental health conditions, ensuring the analysis remains valid without assuming normal distribution. Levene's test for homogeneity of variances was non‐significant across all subscales ( p > 0.05), supporting the assumption of equal variances. Post‐hoc Dunn's tests were used to explore significant pairwise group differences, with Bonferroni corrections applied to adjust for multiple comparisons. This approach provided a robust analysis while controlling for potential Type I errors due to multiple tests. Throughout all analyses, the assumptions of the selected statistical methods were examined. Where assumptions were breeched, appropriate non‐parametric methods were used to ensure robust conclusions. The chosen analytic approach offered both disorder‐specific insights (via regression models) and cross‐diagnostic comparisons (via Kruskal‐Wallis and post‐hoc tests), providing a comprehensive assessment of the role of IPs in mental health illness severity. 3 Results 3.1 Illness Perceptions and Their Associations With Symptom Severity Table presents the associations between IPs and symptom severity across MDD, AN, GAD, SAD and PD, controlling for age, illness duration, gender and BMI (for AN only). For MDD, no IP subscales were significantly related to CES‐D scores; however, longer illness duration predicted greater severity, while older age was associated with lower severity. In AN, higher Treatment Control was linked to lower EAT‐26 scores, whereas higher Personal Control was linked to greater severity. For GAD, higher Personal Control was associated with lower GAD‐7 scores, while greater Concern and longer illness duration were linked to higher severity; older age was associated with lower severity. For SAD, older age predicted lower SIAS scores, with no significant associations for IP subscales. Finally, for PD, no significant associations were observed between IPs, age, illness duration, and PDDS scores. 3.2 Comparing Illness Perceptions Across Mental Health Conditions Table shows the differences between IP dimensions and the five mental health disorders. Significant effects were observed for Timeline, Identity, Coherence, and Emotional Representations. Dunn's post‐hoc comparisons (Table ), adjusted for multiple comparisons, indicated that significant differences were observed between mental health conditions across multiple subscales. On the Timeline subscale, AN showed significantly lower scores compared to all other conditions, with both GAD and MDD groups scoring significantly higher than SAD. For Identity, the AN group scored significantly lower than GAD, MDD and PD. On the Emotional Representation subscale, the AN group demonstrated significantly lower scores compared to GAD and MDD. Finally, although Coherence showed a significant overall group difference, post‐hoc comparisons did not reveal any statistically significant differences between the individual disorders. 4 Discussion The aims of the current study were twofold: (1) to investigate whether IPs were linked to symptom severity in MDD, AN, GAD, SAD and PD and (2) to explore differences and similarities in IPs across these mental disorders. With our first hypothesis we found that IPs were significantly associated with symptom severity only in AN and GAD. Specifically, we found that Personal Control was linked to reduced severity in GAD but increased severity in AN; Treatment Control was negatively associated with severity in AN; and perceived Concern was positively associated with severity in GAD. Consistent with our second hypothesis, our findings supported a largely transdiagnostic pattern; however, important differences also emerged across conditions in Timeline, Identity, and Emotional Representations, with these differences being most pronounced in AN. 4.1 Perceived Personal Control and Treatment Control in Anorexia Nervosa In AN, our study identified significant associations between Personal Control and Treatment Control and illness severity, consistent with previous research highlighting the role of perceived control in ED severity (Gorwood et al. ). Specifically, our results indicate that individuals with AN who perceived higher levels of Personal Control over their condition reported greater eating disorder severity. This suggests that in AN, perceived Personal Control may be maladaptive, reinforcing rigid control over food intake, body weight, and other disordered

Identity, and Emotional Representations, with these differences being most pronounced in AN. 4.1 Perceived Personal Control and Treatment Control in Anorexia Nervosa In AN, our study identified significant associations between Personal Control and Treatment Control and illness severity, consistent with previous research highlighting the role of perceived control in ED severity (Gorwood et al. ). Specifically, our results indicate that individuals with AN who perceived higher levels of Personal Control over their condition reported greater eating disorder severity. This suggests that in AN, perceived Personal Control may be maladaptive, reinforcing rigid control over food intake, body weight, and other disordered behaviours that exacerbate the illness (Agüera et al. ; Haynos et al. ; Pauligk et al. ). Our findings also demonstrated that for the AN sample higher perceptions of Treatment Control were associated with lower eating disorder symptom severity, suggesting that a belief in the efficacy of treatment maybe a protective factor. This aligns with a growing body of literature demonstrating that strong beliefs in the controllability of a condition through treatment often lead to improved adherence, higher treatment expectations, and better clinical outcomes across a range of health issues (von der Warth et al. ; Chan and Mak ). It is important to note that many individuals with AN also experienced comorbid anxiety or depression, which may have shaped the relationship between perceived control and illness severity. Elevated Personal Control may reflect not only eating‐specific cognitions but also a broader tendency toward rigidity and perfectionism compounded by comorbid anxiety. Conversely, beliefs in Treatment Control might be weakened in the presence of comorbid depression, where hopelessness can undermine optimism about treatment efficacy. While comorbidity may have influenced these perceptions, our findings nonetheless highlight the importance of considering Personal Control and Treatment Control within the AN individuals. Our findings suggest that both Personal Control and Treatment Control could be important targets for recovery in AN. Helping individuals with AN develop a more flexible and adaptive sense of control, focused on healthy behaviours rather than rigidity in their disordered eating patterns (Robertson and Thornton ) and greater appreciation for Treatment Control, may reduce the severity of eating disorder symptoms in AN. 4.2 Concern and Personal Control Shape Anxiety Severity in Generalised Anxiety Disorder In our study, a greater perceived sense of Personal Control was associated with lower anxiety severity, while a higher level of Concern was related to increased anxiety symptoms. Ou findings align with previous research, such as the study by Yap et al. ( ), which found that negative perceptions of Personal Control and the perceived Consequences of anxiety significantly contribute to heightened anxiety levels. This may reflect how emotional distress may heighten both the mental and physical strain of anxiety, where intense emotional interpretations and preoccupation can lead individuals to become overly sensitive to perceived threats (Bystritsky and Kronemyer ; Hirsch et al. ). Given the high rates of comorbidity between GAD and depression (Groen et al. ; Ter Meulen et al. ), it is possible that overlapping symptoms (e.g., fatigue, concentration problems) or shared cognitive vulnerabilities influenced our findings. For instance, the positive association between Concern and anxiety severity may partly reflect ruminative processes common to both GAD and depression (Baik and Newman ), making it difficult to disentangle disorder‐specific IPs from transdiagnostic features driven by comorbidity. Furthermore, extended duration of illness and advancing age were both correlated with higher GAD‐7 scores, which reflects our current understanding of a longer duration of untreated illness leading to poorer response to treatment and worse outcomes (Altamura et al. ). Fostering a sense of personal control may empower GAD patients to manage their anxiety more effectively, reducing its overall impact. This reflects the goals of most psychotherapy approaches to anxiety, which aim to provide people with skills to manage their distress and cognitions (Papola et al. ; Nakao et al. ). Conversely, our finding that higher levels of Concern were associated with increased GAD symptom severity suggests that addressing excessive worry about the condition itself may be a crucial therapeutic target. 4.3 Age as a Predictor of Social Anxiety Severity Our study revealed no significant associations between IPs and clinical severity of individuals with SAD. However, we did find that age was significantly and negatively associated with SAD severity. The inverse association between age and SAD severity may reflect the developmental trajectory of the condition, with a growing prevalence of SAD among younger populations (Jefferies and Ungar ). While our study did not find a direct link between IPs and illness severity in SAD, the literature highlights the importance of perceived control and consequences in managing this diagnosis (Dias et al. ; Hur et al. ). Previous research suggests that interventions such as exposure therapy and cognitive restructuring may help shift perceptions of consequences, allowing individuals to more actively engage in

was significantly and negatively associated with SAD severity. The inverse association between age and SAD severity may reflect the developmental trajectory of the condition, with a growing prevalence of SAD among younger populations (Jefferies and Ungar ). While our study did not find a direct link between IPs and illness severity in SAD, the literature highlights the importance of perceived control and consequences in managing this diagnosis (Dias et al. ; Hur et al. ). Previous research suggests that interventions such as exposure therapy and cognitive restructuring may help shift perceptions of consequences, allowing individuals to more actively engage in social situations and develop coping mechanisms (Butler et al. ; Newman et al. ). 4.4 Illness Perceptions in Panic Disorder Do Not Impact Clinical Severity Building on the work of Dias et al. ( ), who demonstrated that PD patients exhibited significantly higher anxiety sensitivity and lower perceived personal and treatment control compared to SAD patients, our study offers additional perspectives with a larger and more diverse sample. However, in contrast to Dias et al.'s findings, our data did not reveal statistically significant relationships between IPs and PD severity. This discrepancy suggests that while PD patients may perceive their condition as having significant negative consequences and a chronic timeline, these perceptions do not necessarily correlate with the severity of their panic symptoms. Several factors may help explain the discrepancy between our findings and those of Dias et al. ( ). One notable difference lies in the sample sizes: our study included 62 individuals with PD, compared to 36 participants in Dias et al.’s study. While our sample is larger and somewhat more diverse, it is still relatively modest in size, which may limit the strength and generalizability of the conclusions. Future studies with larger, multi‐site cohorts will be important to clarify these differences and strengthen the evidence base. Overall, the lack of significant findings for PD and SAD may partly reflect their frequent comorbidity with depression and other anxiety disorders (Kalin ). Comorbid depression, for example, could overshadow disorder‐specific IPs, with depressive cognitions about control or consequences diluting associations within these groups. This heterogeneity may have reduced the likelihood of detecting disorder‐specific IP–severity links. 4.5 Illness Duration and Gender as a Key Driver of Clinical Severity in Major Depressive Disorder Our findings for MDD did not reveal any significant associations between IPs and clinical severity. However, we found that longer illness duration and female gender were associated with greater depressive symptom severity. While the link between illness duration and chronicity aligns with prior research (Monroe and Harkness ; Ten Have et al. ), our finding of gender differences contrasts with literature that often reports no significant differences (Parker et al. ). Our findings highlight the need to consider illness duration in MDD interventions, particularly for long‐standing cases where managing chronic symptoms and preventing recurrence is essential. Although our study did not find specific IPs to be significant, therapies such as Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (Beck ) remain important for targeting cognitive distortions and reducing symptom burden. 4.6 Comparison of Illness Perceptions Across Mental Health Disorders Supporting our second hypothesis, we found that most IP subscales showed transdiagnostic features, with a few disorders displaying unique profiles. AN was particularly distinct from other mental health conditions on Timeline, Identity, and Emotional Representations. When looking at how individuals perceive their illness identity, individuals with MDD often viewed their illness as a more integral part of their identity compared to those with AN. This suggests that MDD may be perceived as a core aspect of the self, potentially due to its pervasive impact on mood and daily functioning (Kendler ), often leading to a profound alteration in self‐concept and daily life. The chronic and relapsing nature of depressive symptoms can deeply affect an individual's sense of self, reinforcing the perception that the illness is an inseparable part of their identity (Kessler and Bromet ; Manber et al. ; Kendler ). In contrast, individuals with AN frequently perceive themselves as having greater control over their condition. This perception is a critical component of their clinical profile, where a sense of control is often overvalued (Gorwood et al. ; Agüera et al. ; Holliday et al. ; Fairburn et al. ). It has been suggested that this belief can manifest as a defence mechanism against the perceived chaos or lack of control in other areas of life, or as part of the cognitive distortions characteristic of the disorder (Fairburn et al. ; Brewerton and Dennis ). The strong focus on control overeating and body image, despite serious health consequences, illustrates a poor insight into the severity and complexity of their condition (Gorwood et al. ; Arbel et al. ; Vandereycken , ). Regarding perceptions of illness duration, individuals with anxiety disorders generally perceived their condition as more

Fairburn et al. ). It has been suggested that this belief can manifest as a defence mechanism against the perceived chaos or lack of control in other areas of life, or as part of the cognitive distortions characteristic of the disorder (Fairburn et al. ; Brewerton and Dennis ). The strong focus on control overeating and body image, despite serious health consequences, illustrates a poor insight into the severity and complexity of their condition (Gorwood et al. ; Arbel et al. ; Vandereycken , ). Regarding perceptions of illness duration, individuals with anxiety disorders generally perceived their condition as more chronic compared to those with AN. This is consistent with the clinical profile of anxiety disorders, where symptoms such as persistent worry and hypervigilance create a continuous state of mental and physical tension (Angst and Vollrath ; Hovenkamp‐Hermelink et al. ). The persistent nature of anxiety symptoms, often exacerbated by triggers and stressors, contrasts with the perception in AN, where a greater sense of control might lead to underestimating the disorder's chronicity. These cross‐disorder comparisons demonstrate the complexity and diversity of IPs, reinforcing why a one‐size‐fits‐all approach is unlikely to be effective in clinical practice. When interpreting these cross‐disorder comparisons, it is also crucial to acknowledge that comorbidity likely influenced group differences. For example, individuals with AN and comorbid anxiety may report higher Concern or Emotional Representations compared to those with ‘pure’ AN, making AN appear more distinct. Similarly, the degree to which MDD was perceived as part of identity may be intensified when occurring alongside long‐standing anxiety disorders. Thus, what appear to be disorder‐specific IPs may in part reflect comorbid clinical features. 4.7 Implications of Findings Our results have important implications for understanding and addressing IPs in clinical practice. Tailoring treatment interventions to target maladaptive IPs, such as perceptions of illness chronicity or lack of personal control, may enhance treatment engagement and improve outcomes for individuals with mental health disorders. Additionally, our findings underscore the importance of considering individual differences in IPs when developing personalized treatment approaches. Given the high prevalence of comorbidity across the disorders examined, interventions may also need to address overlapping or compounded IPs that span multiple conditions. For instance, comorbid anxiety and depression may intensify maladaptive beliefs about uncontrollability or chronicity, while co‐occurring eating and anxiety disorders could reinforce rigid perceptions of personal control. Recognising and targeting these transdiagnostic patterns within comorbid presentations may therefore be critical for optimizing treatment outcomes. Our study's findings are particularly relevant to the ongoing shift towards the recovery model in psychiatry (Davidson et al. ), which emphasizes patient‐centred care and greater involvement of patients in their own treatment and decision‐making processes. The recovery model advocates for a holistic approach that considers the individual's subjective experience of their illness, aiming to empower patients by involving them actively in their treatment plans (Leamy et al. ; Slade et al. ). By elucidating the significant relationships between IPs and clinical severity across various mental health disorders, our research highlights the importance of understanding and addressing these perceptions in clinical practice. Tailoring interventions to align with patients' views and experiences can enhance engagement and adherence to treatment, fostering a sense of ownership and control over their recovery journey (Leamy et al. ). This approach aligns with the recovery model's principles of personal empowerment and collaborative care, promoting not just symptom reduction but also the achievement of a meaningful and fulfilling life despite the presence of mental illness (Anthony ). Therefore, incorporating IP assessments into routine clinical practice could significantly enhance the efficacy of mental health care and support the broader goals of the recovery model. 4.8 Limitations, Strengths and Future Directions This study has several important limitations. First, the cross‐sectional design precludes causal inferences, making it unclear whether IPs shape clinical severity or vice versa. Future research should employ longitudinal or experimental designs to clarify temporal and causal relationships. Second, all data relied on self‐report measures, introducing potential recall bias, social desirability effects, and item misinterpretation. Future work could combine self‐report with clinician‐rated assessments or objective behavioural/biological measures to improve validity. Third, diagnoses were self‐reported, based on prior clinical diagnoses rather than structured clinical interviews, which may affect diagnostic accuracy and overlook comorbidities or illness chronicity. Subsequent studies should incorporate standardized diagnostic interviews to enhance diagnostic precision and capture comorbid patterns. Fourth, although we controlled for illness duration, gender, and with BMI in AN, we did not account for other clinical variables such as treatment status or functional impairment, which could influence both IPs and symptom severity. Future research should integrate these variables to provide a more comprehensive understanding of these relationships. Fifth, we did not systematically assess comorbid conditions. Given the high rates of co‐occurrence among the disorders studied, comorbidity may have significantly influenced both IPs and severity, potentially obscuring or inflating

or illness chronicity. Subsequent studies should incorporate standardized diagnostic interviews to enhance diagnostic precision and capture comorbid patterns. Fourth, although we controlled for illness duration, gender, and with BMI in AN, we did not account for other clinical variables such as treatment status or functional impairment, which could influence both IPs and symptom severity. Future research should integrate these variables to provide a more comprehensive understanding of these relationships. Fifth, we did not systematically assess comorbid conditions. Given the high rates of co‐occurrence among the disorders studied, comorbidity may have significantly influenced both IPs and severity, potentially obscuring or inflating associations. Future studies should incorporate structured diagnostic interviews to assess and control for comorbidity, and examine whether certain disorder combinations (e.g., AN + GAD, MDD + SAD) are associated with distinct IP constellations. Sixth, recruitment from university settings and health organizations may limit generalizability, as participants may not represent more diverse cultural, geographical, or socioeconomic backgrounds. Broader recruitment strategies, including community‐based and cross‐cultural samples, are needed to enhance representativeness and external validity. Finally, the study's strengths should also be acknowledged, which include its cross‐diagnostic examination of IPs across multiple mental health disorders, the use of validated measures, and a large sample enabling robust analyses. By focussing on IPs ‐ a factor often overlooked in mental health research ‐ it offers valuable insights to guide recovery‐oriented, patient‐centred interventions. 5 Conclusion In conclusion, our study underscores the pivotal role of IPs in shaping the clinical severity and treatment outcomes of various mental health disorders. By examining IPs in MDD, AN, GAD, SAD and PD concurrently, we have highlighted patterns and differences that would remain undiscovered in single‐disorder studies, thereby offering a more comprehensive understanding of how IPs intersect with symptom severity. These findings align with the principles of the recovery model, which advocates for empowering patients through active involvement in their treatment plans and acknowledging their subjective experiences. Nevertheless, findings should be interpreted with caution given the high levels of comorbidity across the mental disorders assessed. Addressing maladaptive IPs, may enhance therapeutic engagement and effectiveness, ultimately fostering a more holistic and person‐centred approach to mental health care. Ethics Statement Ethical approval was obtained from the University of Melbourne with an Ethics Committee HREC number: 1853137.6. Consent Informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to their involvement for use of their data and publication. Conflicts of Interest The authors declare no conflicts of interest. chunks.content: Introduction Cancer has emerged as a significant public health challenge and societal concern in the 21st century, posing substantial economic implications. In February 2024, the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) published the most recent global cancer data, showing nearly 20 million newly diagnosed cancer cases worldwide, leading to around 9.7 million fatalities. Forecasts suggest that by the year 2050, the annual number of new cancer diagnoses could rise to 35.281 million. Studies indicate that 30–50 % of cancer patients experience sleep disturbance, a prevalence substantially higher than that found in healthy individuals. , , , Notably, surgery, a primary treatment for cancer, can exacerbate postoperative sleep disturbance (PSD). Sleep disturbance is one of the significant risk factors for poor prognosis in cancer patients during the perioperative period, , leading to poor wound healing, cognitive decline, increased length of hospital stay and medical expenses, and increased risk of cancer recurrence. , , , Maintaining good sleep helps to improve immune response, promote cognitive function recovery, and regulate body metabolism. These benefits have significant positive impacts on postoperative rehabilitation and overall health. Therefore, assessing the incidence of sleep disturbance in cancer patients and fully understanding the postoperative sleep quality and its influencing factors are of great significance for improving the treatment response and quality of life and reducing the occurrence of complications in cancer patients. This study aims to assess the incidence of sleep disturbance in cancer patients one week after surgery, as well as preoperative factors (e.g., baseline characteristics), social psychology, environment, and postoperative-related factors, to determine the independent risk factors for PSD. Methods Participants This was a prospective observational study conducted at the First Affiliated Hospital of Wenzhou Medical University. The study protocol was approved by the hospital’s Institutional Review Board (Approval No: KY2021–102) and was registered in the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (ChiCTR2100054013). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants before their enrollment in the study. From October 2021 to June 2023, we consecutively screened adult patients (ASA I-III) scheduled for elective surgery. The study protocol pre-specified the inclusion of four major cancer types—thyroid, breast, lung, and digestive system (e.g., gastric, colorectal)—to ensure a representative cohort. Inclusion criteria: (1) ASA classification of grades I to III; (2) Age ≥ 18 years old; (3) Conscious and able to communicate without difficulty. Exclusion criteria: (1) Having neurological and mental disorders; (2) Having a history of alcohol abuse, drug abuse, or opioid dependence; (3) Pregnant or lactating women; (4) Having significant cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases, respiratory system diseases, liver and kidney diseases. Elimination criteria: (1) The surgery was not carried out as planned; (2) The postoperative pathological result was benign. Data collection and questionnaires Collecting the demographic information of patients includes age, gender, body mass index (BMI), educational level, occupation, smoking status, drinking status, physical exercise, whether having medical insurance, whether suffering from hypertension, diabetes, heart disease, or stroke; whether the patient was aware of their cancer diagnosis, whether there is preoperative chronic pain, disease-related factors such as the type of cancer; environmental factors such as room noise, interference from room lighting, interference from electrocardiogram monitoring equipment in the room, confined space; anesthesia and surgery-related factors such as operation time, anesthesia time, medical care procedures, postoperative difficulty in moving, postoperative discomfort in body position, etc, and postoperative complications such as moderate to severe postoperative pain, sore throat, back pain, postoperative fever, coughing and expectoration, and postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV). The Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) scale was used to assess the sleep status of the patients. In this study, the modified Chinese version of the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) scale was employed for the assessment, with a PSQI score of ≥ 6 serving as the indicator for sleep disturbance. The emotional state of patients during the perioperative period was evaluated using the Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS). According to the total score of SAS, a score of ≥ 50 was considered indicative of an anxious state. The acute and chronic pain conditions of the patients were evaluated using the Numerical Rating Scale (NRS). This scale uses a 0–10 scale to assess the severity of pain (where 0 and 10 represent no pain and the maximum pain, respectively), 1–3 points indicate mild pain, 4–6 points indicate moderate pain, and 7–10 points indicate severe pain. If doctors or other healthcare professionals had previously diagnosed and informed the participants that they had congestive heart failure, coronary heart disease, angina pectoris, or a heart attack, they were considered to have heart disease. Preoperative chronic pain was defined as pain that persisted or recurred for more than 3 months. Physical exercise was defined as exercise lasting more than two hours per week on three occasions. A confined space was defined as the enclosed ward environment of the hospital. Two trained researchers collected all

If doctors or other healthcare professionals had previously diagnosed and informed the participants that they had congestive heart failure, coronary heart disease, angina pectoris, or a heart attack, they were considered to have heart disease. Preoperative chronic pain was defined as pain that persisted or recurred for more than 3 months. Physical exercise was defined as exercise lasting more than two hours per week on three occasions. A confined space was defined as the enclosed ward environment of the hospital. Two trained researchers collected all data from electronic medical records and through structured interviews with patients and their families. Environmental factors were collected through patient interviews. The researchers asked the following standardized questions, and the patients answered ‘yes’ or ‘no’ based on their personal experiences during the postoperative hospital stay: (1) Ward noise: “Did the noise in the ward (such as the voices of other patients, the operations of medical staff, the footsteps in the corridor, etc.) interfere with your rest or sleep?”; (2) Interference of lights: “Did the lights in the ward (such as night lighting, light from outside entering the room, or lights turned on by medical staff during rounds) interfere with your rest or sleep?”; (3) Interference from the device: “Do the medical devices in the ward (such as the alarm sounds of the electrocardiogram monitor, the ticking sounds of the infusion pump, etc.) cause you any disturbance or interfere with your sleep?”; (4) Confined spaces: “Do you feel depressed or uncomfortable in the enclosed ward environment of the hospital?”. Data collection and time points Data were collected at two main time points by two trained researchers to ensure consistency. Preoperative Assessment (T0): Conducted on the day before surgery (15:00–17:00). The PSQI was used to assess sleep quality over the past month to establish a baseline. The SAS was used to evaluate the preoperative anxiety state. Postoperative Assessment (T1): Conducted on postoperative day 7 [POD 7 (15:00–17:00)]. The PSQI was used to assess sleep quality from POD 1 to POD 7 (i.e., the first postoperative week). The SAS was used to evaluate the anxiety state during the postoperative period. Pain Assessment: The NRS for pain at rest was assessed twice daily (8:00–10:00 and 18:00–20:00) from POD 1 to POD 7. The highest NRS score recorded during this period was used to define the variable “moderate-to-severe postoperative pain” (NRS ≥ 4). We provide a detailed description of the specific operation methods for PSQI (assisted by researchers), SAS (based on patient self-assessment), and NRS (inquiry using a scoring card by researchers). Regarding blinding: The researchers who collected the information were unaware of the patients’ sleep conditions before the surgery. During the evaluation process, measures to reduce bias through standardized procedures were emphasized. Outcome measures Primary Outcome: The incidence of postoperative sleep disturbance (PSD), defined as a Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) global score of ≥ 6, assessed on postoperative day 7. Secondary Outcomes: To identify independent factors associated with PSD through univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses; To compare the baseline characteristics and clinical profiles between patients with and without PSD. Sample size consideration The sample size was estimated a priori for the planned logistic regression analysis. Based on existing literature, we assumed a PSD incidence of approximately 50 %. Using the conservative ‘events per variabl’ (EPV) criterion of 10, and anticipating up to 10 predictor variables in the final model, a minimum of 100 patients with PSD were required. This corresponds to a total sample of 200 patients. To account for an estimated 20 % dropout rate, we planned to recruit at least 250 patients. The final analysis included 296 patients. The sample size of our study was to the requirements. Handling of missing data It reports the extent of missingness for all key variables ( ). Due to the very low rate of missing data (≤ 1 %), we used a single imputation method to retain the full sample (n = 296) for the binary logistic regression, thereby maximizing power and minimizing bias. Statistical analysis In this study, a database was established using Access 2019, and all data were input after being verified by the two researchers. After preliminary verification, the data were statistically analyzed using SPSS software for Windows version 26.0. Normally distributed data are presented were presented as mean ± standard deviation (mean ± SD), and were compared between groups using the two independent samples t -test. Measurement data with skewed distribution were expressed as median and interquartile range [IQR], and compared between groups using non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney U test). Count data were expressed as the number of cases and percentage, and compared between groups using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact probability test. Normally distributed data are presented were presented as mean ± standard deviation (mean ± SD), and were compared between groups using the two independent samples t -test. Measurement data with skewed distribution were expressed as median and interquartile range [IQR], and compared between groups using non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney U test). Count data were expressed as the number of cases and percentage, and compared between groups using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact probability test. In the univariate analysis, variables related to sleep disturbance were selected ( P < 0.05), and binary logistic regression analysis was performed on these variables to detect independent influencing factors related to sleep disturbance. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (ROC) was used to evaluate the discriminative ability of the model. The Brier score and calibration curve assessed the model’s calibration ability. A P -value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Result A total of 380 cancer patients scheduled for surgery were collected. 40 patients were excluded (25 of whom had lost follow-up, 13 had communication disorders after surgery, and 2 died within one week after surgery), and 44 patients were also excluded (26 of whom had delayed surgeries and 18 had benign postoperative pathological results). Finally, 296 patients were included in the statistical analysis, including 72 patients with thyroid cancer, 60 patients with breast cancer, 69 patients with lung cancer, and 95 patients with digestive system cancers ( ). The distribution of PSQI scores of the two groups of patients after surgery Among the 296 cancer patients, 193 cases (65.2 %) had sleep disturbance (PSQI ≥ 6) one week after surgery. There were significant differences in the total scores and 7 subcategories of PSQI scores between the two groups of cancer patients with and without sleep disturbance ( ). Comparison of baseline characteristics between the two groups of patients with and without sleep disturbance Among the 296 cancer patients who underwent surgery, 108 were male (36.5 %) and 188 were female (63.5 %). In the sleep disturbance group, 55.4 % of the patients were unemployed and lacked job security, which was significantly higher than that in the group without sleep disturbance (41.7 %, P < 0.001); notably, 82.9 % of the patients in the sleep disturbance group had an education level below high school, which was significantly higher than that in the group without sleep disturbance; the proportion of patients who exercised before the surgery was significantly higher in the sleep disturbance group (64.8 %) than in the group without sleep disturbance(38.3 %, P < 0.001); the proportion of patients in the sleep disturbance group who had sleep disturbance before the surgery was as high as 81.9 %, which was significantly higher than that in the group without sleep disturbance(18.4 %, P < 0.001) ( ). Comparison of surgical and postoperative related factors between the two groups of patients with and without PSD Most patients (61.5 %) experienced mild pain after the surgery, while 38.5 % of the cancer patients experienced moderate to severe pain. Compared with the patients in the group without sleep disturbance, the patients in the sleep disturbance group had longer operation and anesthesia times (97 (65.5–145) vs 119 (73–166.5), P = 0.028; 153 (98.5–203.5) vs 127 (88–175), P = 0.015), were more affected by ward noise (43.6 % vs 60.6 %, P = 0.005) and postural discomfort (38.8 % vs 52.3 %, P = 0.027), and more experienced the confined space of the ward (9.7 % vs 19.7 %, P = 0.026). The incidence of moderate to severe pain after surgery in the sleep disturbance group was significantly higher than that in the group without sleep disturbance (45.1 % vs 26.2 %, P < 0.001); the incidence of postoperative anxiety was also significantly higher than that in the group without sleep disturbance (11.9 % vs 1.9 %, P = 0.007). This indicates that there are significant differences between cancer patients with and without sleep disturbance in terms of operation time, anesthesia time, occurrence of moderate to severe pain after surgery, postural discomfort after surgery, postoperative anxiety level, and environmental-related factors such as ward noise and confined ward space ( ). To explore the role of modifiable postoperative factors, we conducted a sub-analysis of the 119 patients who had no preoperative sleep disturbance (preoperative PSQI < 6). Among these patients, 35 (29.4 %) developed new-onset PSD (postoperative PSQI ≥ 6). The results highlight that in this group, postoperative pain, anxiety, and ward noise emerge as the significant and clinically relevant modifiable factors. In the single-factor analysis, education level, occupation, preoperative physical exercise, preoperative sleep disturbance, operation time, anesthesia time, cancer type, ward noise, confined space, postural discomfort, moderate to severe postoperative pain, and postoperative anxiety were significantly associated with PSD in cancer patients ( , ). The final model incorporated the following variables: age, gender, operation time, anesthesia time, type of surgery, education level, occupation, preoperative physical exercise, preoperative sleep disturbance, hypertension, ward noise, confined space, postural discomfort, Interference of lights, moderate to severe postoperative pain, and postoperative anxiety. Binary logistic regression analysis demonstrated that postoperative moderate to severe pain (OR [95 % CI]: 2.95 [1.19–7.30], P = 0.019), ward noise (OR [95 % CI]: 3.03 [1.41–6.52], P = 0.004), postoperative anxiety (OR [95 % CI]: 9.07 [1.33–61.69], P = 0.024), and preoperative sleep disturbance (OR [95 % CI]: 36.09 [15.59–83.53], P < 0.001) were significantly associated with increased odds of PSD. Compared with those with education levels of high school or below, cancer patients with higher education levels (OR [95 % CI]: 0.19 [0.08–0.50], P < 0.001) were associated with a lower likelihood of PSD, different types of surgeries also had certain effects on the occurrence of PSD in cancer patients, and compared with patients undergoing thyroid and breast surgeries, patients undergoing thoracic surgery had a lower possibility of PSD (OR [95 %CI]: 0.27 [0.09–0.85], P = 0.024). According to the results of the binary logistic regression analysis, postoperative moderate to severe pain, preoperative sleep disturbance, educational level, type of cancer surgery, postoperative anxiety state, and ward noise are independent influencing factors for PSD in cancer patients. The ROC value of the model was 0.905 (95 % CI [0.892–0.913], p < 0.001), which indicated the model had adequate discrimination ability ( A). The calibration graphic and the Brier score (0.139) revealed a good fit for the model ( B). Exploratory analysis Given that preoperative sleep disturbance showed a strong predictive power, we conducted a stratified analysis to explore whether there were differences in postoperative predictive factors between patients with and without preoperative sleep disturbance (See in the Appendix). The result analysis revealed that in the subgroup of patients without preoperative sleep disturbance (n = 119), noise in the ward became a more prominent risk factor. Discussion Sleep quality during the perioperative period directly influences postoperative recovery in cancer patients. However, existing studies on this topic are relatively scarce and often limited to specific cancer types. Our study is among the first to systematically include patients with various cancer types (e.g., thyroid, breast, lung, and digestive system cancers) and to analyze the type of cancer surgery as a potential influencing factor, thereby exploring the risk factors that collectively affect perioperative sleep quality. Our research results show that the incidence of PSD among different cancer patients is as high as 65.2 %, which is much higher than that of the general healthy population. , Among them, postoperative moderate to severe pain, preoperative sleep disturbance, education level, cancer surgery type, postoperative anxiety state, and ward noise are independent influencing factors of sleep disturbance. Although different types of surgeries have different effects on patients' postoperative sleep quality, our research found that, compared to different types of surgeries, the degree of postoperative pain shows a stronger association with sleep disturbance. In this study, 38.5 % (114 cases) of patients experienced moderate to severe pain, and 76.3 % (87 cases) of these patients had sleep disturbance. The sleep disturbance after lung cancer surgery may be related to the pain caused by intubation during thoracic surgery, coughing, and the sensation of foreign bodies, which leads to sleep interruption. Interestingly, in this study, the incidence of PSD in patients undergoing thoracic surgery was lower than that in patients undergoing thyroid and breast surgeries. The sleep disturbance after lung cancer surgery may be related to the pain caused by intubation during thoracic surgery, coughing, and the sensation of foreign bodies, which leads to sleep interruption. Interestingly, in this study, the incidence of PSD in patients undergoing thoracic surgery was lower than that in patients undergoing thyroid and breast surgeries. This might be since during lung surgeries in this hospital, opioid or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are routinely used during the operation, combined with nerve block techniques to provide auxiliary analgesia, to alleviate the postoperative pain of patients, thereby having a positive impact on their sleep conditions. In contrast, patients undergoing breast or thyroid surgeries may have an increased incidence of PSD due to the hormonal level fluctuations caused by the surgery and the depression and anxiety that occur during the waiting for pathological results after the surgery. The impact of pain on sleep is bidirectional, and the two interact with each other. Previous experimental studies suggest that sleep disturbance can lead to an increase in the secretion of interleukin 6 and tumor necrosis factor α, which may cause the occurrence of pain and hyperalgesia ; conversely, pain is also known to contribute to a decline in sleep quality and delay the recovery of the disease. Therefore, our findings suggest that interventions aimed at alleviating postoperative pain, such as multimodal analgesia, might also have a beneficial effect on improving PSD, promoting the recovery of the neurological and cognitive functions of perioperative patients, maintaining brain health and quality of life. , Previous studies have shown that people with lower educational levels are more likely to have sleep disturbance. This study also obtained similar results. We found that a high level of education is a protective factor for preventing sleep disturbance. Compared with low levels of education, higher education can significantly reduce the incidence of sleep disturbance. This may be because people with good education can maintain a healthy lifestyle, while lower education may lead to a decline in their quality of life, including sleep quality. Moreover, people with lower educational levels have a lower awareness of surgery and prognosis, resulting in a lack of confidence in disease prognosis, and subsequently showing fear and worry, which in turn affects the sleep state. , Studies have found that 36 % of hospitalized patients reported new-onset insomnia, of which 10 % were clinical insomnia and severe insomnia. Several hospital-related environmental factors—such as noise, lighting, and confined spaces—have been identified as significant contributors to sleep disturbance. , , , Inappropriate light interference can affect the secretion of melatonin and trigger stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system, which may also affect sleep quality. In this study, we found significant differences between the two groups of patients in terms of factors such as ward lighting noise and ward confinement, but after regression analysis, only ward noise was an independent risk factor for sleep disturbance in cancer patients after surgery. The discrepancy between our findings and those of previous studies may be attributed to variations in hospital settings, ward design, disease-specific symptoms, and conceptual differences in assessing sleep quality ; noise can lead to fragmented sleep and reduce the time of high-quality sleep and total sleep time. Furthermore, stratified analysis revealed that, among patients without preoperative sleep disturbance, ward noise exhibited a significantly stronger association with PSD. This underscores the critical need to actively optimize the hospital environment and minimize noise exposure to prevent new-onset sleep disturbance in this vulnerable subgroup. In contrast, for patients with preexisting sleep issues, their condition may be more closely linked to chronic underlying factors; perioperative management in these cases should integrate long-term sleep treatment strategies alongside acute interventions. Therefore, improving the ward environment and taking appropriate measures to reduce noise exposure can effectively improve the sleep quality of patients during the perioperative period. The PSQI questionnaire is a self-assessment questionnaire, which is an effective method for assessing patients' sleep quality in research and clinical practice. , Previous studies have tested the reliability and validity of this scale and confirmed that it applies to Chinese patients. , Additionally, Broderick et al. found that there were no significant differences in PSQI scores within 7–28 days of the reporting period. In this study, we evaluated the sleep quality of patients before and one week after surgery. A total of 193 patients (65.2 %) had sleep disturbance one week after surgery. The preoperative PSQI score was significantly associated with PSD, which might be since cancer patients already have some degree of sleep problems before surgery. The harmful stimuli brought by surgery and anesthesia would aggravate these problems, thereby causing sleep disturbance after surgery. A total of 193 patients (65.2 %) had sleep disturbance one week after surgery. The preoperative PSQI score was significantly associated with PSD, which might be since cancer patients already have some degree of sleep problems before surgery. The harmful stimuli brought by surgery and anesthesia would aggravate these problems, thereby causing sleep disturbance after surgery. This study also found that cancer patients with sleep disturbance are more prone to anxiety after surgery. Anxiety levels are closely related to subjective sleep quality disturbance, and the incidence of perioperative anxiety in cancer patients is higher than that in the general population. , Anxiety is a common preoperative symptom among patients awaiting surgery, possibly related to the pain and discomfort caused by the disease itself. In addition, cancer patients' concerns and fears about the disease and surgery, changes in postoperative quality of life, and the complexity of the economic aspects of disease treatment are all important reasons for the occurrence of anxiety in perioperative patients. Previous studies have confirmed that anxiety is associated with shortened sleep time, daytime fatigue, and insomnia. , Cancer patients' anxiety symptoms are most likely to manifest as sleep disturbance, and sleep disturbance can also exacerbate anxiety. A meta-analysis of 51 cohort studies found that anxiety is associated with a higher cancer-specific mortality rate and poorer cancer survival rate. During the clinical process, enhancing the dissemination of patients' surgical knowledge, combined with cognitive behavioral therapy, may have a positive effect on improving the sleep quality of cancer patients. Medical staff can alleviate patients' concerns about the disease by establishing a strong doctor-patient relationship, eliminating the unfamiliarity with the environment, and explaining the treatment process. As a cross-sectional study assessing PSD and their associated factors at a specific time point, the temporal sequence between some factors and sleep disturbance remains unclear. For instance, while we postulate that postoperative pain and anxiety contribute to sleep disturbance, it is also plausible that pre-existing or incident sleep disturbance lowers pain thresholds, , and exacerbates anxiety symptoms, , indicating a potential for reverse causality. The strong association observed with preoperative sleep disturbance underscores the complex, bidirectional relationship between psychological state, physical symptoms, and sleep. Future longitudinal studies with repeated measurements are needed to elucidate the precise temporal and causal pathways linking these factors. Epidemiological studies have shown that factors such as work, exercise, age, and gender are associated with the incidence of sleep disturbance. , In our current study, these factors were not identified as independent risk factors for sleep disturbance in cancer patients after surgery in the results of the binary logistic regression analysis. This study has several limitations. First, its observational and cross-sectional design precludes definitive causal inferences regarding the identified associations. Although we adjusted for known confounders, the possibility of residual confounding persists, particularly due to the lack of systematically collected data on anesthesia and analgesia details (e.g., opioid dosage, regional techniques). These unmeasured factors may have influenced both pain and sleep outcomes. Second, while patient-reported measures appropriately capture perceived environmental disturbance, they are subject to recall bias and lack validation by objective tools such as actigraphy or sound level meters. Finally, the single-center design may limit the generalizability of our findings. Furthermore, while the sample size was adequate for the primary analysis, it hampered reliable exploration of risk factors within specific patient subgroups (e.g., by cancer type or surgery), rendering such analyses potentially underpowered. Future multi-center studies with larger samples are needed to incorporate longitudinal assessments, objective monitoring, detailed perioperative data, and to enable adequately powered subgroup analyses and extend our results. Conclusions This study revealed a high incidence (65.2 %) of PSD among cancer patients. Independent factors associated with PSD included moderate-to-severe postoperative pain, postoperative anxiety, preoperative sleep disturbance, and ward noise. Clinically, these findings underscore the importance of screening high-risk patients—particularly those with pre-existing sleep issues, lower education levels, or those undergoing specific surgeries—and implementing proactive interventions. Promising, modifiable targets for such interventions include multimodal analgesia for pain, psychological support for anxiety, and environmental modifications to reduce noise, all of which may improve sleep quality and potentially enhance postoperative recovery in this vulnerable population.
