with doxycycline, both of which provide effective coverage against N. gonorrhoeae , C. trachomatis , and anaerobic bacteria. Other options include azithromycin for a 7-day course combined with metronidazole for 14 days, ampicillin plus clindamycin with gentamicin, levofloxacin plus metronidazole, or imipenem with cilastatin [ ]. These regimens may serve as comparably effective alternatives when first-line therapies are contraindicated or unavailable. Due to the discomfort often associated with intravenous infusion, doxycycline is preferably administered orally when tolerated, as its oral formulation offers bioavailability comparable to that of the intravenous form [ ]. Transition to oral therapy should be considered after 24 to 48 h of sustained clinical improvement. The recommended oral regimens consist of doxycycline combined with metronidazole to complete a total 14-day course of therapy. For patients unable to tolerate doxycycline, azithromycin may be used as an alternative, while clindamycin can substitute for metronidazole to maintain anaerobic coverage [ ]. Despite less robust evidence, European guidelines recommend a 14-day regimen of IV ofloxacin plus IV metronidazole as an alternative treatment option for PID [ ]. On the contrary, the CDC does not recommend quinolones for routine PID treatment due to the increasing prevalence of quinolone-resistant N. gonorrhoeae. However, in select cases—such as patients with cephalosporin allergy or low risk of gonorrhea—close follow-up-quinolone-based regimens may be considered. In these circumstances, levofloxacin or moxifloxacin combined with metronidazole for 14 days may be used [ ]. 7.1.2. Non-Hospitalized Patients Outpatient therapy is appropriate for females with mild to moderate pelvic in PID who can tolerate oral medications and are likely to adhere to the treatment regimen. The recommended approach includes a single intramuscular (IM) dose of a long-acting cephalosporin, preferably ceftriaxone, combined with doxycycline for 14 days and metronidazole for 14 days. Alternative cephalosporins that may be used include cefoxitin, cefotaxime, or ceftizoxime. For patients who cannot tolerate doxycycline, azithromycin can be substituted for a complete 14-day course, although it should still be combined with a cephalosporin and metronidazole [ ]. Emerging data on alternative treatments, including morinidazole in combination with levofloxacin, suggest promising efficacy and safety profiles, particularly in the context of increasing resistance to standard agents such as metronidazole [ ]. 7.2. Enteric Pathogens In certain cases, the formation of a TOA arises from localized extension of infection secondary to uncontrolled inflammatory bowel disease, appendicitis, adnexal surgery, or, less commonly, hematogenous spread from distant organs [ , ]. The microbiology profile of TOAs tends to be polymicrobial, involving organisms such as E. coli , aerobic streptococci , B.fragilis , Prevotella , and other anaerobes. Thus; antimicrobial regimens must provide adequate coverage for this broad spectrum of organisms [ ]. Although management generally adheres to CDC-recommended guidelines, there is rising concern regarding potential resistance of bowel flora to agents such as cefotetan and cefoxitin [ ]. Given that bowel flora are often involved in TOA pathogenesis and the classification of TOA as a serious intra-abdominal infection, broader-spectrum regimens such as ertapenem [ ], meropenem, or piperacillin-tazobactam may represent more effective therapeutic options [ , ]. Empiric therapy for Enterobacterales should be stratified by illness severity, patient specific factors (allergies, immunocompromise) [ ] and Pseudomonas risk factors which include recent hospitalization, devices, recent IV antibiotics, immunosuppression [ , ]. In stable, immunocompetent patients without healthcare exposures, a broad-spectrum single agent (e.g., a third- or fourth-generation cephalosporin) is appropriate. With healthcare exposures or immunosuppression and in cases of sepsis/septic shock a single antipseudomonal β-lactam (e.g., cefepime/ceftazidime, piperacillin–tazobactam, or a carbapenem) is preferred. For severe β-lactam allergy, aztreonam or a fluoroquinolone may serve as equal alternatives. Severe sepsis/septic shock warrants empiric combination coverage for Gram-negatives (β-lactam plus aminoglycoside rather than fluoroquinolone) [ ]. Carbapenem therapy with meropenem, imipenem–cilastatin, or ertapenem is favored for extended spectrum b lactamases (ESBL)-E infections [ ]. Ceftolozane–tazobactam, a newer antipseudomonal β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor has excellent activity against multidrug-resistant P. aeruginosa , including many strains resistant to piperacillin–tazobactam, ceftazidime, or cefepime though it does not overcome carbapenemase producers [ ]. When AmpC β-lactamase production is suspected in organisms with a moderate risk profile, cefepime is an appropriate treatment option [ ]. For Class A (KPC) β-lactamases, preferred regimens include meropenem–vaborbactam, ceftazidime–avibactam, or imipenem–cilastatin–relebactam, with cefiderocol as an alternative. For Class B (MBLs such as NDM/VIM/IMP), the preferred approach is ceftazidime–avibactam combined with aztreonam, or cefiderocol as monotherapy. For Class D (OXA-48–like) producers, ceftazidime–avibactam is preferred, with cefiderocol as an alternative [ ]. 7.3. Anaerobic Pathogen Associated Infections In case of anaerobic infections, metronidazole is a first-line option. Clindamycin covers many anaerobes but rising resistance in B. fragilis makes it less reliable than metronidazole, β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor (BL/BLI) combinations, or carbapenems for empiric therapy. BL/BLI regimens (e.g., amoxicillin–clavulanate, ampicillin–sulbactam, ticarcillin–clavulanate, piperacillin–tazobactam) also provide broad anaerobic coverage. Among cephalosporins, second-generation agents (cefoxitin, cefotetan, cefmetazole) are more active against B. fragilis but, due to increasing

(MBLs such as NDM/VIM/IMP), the preferred approach is ceftazidime–avibactam combined with aztreonam, or cefiderocol as monotherapy. For Class D (OXA-48–like) producers, ceftazidime–avibactam is preferred, with cefiderocol as an alternative [ ]. 7.3. Anaerobic Pathogen Associated Infections In case of anaerobic infections, metronidazole is a first-line option. Clindamycin covers many anaerobes but rising resistance in B. fragilis makes it less reliable than metronidazole, β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitor (BL/BLI) combinations, or carbapenems for empiric therapy. BL/BLI regimens (e.g., amoxicillin–clavulanate, ampicillin–sulbactam, ticarcillin–clavulanate, piperacillin–tazobactam) also provide broad anaerobic coverage. Among cephalosporins, second-generation agents (cefoxitin, cefotetan, cefmetazole) are more active against B. fragilis but, due to increasing resistance, are not recommended for empiric treatment and are used primarily for surgical prophylaxis. Carbapenems (imipenem, meropenem) offer excellent anaerobic and aerobic coverage with meropenem slightly more active against Gram-negatives. Fluoroquinolones (notably levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) have some anaerobic activity and good tissue penetration, but rising resistance limits their role; they are generally reserved for situations such as β-lactam allergy (especially in children) when alternatives are unsuitable [ ]. 7.4. PID Due to Actinomycosis The risk of infection by Actinomyces spp. appears to be increased among IUD users, although the exact risk remains unknown. It is important to note that a positive culture or the presence of Actinomyces -like organisms on a Pap test does not necessarily warrant antimicrobial therapy or IUD removal; intervention being recommended only in the presence of clinical evidence of infection [ ]. An initial course of intravenous antibiotics for at least two weeks—often extended to 6 weeks—is generally recommended depending on disease severity. Penicillin G remains the recommended IV regimen [ ]. IV ampicillin and IV ceftriaxone remain reasonable alternatives [ , ]. In case of penicillin allergy, the selection of alternative agents depends on the type and severity of the allergic reaction. For patients with a non-severe or IgE-mediated allergy, ceftriaxone is generally employed as first line IV therapy [ , ]. However, for patients with severe non-IgE-mediated hypersensitivity reactions doxycycline is preferred, and IV carbapenems such as ertapenem may be considered in consultation with an allergist [ ]. Oral regimens include penicillin V or amoxicillin [ , ]. In cases where co-pathogens are suspected amoxicillin-clavulanate is an appropriate option [ ]. For penicillin-allergic patients, doxycycline, tetracycline, erythromycin, or azithromycin, have demonstrated in vitro efficacy and have been associated with successful outcomes in limited cases [ , , ]. The duration of therapy for classic actinomycosis typically ranges from two to six months for mild disease and six to twelve months for severe disease, with treatment continuing for at least one to two months after clinical and/or radiologic resolution of the infection. Longer courses, extending up to 12–18 months, may be required for complicated, invasive infections or in immunocompromised hosts, including those with HIV [ , ]. Shorter durations of therapy for actinomycosis may be considered in select cases, particularly when adequate surgical resection of infected tissue has been performed and bone involvement is absent. Early recognition, rapid clinical response, and smaller, less indurated lesions further support abbreviated therapy. In pelvic actinomycosis associated with IUD use, a reduced treatment course may be sufficient, especially when the IUD is promptly removed and the infection remains localized [ , , ]. 7.5. PID Due to Tuberculosis Management of FGTB follows the same principles as treatment of drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis, in accordance with WHO and CDC/IDSA guidelines [ ]. For drug-susceptible cases, the recommended regimen consists of six months of first-line anti-tuberculous therapy: an intensive phase of two months with isoniazid (H), rifampicin (R), pyrazinamide (Z), and ethambutol (E), followed by a four-month continuation phase with isoniazid and rifampicin (2HRZE/4HR) [ ]. 7.6. PID Due to CMV PID due to CMV is rarely suspected in immunocompetent adults, although a few cases have been reported [ ]. However, in immunocompromised populations, including individuals with HIV infection, CMV may cause severe and potentially life-threatening disease. In such cases, early recognition and timely initiation of antiviral therapy are critical [ , ]. For mild to moderate disease, in patients able to tolerate oral therapy, valganciclovir is the preferred treatment. For severe or life-threatening cases, intravenous ganciclovir is recommended, with transition to oral valganciclovir once clinical improvement is achieved. In patients who cannot tolerate first-line therapy, second-line options include maribavir or foscarnet, with the choice guided by disease severity, viral load, and drug related toxicity [ ]. 7.7. PID Due to Parasitic Infection Infection due to Enterobius vermicularis or other parasites should be considered as a potential cause of PID, particularly in cases with unusual presentations or when common bacterial pathogens are not identified [ , ]. Treatment of Enterobius vermicularis infection includes anti-helminthic therapy with albendazole, mebendazole, or pyrantel pamoate [ ]. Treatment for Entamoeba involves systemic therapy with metronidazole for 7–10 days, followed by a luminal agent for 7–20 days depending

tolerate first-line therapy, second-line options include maribavir or foscarnet, with the choice guided by disease severity, viral load, and drug related toxicity [ ]. 7.7. PID Due to Parasitic Infection Infection due to Enterobius vermicularis or other parasites should be considered as a potential cause of PID, particularly in cases with unusual presentations or when common bacterial pathogens are not identified [ , ]. Treatment of Enterobius vermicularis infection includes anti-helminthic therapy with albendazole, mebendazole, or pyrantel pamoate [ ]. Treatment for Entamoeba involves systemic therapy with metronidazole for 7–10 days, followed by a luminal agent for 7–20 days depending on the drug. Alternatives to metronidazole include tinidazole, ornidazole, or nitazoxanide [ ]. 7.8. Surgical Management Although universally accepted guidelines are lacking, certain clinical scenarios may warrant surgical management in PID. Indications include pelvic peritonitis or TOAs, particularly when abscess size exceeds 3–4 cm, or when severe complications such as rupture or septic shock occur. In these cases, prompt initiation of antimicrobial therapy and abscess drainage—preferably via imaging-guided transvaginal approach—should not be delayed. If severe signs are present, surgical intervention, ideally by laparoscopy, may be required, with drainage preferred over excision [ ]. In some cases, inflammatory markers CRP and ESR may help guide management and decisions regarding surgical intervention, as elevated levels have been associated with greater disease severity, larger abscess size, and prolonged hospitalization [ , , ]. Despite factors such as fever, larger abscess size, and higher inflammatory markers being predictive of treatment failure, scoring systems incorporating these parameters have demonstrated poor discriminatory capacity [ ]. When surgical intervention is required, laparoscopic surgery appears to offer advantages over open laparotomy. Reported benefits include shorter operation times, reduced need for blood transfusions, and a shorter hospital stay, without increasing the risk of surgical complications, revision surgery, or in-hospital mortality [ ]. 8. Complications and Prognosis PID is strongly associated with long-term complications, including chronic pelvic pain, infertility, and ectopic pregnancy, and these adverse outcomes may occur not only when treatment is delayed but also despite timely and complete therapy, with affected individuals remaining at risk for recurrent episodes and ongoing morbidity [ , ]. TOA is a severe complication of PID and could lead to morbidity and occasional mortality. Clinical presentation of TOA is similar to that of PID, with the addition of a pelvic mass often noted on examination or imaging [ , ]. TOA’s typical symptoms include fever, abdominal pain, adnexal mass, and abnormal vaginal discharge; thus, obtaining a detailed medical history and performing a thorough clinical examination is mandatory. An auxiliary transabdominal or transvaginal ultrasound may be useful, while in case of diagnostic difficulties, a CT and then an MRI may be helpful [ , ]. A history of PID has been identified as an independent predictor of chronic pelvic pain (CPP) in women [ , ]. CPP occurs in 18–36% of cases and can increase up to 67% in women who experience three or more episodes of PID [ , ]. The underlying mechanisms of CPP are not fully understood, though it is generally thought to result from adhesive disease and damage to the fallopian tubes and ovaries caused by the infection, chronic inflammation due to host immunological responses, or recurrent infections as a consequence of repeated exposures and weakened host defenses [ , ]. Approximately one-third of individuals with PID develop CPP within three years, with more than half experiencing highly intense pain, which is often accompanied by impairments in physical function, overall health, vitality, social engagement, and psychological well-being [ , ]. CPP management may include analgesia, hormonal suppression, and physiotherapy of the pelvic floor, whereas peripheral nerve blocks and sacral nerve neuromodulation may be essential in selected cases. Individuals with PID might experience hydrosalpinx, a condition resulting from inflammation where the injured fallopian tube may get obstructed by surgery, adhesions, accumulate sterile fluid, and increase in size. The hydrosalpinx persists even after the PID is resolved. In individuals receiving in vitro fertilization (IVF), hydrosalpinx adversely affects pregnancy rates, implantation success, early pregnancy loss, preterm delivery, and live births [ ]. Infertility should always be recognized as a potential long-term complication of PID, and women with a history of PID should undergo early assessment when planning pregnancy to enable timely discussion of diagnostic and therapeutic options in case spontaneous conception is not achieved [ ]. According to the PID Evaluation and Clinical Health (PEACH) trial, the incidence of infertility among participants with PID was 18% after a three-year follow-up [ ]. PID seems to be positively associated with infertility and interestingly, women with a history of PID treatment are considerably more likely to experience infertility compared to women without a history of PID [ ]. early assessment when planning pregnancy to enable timely discussion of diagnostic and therapeutic options in case spontaneous conception is not achieved [ ]. According to the PID Evaluation and Clinical Health (PEACH) trial, the incidence of infertility among participants with PID was 18% after a three-year follow-up [ ]. PID seems to be positively associated with infertility and interestingly, women with a history of PID treatment are considerably more likely to experience infertility compared to women without a history of PID [ ]. Potential mechanisms leading to infertility following PID include the upward spread of infection from the cervix to the upper reproductive tract. Disruption of the endocervical mucous plug, mid-cycle uterine peristalsis, and retrograde menstrual flow can facilitate pathogen migration into the pelvis, causing tubal damage and impaired fertility [ ]. PID has been associated with an increased risk of adverse pregnancy outcomes, including ectopic pregnancy, with studies showing that women with a history of PID have more than twice the risk compared to those without PID [ , ]. Repeated PID episodes are leading to ongoing injury to fallopian tube and pelvic tissues. Every infection increases tubal adhesions and scarring, resulting in progressively greater infertility rates and ectopic pregnancy [ , ]. The likelihood of ectopic pregnancy rises with the frequency and severity of PID episodes [ ]. Of note, non-STI-related PID typically leads to milder peri-tubal adhesions and partial tubal blockages, resulting in a moderate risk of infertility and a relatively weaker association with ectopic pregnancy compared to STI-related PID [ , ]. The association between PID and ovarian cancer remains uncertain. It is indicated that, PID correlates with a heightened risk of ovarian cancer and particularly higher risk in patients with five or more PID episodes [ ]. Additionally, there was an increase in borderline ovarian tumors and variations in both serous and non-serous types, however non-STI PID is not associated with ovarian cancer risk, suggesting etiological differences [ , ]. However, if PID independently increases ovarian cancer risk, it can also raise the likelihood of low parity and infertility, which are additional risk factors for ovarian cancer. This is related with evidence suggesting that fallopian tubes, not ovaries, are primarily involved in most cases of related carcinomas [ , ]. Perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh Curtis Syndrome), which is actually inflammation of the liver capsule and the peritoneal surfaces in the anterior right upper quadrant, is typically associated with STIs such as N. gonorrhoeae , C. trachomatis , and possibly M. genitalium , and is generally not observed in cases of non-STI-related PID [ , ]. Overall, the prognosis of non-STI-related PID is closely linked to early recognition, accurate diagnosis, and timely treatment. Most patients have an excellent outcome when appropriate antimicrobial therapy is initiated promptly, whereas delayed or inadequate management increases the risk of complications such as TOAs, infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain, and, less commonly, ovarian malignancy. Ultimately, when the index of suspicion for PID is high, the appropriate diagnostic algorithm is applied, and effective therapy is administered, the long-term prognosis is generally favorable, with preservation of reproductive health and overall quality of life [ ]. 9. Follow-Up and Monitoring PID is essential to be treated timely and effectively due to the high risk of long-term sequelae [ ]. In the absence of strong indications for hospitalization, such as pregnancy, ineffective outpatient treatment, or severe clinical manifestations, mild to moderate PID can be treated on an outpatient basis with a focus on follow-up. More specifically, a clinical reassessment within 48–72 h should be performed, when a substantial improvement in signs and symptoms is expected [ , , ]. Otherwise, further evaluation should be undertaken with a focus on imaging and repeat clinical assessment, to rule out for potential complications [ ]. A high level of suspicion should be maintained for the development of TOAs. Patients with TOAs require IV antibiotic therapy, and significant improvement is expected within 24–48 h, after which a transition to oral antibiotics may be considered. Oral antibiotic therapy continues for at least 14 days. Daily monitoring of the leukocyte count is required to evaluate the process in case of worsening symptoms. In case of no clinical and laboratory improvement, drainage may be necessary. Surgical intervention is needed in case of a ruptured TOA or if the patient is deteriorating [ ]. Long-term follow-up is equally important. Infertility may occur due to proximal and/or distal disease of the fallopian tube [ ]. When evaluating an individual with a PID history and infertility issues, hysterosalpingography should be performed without delay, and solutions, including surgery, could be assessed [ ]. Similarly, high index of suspicion should be raised for ectopic pregnancy or presence of ovarian cancer when evaluating an individual with PID history. 10. Prevention Prevention of non-STI-related PID requires a multifactorial approach. One

Infertility may occur due to proximal and/or distal disease of the fallopian tube [ ]. When evaluating an individual with a PID history and infertility issues, hysterosalpingography should be performed without delay, and solutions, including surgery, could be assessed [ ]. Similarly, high index of suspicion should be raised for ectopic pregnancy or presence of ovarian cancer when evaluating an individual with PID history. 10. Prevention Prevention of non-STI-related PID requires a multifactorial approach. One of the most critical strategies involves the strict application of aseptic techniques during obstetric and gynecological procedures, as post-procedural infection represents a major contributor to PID of non-sexual origin [ ]. It is vital for surgical personnel to wear sterile attire, including sterile gloves, gowns, and other protective gear, to avoid contamination of the surgical field. The sterilization of surgical instruments is critical [ ]. Minimally invasive surgical procedures must be preferred, if possible, in terms of minimizing the risk of infection as well as minimizing the risk of long-term consequences, such as infertility, attributed to scar tissue formation [ ]. Patient education is essential and among others includes post-surgical scrupulous wound care and prompt recognition of symptoms indicating infection, and seeking medical attention [ ]. Antibiotic prophylaxis is also important in terms of prevention, though it is not routinely recommended and is tailored to the procedure and the risk factors [ ]. In a meta-analysis regarding perioperative antibiotics to avoid infection following a first-trimester abortion, the utilization of preventive antibiotics decreased infection rates after abortion by 41% [ ]. The protective impact of antibiotics was evident irrespective of which subgroup was examined including women with a history of PID, women without a documented history of PID and females who received positive results for chlamydial infection during the procedure [ ]. For uterine evacuation following abortion or miscarriage, administration of doxycycline or metronidazole, optionally combined with azithromycin in selected high-risk cases, is recommended [ ]. Prophylaxis is also indicated for hysterectomy, typically as a single dose of a first- or second-generation cephalosporin, often combined with metronidazole [ ]. In contrast, routine antibiotic prophylaxis is not indicated for hysterosalpingography. However, for patients with a prior history of PID, doxycycline or azithromycin are recommended prior to the procedure. Other gynecologic and obstetric interventions, including intrauterine device insertion, endometrial biopsy, and routine hysteroscopy, generally do not require prophylactic antibiotics [ ]. Beyond procedural and pharmacological interventions, public health awareness plays a pivotal role in PID prevention. Educational campaigns targeting both the public and healthcare providers are essential, as they increase recognition of symptoms, improve timely access to care, and reduce the risk of complications such as infertility, chronic pelvic pain, or sepsis [ ]. A unique reference should be made to the education of special populations, as prompt recognition and effective management are essential [ , ]. While this review addresses PID of non-sexual origin, raising awareness of the sexually transmitted causes remains equally important. Public health education should emphasize safe sexual practices, including the correct and consistent use of barrier contraceptive methods. The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends annual screening for N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis in all sexually active women under 25 years of age, as well as in women aged 25 years and older who possess additional risk factors for infection. [ ]. 11. Future Directions Even with advancements in non-STI PID studies, significant challenges remain. Studies depend on data that do not have microbiological validation- examination of 11.7 million cases excluding STI/BV testing [ ]. Hospital-centric research tends to emphasize severe clinical image, underestimating milder or subclinical cases. Low-income countries fall behind in consistently monitoring non-STI PID, further complicated by diagnostic inequalities (limited laparoscopy/PCR availability). These limitations hinder prevalence and targeted interventions, particularly in areas with low socioeconomic status, where the incidence of non-STDs may be highest. Enhanced monitoring that includes pathogen identification is urgently required for precise epidemiological evaluation [ , ]. A diagnostic gap persists in PID, as existing methods primarily identify only a restricted subset of causative pathogens, thereby failing to comprehensively characterize the broader vaginal microbiota [ , ]. Traditional diagnostic methods, such as microscopy and culture, commonly present low sensitivity and specificity. In contrast, modern approaches, including multiplex PCR and Next-Generation Sequencing, offer enhanced sensitivity, allowing early and precise identification of both sexually transmitted and polymicrobial contributors. On top of that, AI-based approaches can enhance PID management by integrating microbiome profiling to predict disease risk, guide individualized therapy, and facilitate remote monitoring through mobile health platforms [ ]. the broader vaginal microbiota [ , ]. Traditional diagnostic methods, such as microscopy and culture, commonly present low sensitivity and specificity. In contrast, modern approaches, including multiplex PCR and Next-Generation Sequencing, offer enhanced sensitivity, allowing early and precise identification of both sexually transmitted and polymicrobial contributors. On top of that, AI-based approaches can enhance PID management by integrating microbiome profiling to predict disease risk, guide individualized therapy, and facilitate remote monitoring through mobile health platforms [ ]. In this context, the vaginal microbiome is crucial for maintaining reproductive health. Dysbiosis, characterized by decreased Lactobacillus abundance and a shift toward a more diverse, pathogen-rich microbial community, including S. aureus , K. pneumoniae , E. faecalis , and E. coli , has been associated with infertility, particularly in women with PID or idiopathic infertility [ ]. Metagenomic analysis of cervical and vaginal microbiota may be useful for detecting changes, such as reduced Lactobacillus abundance and increased bacterial diversity [ ]. Deep-sequencing technologies may assist in predicting treatment outcomes and recurrence risk, informing strategies to reduce the recurrence rate of BV and consequent PID [ ]. The development of noninvasive, biomarker-based diagnostics represents a promising avenue for improving PID detection. Candidate biomarkers include lipopolysaccharides (LPS), and interleukin-6 (IL-6). Both markers are detectable in endometrial tissue, and could serve as effective diagnostic tools, although upscaling would not be easily implemented [ ]. 12. Conclusions Although originally thought to be primarily a sexually transmitted disease, the rising prevalence of non-STI-related PID highlights the importance of recognizing alternative etiologies. Non-STI-related PID is associated with BV, IUD use, postpartum and post-procedural infections, as well as a diverse array of bacterial, viral, and parasitic pathogens. Currently, no specific clinical guidelines exist for the diagnosis or management of non-STI-related PID, presenting significant challenges for clinicians in tailoring therapy. Empiric treatment frequently relies on extrapolation from STI-based protocols, highlighting the urgent need for evidence-based recommendations that address non-STI etiologies. Given the potential for serious complications such as infertility, chronic pelvic pain, and recurrent infections, future research should prioritize strategies for early diagnosis, accurate identification of causative pathogens, and optimization of therapeutic approaches for non-STI PID.

documents.title: Falls Prevention Older People

chunks.content: 1 Introduction The injury patterns observed in older adults at home differ from those in other age groups; this risk level may be in part due to factors such as decreased functional capacity, increased dependency on daily activities, the presence of chronic illnesses, and various physical, sensory, and cognitive changes [ ]. Furthermore, since older people spend most of their time at home, they are more vulnerable to injuries associated with their home environment [ , ]. These injuries rank as the second most prevalent type of injuries, following traffic‐related accidents, and account for 7.7%–67.9% of all injuries globally, including in Iran [ , , , , , , ]. The majority of fatalities that occur in the home are due to injuries from falls, poisoning, burns, and fires, accounting for 86%–90% of cases. This issue is particularly prevalent among older adults with disabilities, and the frequency of these incidents varies by geographical location [ , , ]. Among the older population, the incidence of at least one home environment injury ranges from 8% to 16% within a month and increases to between 23% and 60% over the span of a year [ , ]. Around 55% of older adults are at risk of home‐related injuries, besides thousands of people of all ages die globally each year as a result of unintentional home‐related injuries [ ]. Compared to children, who, along with older adults, represent two high‐risk age groups for home injuries, the mortality proportions for seniors aged 65–84 and those over 85 are 10 and 50 times higher than that of children under 14, respectively [ ]. In the United States, a fatal or debilitating injury occurs at home every 18 min and 4 s, with 82% of these incidents happening to older adults [ , ], which can reduce independence and quality of life [ ]. As a result, there has been a rise in emergency room visits, hospital admissions, and longer hospital stays for older individuals due to environmental hazards and home safety issues. This has placed strain on the healthcare system and increased the economic burden on society while raising individual costs [ , , , , ]. For many people, the desire to age gracefully while maintaining independence and living in their own homes is a significant goal. However, the importance of a safe home environment in daily living and the prevalence of various injuries associated with aging, particularly in developing countries, are often not fully recognized [ , ]. Though living environments are generally perceived as safe and secure, research suggests that this belief is often mistaken, nonetheless, unsuitable design or structurally inappropriate modifications to the home environment can contribute to a higher risk of unintentional injuries among the older population [ , ]. On the other hand, the high prevalence of home injuries among older adults has led several studies to identify age as a significant risk factor for unintentional injuries [ , ]. In this regard, a higher proportion of elderly individuals suffering from various health conditions, including heart disease, hyper blood pressure and diabetes, reduces their chances of recovering from nonfatal injuries, in other words the existence of multiple unmanaged disorders and diseases increases their risk of mortality [ ]. Various factors contribute to injuries occurring at home. Research indicates that individual and social factors play a major role. These include being female, living alone, having a low socioeconomic status, suffering from chronic and musculoskeletal conditions, decreased functional reserve [ , , ], and facing various home environmental risks. For example, seniors living in homes with more than five risks are 2.8 times more likely to sustain at least one injury compared to those residing in homes with fewer risks [ , ]. Other studies have shown that factors such as age over 75, living in rural regions, cohabiting with family members, low literacy levels, and having health insurance are associated with higher injuries, in other words, previous research has indicated significant association between home environment injury and the mentioned factors [ , ]. It's important to recognize that we can greatly reduce and prevent unintentional older adults' injury in the home environment by improving living conditions and increasing safety measures [ , ]. Home environment injuries in older adults can result from various factors such as social, environmental, structural, physical, individual, and behavioral influences. Therefore, taking a multifaceted approach to injury prevention that addresses these factors is crucial [ , ]. To ensure the safety of the home environment, it's important to recognize and address potential hazards. These hazards include loose carpets, uneven flooring, and unsafe staircases, all of which can increase the risk of slips and falls [ ]. [ , ]. Home environment injuries in older adults can result from various factors such as social, environmental, structural, physical, individual, and behavioral influences. Therefore, taking a multifaceted approach to injury prevention that addresses these factors is crucial [ , ]. To ensure the safety of the home environment, it's important to recognize and address potential hazards. These hazards include loose carpets, uneven flooring, and unsafe staircases, all of which can increase the risk of slips and falls [ ]. Other risk factors in the home environment include malfunctioning electrical devices, improper cooking practices, slippery floors, inadequate lighting, and damaged steps. Addressing these issues is crucial for reducing the risk of injuries among older individuals [ , , , ]. However, in less developed and developing countries, concerns about the environmental conditions and safety of their living spaces have not been given as much priority as other areas. The occurrence of unintentional injuries and the associated factors varies significantly across different cultures. In the context of Iran, few studies have examined the safety conditions of older adults' homes, primarily relying on hospital and health system data from all age groups [ , , , , ] or investigating a specific type of injury, such as falls in older adults [ , , ]. Therefore, the objective of this study was to identify injury patterns and influencing factors among older adults living in the community in Tabriz City. 2 Methods 2.1 Study Design and Setting Iran, situated in the Middle East, 1,648,195 km², ranking as the fourth largest nation in Asia and the second in Western Asia. The country includes a cultural diversity, comprising various ethnic and linguistic groups under a shared Iranian identity. Since 1956, Iran's population has risen from approximately 19 million to over 84 million by 2020, positioning it as the 17th most populous country globally. However, the fertility rate has dropped from 6.5 to just above 2 over the last two decades, leading to a growth rate of about 1.39% in 2018. As of 2022, the population reached 85,891,580, with a sex ratio of 1.03 and a life expectancy of 70.1 years. Historical events, including the 1978 revolution and the 1980 war, have notably influenced demographic trends [ ]. The current study is a cross‐sectional study of 350 older adults, from 350 households, residents of Tabriz city. Tabriz is the capital of the East Azerbaijan province and Iran's fourth‐largest city overall. It is located in northwest Iran and has a population where more than 10% are over 60 years old, with a total population of 1,603,799, including 170,135 people over the age of 60 in 2021 [ ]. The study used stratified random sampling to select participants. Initially, the total number of samples was allocated based on the population of urban health centers, focusing on individuals aged 60 and above, and grouped by age and gender. The contribution of each strata was calculated using the formula ni = ki/N * n , and eligible older individuals attending these centers were included in the study by simple random sampling. The sample size was determined using Cochran's formula ( p = 0.3, d = 0.05, z = 1.96) and was initially estimated as 322 individuals. However, it was increased to 350 individuals to improve accuracy. In the next step, the calculated study subjects were selected from the pool of older adults using Iran's Health Information System (SIB). The SIB has been operational for 10 years within the Ministry of Health and Medical Education, facilitating the electronic management and documentation of health information and records for the Iranian population. This system is implemented across various health centers throughout the country. Healthcare professionals, including doctors, health experts, midwives, psychologists, nutritionists, Iranian rural health workers (Behvarz)‎, and other health professionals, are required to log all services provided to persons into this system. This resulted in a sample size that accurately represented 350 older individuals from the Tabriz Older People Health Survey. 2.2 Data Collection All eligible older adults who met our inclusion criteria were invited to participate in a face‐to‐face interview and home evaluation visits. Data collection was carried out by researchers (M.A. and trained researchers) from January 2024 to May 2024. The interviews were conducted in two intervals—from 9:30 a.m. to 1 p.m. and from 2:30 p.m. to 6:30 p.m. After coordinating via phone and explaining the plan and its objectives, the researchers visited the residences of the older individuals. Upon entering their homes and obtaining either oral or written informed consent, they gathered essential information regarding the participants' living situations. 2.3 Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria All study participants were older adults over the age of 60, residing in Tabriz city for at least 6 months, and willing to participate in this study. Exclusion criteria included hearing or mental problems, and

The interviews were conducted in two intervals—from 9:30 a.m. to 1 p.m. and from 2:30 p.m. to 6:30 p.m. After coordinating via phone and explaining the plan and its objectives, the researchers visited the residences of the older individuals. Upon entering their homes and obtaining either oral or written informed consent, they gathered essential information regarding the participants' living situations. 2.3 Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria All study participants were older adults over the age of 60, residing in Tabriz city for at least 6 months, and willing to participate in this study. Exclusion criteria included hearing or mental problems, and cognitive impairment as determined by an abbreviated mental test. Older adults who did not want to participate in the study were also excluded. 2.4 Measurement Tools 2.4.1 Demographic Information A checklist collecting demographic data, including age, gender, education level, job, marital status (married, single, widowed, divorced), year and hours of residency at home, visiting relatives status (children, relatives, friends in daily, weekly, monthly, yearly, and non), living status (single, with spouse, spouse/child or children, child, or children), income or supportive financial resource (0, 1‐100$, $100–$200, and $200 and more per month in 2023), assistive device/s (glasses, ear aid, walker, two or more than two device), injury occurrence, type, situation, time, place, body in the last week, month, 3 months, and 6 months), diseases and drugs, prescribed medications per day, (less than 2, 3 or more and non), smoking status (yes/no), health problem/s, and health perception were collected for the older adults completing the questionnaire [ , ]. 2.4.2 AMTS (Abbreviated Mental Test Score) The current questionnaire is identical to the Mini Mental State Examination (MMSE) questionnaire for concurrent validity assessments. Additionally, it is the most suitable questionnaire for illiterate older adults. Elderly individuals with cognitive impairment were established as exclusion criteria for the study. Consequently, this tool was utilized for cognitive screening and the exclusion of samples, allowing for the collection of precise information covering timeframes from 1 week to the past 6 months, while ensuring ease of use and rapid application for all elderly participants. A total score of less than 6 in AMTS indicates cognitive impairment likelihood, while a score of more than 6 does not. Furthermore, this scale has been validated for use with Iranian older individuals. The total Cronbach's α coefficient was 0.90 [ ]. 2.4.3 ADL (Activities of Daily Living), KATZ The ADL index assesses individuals based on their level of independence in performing daily activities. Each item is scored as dependent (0 points), needs help (1 point), or independent (2 points). The overall score ranges from 0 to 16, and individuals are categorized as dependent (0–7 points), needing help (8–11 points), or independent (12–16 points). This scale has been validated for use among older individuals in Iran. Total Cronbach's α coefficient was 0.80 [ ]. 2.4.4 IADL (Instrumental Activities of Daily Living), Lawton Instrumental activities of daily living (IADL) are activities that enable individuals to live independently within a community. This scale had eight items, including shopping, responsibility for own medications, mode of transportation, laundry, food preparation, housekeeping, ability to use telephone, and ability to handle finances. For each item, there are three choices: unable to perform (zero points), with minimal assistance (1 point), and independently (2 points). The total score for the IADL index ranges from 0 to 16, placing individuals into one of three groups: dependent (0–7 points), requiring assistance (8–11 points), and independent (12–16 points). This scale has been validated for use among the elderly population in Iran. Cronbach's alpha = 0.96 [ ]. 2.4.5 Loneliness Scale (Six‐Item Jong Gierveld) The loneliness scale contains six items with three response options: no, more or less, and yes. There are three negatively framed and three positively framed items. The questionnaire assesses emotional loneliness and social loneliness. Items 1, 5, and 6 are about emotional loneliness, while items 2, 3, and 4 are about social loneliness. A score of zero means no loneliness, while a score of six indicates extreme loneliness. The internal consistency coefficient for older adults is 0.76, and the scale has been confirmed for use with older people in Iran. Internal consistency was 0.698 [ ]. 2.4.6 Cougar Home Safety Assessment (CHSA) 5.0 The checklist, consisting of 74 items, addresses various hazard areas including fire hazards/carbon monoxide, emergency/medical, electrical, flooring/hallways, kitchen, bathroom(s), closets/storage areas, parking areas/entrances, bedroom, and disaster preparedness [ ]. The final categorization of this checklist was determined by the Elmeri index. 2.5 Statistical Analysis Data analyses were conducted by using IBM SPSS version 25 and STATA version 16. Descriptive results were reported as frequencies and percentages. The difference in demographic variables, ADL, IADL, loneliness, and CHSA by home injury variables was assessed by using χ 2 . A p value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

The final categorization of this checklist was determined by the Elmeri index. 2.5 Statistical Analysis Data analyses were conducted by using IBM SPSS version 25 and STATA version 16. Descriptive results were reported as frequencies and percentages. The difference in demographic variables, ADL, IADL, loneliness, and CHSA by home injury variables was assessed by using χ 2 . A p value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant. We conducted a comprehensive analysis to investigate the most common types of home‐related injuries among older adults at all times, focusing on factors such as gender, IADL, the availability of potential caregivers, and home safety. Binary logistic regression is used to estimate the likelihood that an observation belongs to one of two categories of a dichotomous dependent variable, utilizing a combination of categorical or continuous independent variables. This method is particularly beneficial when the goal is to predict the existence or non‐existence of a specific characteristic based on the values of various predictor variables, especially when the dependent variable is dichotomous. In this study, the binary logistic regression model was selected as the dependent variable had two response options (Yes vs. No) regarding home injuries among older adults. The χ 2 tests were performed for preliminary exploratory analysis and utilized to investigate and identify the relevant variables for constructing the final multiple regression model. At this point, selected variables were incorporated into the regression model. The findings from the analyses conducted in this study are presented in Table . Model fitness was assessed by checking the Confusion Matrix, Pseudo R‐squared Values, Deviance Residual analysis, and ROC/AUC investigation. Multicollinearity was also assessed through estimation of the variance inflation factor for each variable in the final model. 3 Results Out of 350 respondents living in 350 households, 177 (50.5%) participants experienced at least one type of home‐related injury. The majority of the respondents were aged between 60 and 74 years, and 54 (15.4%) belonged to the no‐income group. Married individuals comprised the majority, with 249 (71.1%) of the respondents, among whom 60% (171) were male, and also 47.1% (165) of respondents were illiterate (Table ). Additionally, 12.6% (44) reported having vision problems. Most older individuals (258, or 83.7%) had “no or one potential caregiver”. Furthermore, approximately 91% (319) visited their children, 21% [74] visited relatives, and 64.2% (224) visited friends on a daily or weekly basis. Nearly 45% (157) of respondents reported having no assistive devices, while 56.9% (199) took three or more prescribed medications each day. As indicated in Table , most respondents were independent in their ADL and IADL. The prevalence of injuries varied based on several factors, including the time period (week, 1 month, 3 months, 6 months), type of injury (falling, burning, cutting), situation (cooking, bathing, gardening, other ADL and IADL, sudden incidents), time of day (0–6 a.m., 6–12 a.m., 12–6 p.m., 6–12 p.m.), affected body part (head, hand, leg, hand and leg, lower body), and location of the injury (kitchen, hallway, bedroom, bathroom, balcony or terrace, outdoors) (see Table ). Among the injured older adults at all times, a majority (88 individuals or 43.3%) experienced falls as the cause of their injuries, followed by cuts (77 individuals or 37.9%), while burns accounted for the lowest proportion (38 individuals or 18.7%). Among our sample, we found that 264 participants (75.4%) were independent, 56 (16.0%) required assistance, and 30 (8.6%) were dependent. Based on binary logistic regression, results indicated that a higher proportion of females who needed help with IADLs and had no or only one caregiver suffered more injuries compared to other groups. Additionally, injuries were more prevalent in homes with low safety measures, particularly in areas such as bedrooms, closets, and those involving fire hazards (Table ). We discovered that women face a 5.1 times higher risk of injury than men, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 2.38–11.08. Older adults who needed assistance with IADLs had at least 7.81 times greater risk of injury compared to independent individuals, with a CI of 7.81–118.24. The risk of injury was 6.1 times higher among older adults with no or only one potential caregiver compared to those with more than one potential caregiver, with a CI of 2.56–14.96. Overall, the likelihood of injury increases in areas of the home with inadequate safety measures, especially when using fire or heat in spaces like the kitchen, highlighting a greater risk compared to other safety domains in the homes of older adults (Table ). 4 Discussion The growing heterogeneity in the elderly population, coupled with their preference to remain in their own residences, underscores the increasing significance of home safety and suitability.

Recent initiatives by professionals in gerontology and home safety focus on enabling older adults to stay in their familiar environments while offering tailored services. Additionally, it is crucial to address the capacity for adaptation and the mitigation of home safety risks. This study aimed to examine the physical deterioration of the living environments of elderly individuals in Tabriz city. This study was the first to investigate injury patterns and influencing factors among older adults living in the community in Tabriz City, Iran. It employs comprehensive information regarding socio‐demographic characteristics, chronic disease conditions, lifestyle, living environment, ADL, IADL, and a home safety index. The prevalence of unintentional injuries among urban older adults over the past 6 months, 3 months, and 1 month were recorded at 10.6%, 19.1%, and 20.9% respectively. In this regard, the decrease in the occurrence of home environment injuries over the 3 and 6 months can be attributed to two factors: firstly, the elimination of repeated injuries during the third and sixth months by research team and analysis process; secondly, while this study required participants to achieve a suitable score on the AMT for inclusion, there remains a potential for recall bias, which may influence the results regarding older individuals reporting home environment injuries impacting more than 1 month. On the other hand, the reported prevalence of home environment injuries in various studies over 1‐year periods ranged from 5.8% to 20.6% [ , , ]. The observed differences in injury prevalence may be attributed to several factors, including the varying time frames for injury assessment in this study compared to others, the use of distinct checklists for evaluation, seasonal influences, cultural factors, the types of residences occupied by the elderly participants, and the differing definitions of home environment injuries among the older population. This study established that falls are the predominant type of injury occurring in home settings, aligning with findings from various prior studies [ , , , , , ]. Previous domestic studies have primarily focused on older adults in specific city or community environments, where falls were identified as the most frequent type of injury [ , ]. The evidence suggests that the significant occurrence of falls, along with the existing scientific literature, can be attributed to its multifactorial nature, encompassing internal, external, and environmental factors. This complexity complicates the management of all contributing elements. Nevertheless, older adults with fewer or more clearly defined risk factors for falls are likely to have better control over their situation compared to those with multiple or less identifiable risks. Cuts were the second most common type of injury, aligning with findings from other research focused on injuries occurring in home environments [ , , ]. The higher incidence of cuts may stem from comprehensive data collection by researchers in older adults' homes, capturing all injuries regardless of severity, unlike many earlier studies that relied on hospital data [ , ] as well as, may be attributed to the population's tendency to use knives and other sharp‐edged instruments for cooking and home maintenance tasks. Many older individuals prefer using hand saws or knives over scissors for gardening, tree care, and chopping vegetables and potatoes at home. As a result, they are more susceptible to knife‐related injuries while performing ADL and IADL. Additionally, because they frequently use knives to prepare food, they also face an increased risk of burns while using the stove. Some research indicates that domestic injuries are more commonly experienced by women, similar to the findings of the current study [ , , , ], while other study highlights a greater prevalence among older men [ ]. This trend can probably be attributed to the fact that women generally spend 2–10 times more time at home than men, making them more likely to experience injuries [ , ]. In traditional societies like Iran, they often bear the primary responsibility for household chores and caregiving tasks such as cooking and cleaning [ ]. Additionally, the study found that certain factors, such as being single, having a lower educational background, and limited financial resources, are more common among women. These issues increase their risk of experiencing injuries compared to men. When examining the interplay of these factors among older

This trend can probably be attributed to the fact that women generally spend 2–10 times more time at home than men, making them more likely to experience injuries [ , ]. In traditional societies like Iran, they often bear the primary responsibility for household chores and caregiving tasks such as cooking and cleaning [ ]. Additionally, the study found that certain factors, such as being single, having a lower educational background, and limited financial resources, are more common among women. These issues increase their risk of experiencing injuries compared to men. When examining the interplay of these factors among older women in Iranian society, especially in Tabriz, it becomes evident that injuries in the home environment are more prevalent and can lead to severe, long‐lasting consequences. Various studies suggest that older Iranian men are more likely to remarry after the death of a spouse. In contrast, widowhood for older Iranian women often leads to a high likelihood of remaining alone for the rest of their lives [ , , ]. As well as, the higher occurrence of home injuries among women appears to be linked to higher rate of urinary incontinence and frailty, as demonstrated in prior research along with controlling confounder variables [ ]. Furthermore, over the past several decades, socioeconomic conditions in Iran have led to women generally achieving lower levels of education, employment, and income compared to men. This complex issue significantly contributes to the higher occurrence of injuries in the home environment among older adults. The variables presented in Tables and , along with the home safety checklist domains, were analyzed to identify injury patterns using binary logistic regression. The findings indicate that gender, IADL, and potential caregivers significantly influence injury likelihood, with females and caregivers showing increased risk, while safety improvements in specific areas reduce injury likelihood. Subsequently, study findings revealed that older women are more susceptible to unintentional injuries than older men, consistent with previous research [ , ]. Moreover, older adults who need assistance face an increased risk of such injuries, likely due to their reduced independence, which raises the chances of falls, cuts, or burns. Having few or no caregivers may further elevate the risk of these incidents. Related studies [ , ] highlighted the connection between assistance needs in IADL tasks and the occurrence of unintentional injuries, emphasizing that difficulties in daily activities can lead to more home injuries and affect overall health negatively. It is worth noting that the initial analyses revealed a statistically significant relationship between age and injuries; however, this significance diminished when other factors and home safety effects were considered. Specifically, individuals aged over 75 exhibited a higher risk of sustaining injuries in the home environment compared to younger age groups, with an odds ratio of 2.25. Nevertheless, upon incorporating environmental factors into the regression model, the age variable lost its significance and was excluded from the final model. This outcome may be attributed to the observation that enhancing home safety measures can mitigate the impact of age on injury risk. The safety conditions in bedrooms, storage areas, and fire hazards in homes of older adults are inversely correlated with environmental injury levels. The results of this investigation aligned with the findings of the Tekin and Kara study [ ]; however, they diverged from those of the Lim et al. study [ ], which identified the kitchen as the primary location of injuries. Enhanced safety in these zones leads to a notable reduction in resident injuries. Studies show these areas often pose risks due to poor lighting and less supervision. Factors like nighttime drowsiness and frequent urination further elevate the risk of harm [ , , ]. This study has notable limitations. It was conducted shortly after the COVID‐19 pandemic, which may have affected participants' responses due to factors like the loss of loved ones, extended quarantines, changes in social interactions, and government financial support initiatives targeting older adults. Additionally, the mixed‐gender interviewing team might have caused discomfort for some participants, particularly those living alone in certain areas of Tabriz, leading to refusals. As well as, older individuals with cognitive impairment, as identified by the AMT, were excluded from the study. However, the retrospective nature of the some of questionnaires and the potential unsuitability of the tool for all groups of older people, along with the dependence of those on self‐reported data, represent recall bias probability and additional limitation of the research. So, future research should include most sample studies or meta‐analysis of little sample studies to better understand home hazards for older adults. In developing countries like Iran, implementing programs to empower older adults and ensure safe home environments could effectively improve their quality of life. 5 Conclusion Ensuring the safety of the home environment is crucial for preventing falls and injuries among older adults. So, future research should include most sample studies or meta‐analysis of little sample studies to better understand home hazards for older adults. In developing countries like Iran, implementing programs to empower older adults and ensure safe home environments could effectively improve their quality of life. 5 Conclusion Ensuring the safety of the home environment is crucial for preventing falls and injuries among older adults. This involves developing and implementing technologies specifically designed to predict falls in residential settings. Additionally, it is important to create opportunities for physical activity and enhance social engagement for older adults, especially older women, through targeted policies and awareness campaigns. For those who have any problem on IADL, providing clear guidance on their proper use is essential, and these devices and infrastructures should be tailored to the recommendations of relevant specialists. Furthermore, to support older individuals living alone, governments and organizations focused on elder care should offer tax benefits or incentives for family members, volunteers, or caregivers. Such measures can help reduce the time older adults spend isolated, ultimately decreasing the incidence of falls and other injuries in their homes. chunks.content: Key messages • What is already known on this topic – Mental health disorders are known to be associated with chronic infections. However, clear evidence of persistent infections and disturbances in brain biochemistry is rarely reported. • What this study adds – We present a case of tick-borne disease with mental health disorder and substance abuse which led to a homicide-suicide event. Persistent spirochetes were identified in autopsy tissues, along with quinolinic acid accumulation in the brain. A patient database further demonstrates the propensity of borreliosis patients to become suicidal and/or homicidal. • How this study might affect research, practice or policy – Consideration of borreliosis as a contributor to mental health disorders in endemic areas could lead to reduced morbidity and mortality if a diagnosis is confirmed and the infection is adequately treated. 1Introduction Infectious diseases, including Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome, tuberculosis, and COVID-19, contribute to substance abuse and addictive disorders [ , , ]. Lyme disease/Lyme borreliosis (LD) and addictive disorders have been reviewed [ ], and studies show an association between LD and substance abuse [ , , , ], with some people becoming dependent upon psychoactive substances [ ]. Borreliosis is a tick-borne infection caused by Borreliaceae family spirochetes that includes Lyme disease (LD) and relapsing fever (RF) [ ]. LD is the most common vector-borne illness in the United States (US) with an annual incidence of approximately 476,000 [ , , , ]. RF is widespread, found on five continents [ ]. Late-stage persistent manifestations of borreliosis, such as musculoskeletal, cardiac and neurologic symptoms, may result from diagnostic and treatment delays [ , , , , ], with patients remaining ill for prolonged periods [ , , ]. Substance use disorders (SUD) are chronic, relapsing disorders characterized by compulsively seeking a substance, thing, or activity, that continue despite harmful consequences, resulting in long-lasting changes in the brain. SUD are complex brain disorders and a mental illness, with severity dependent on the number of symptoms [ ]. Substances with potential for abuse include opioids, alcohol, sedatives, marijuana, and stimulants. Those at risk for addiction describe a very different reaction to potentially addictive substances compared to those not at risk, with patients sometimes stating that they feel more normal/alive when exposed to their substance of abuse. In the US, 46.3 million people (16.5 % of the population) met the DSM-5 substance use disorder criteria [ ], and over 111,000 died from overdoses [ ]. A recent large-scale study using Danish patient registries demonstrated that individuals with LD as a group had higher rates (28 %) of any mental disorder, including depression and suicidality (75 % higher rate of suicide), compared to those without LD [ ]. An earlier study focused on patients with intrathecal antibody indicative of neuroborreliosis and found no significant differences in seeking psychiatric care or medictions between those patients and the general population [ ]. While the study populations and outcome measures are drastically different, the reports highlight the value of large-scale studies in determining risk of mental illness following infection. One hypothesis explaining the impact of chronic infectious disease upon mental functioning is chronic inflammation and increasing indoleamine-2,3-dioxygenase (IDO), adversely altering tryptophan catabolism and the kynurenine pathway (KP). This association between chronic infections and tryptophan catabolism plays a vital role in both health and disease [ ]. The majority of available l -tryptophan (L-TrP) is metabolized through the KP, and ∼5 % is converted to serotonin. IDO is the first and the rate-limiting step, which branches with the synthesis of kynurenic acid (KA), anthranilic acid, or 3-hydroxykynurenine (3-HK) and downstream metabolites including quinolinic acid (QA). While KA, an NMDA (N-methyl- d -aspartate) receptor antagonist, is thought to be neuroprotective, QA, an NMDA agonist, is neurotoxic. NMDA is a receptor for glutamate, the primary excitatory neurotransmitter in the brain. Reduced NMDA activity can cause cognitive defects, while overstimulation can lead to neuronal death and neurodegeneration [ ]. Thus, the induction of this pathway has both protective and harmful consequences [ , ]. Clearly, the possible association between SUD and Borrelia infection deserves greater attention. Here we review a fatal case of borreliosis and substance abuse, comparing patient history to symptoms from LD patients. We also evaluate brain tissue for microglial activation and QA, and interrogate postmortem tissue for Borrelia using immunoflouresence (IFA) and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) [ , ]. 2Materials and methods Autopsy tissue: Autopsy tissue was obtained from the Lyme Disease Biobank (LDB) through their partnership with the National Disease Research Interchange (NDRI). University of Pennsylvania (IRB#5 FWA00004028) approved the authorization/consent forms for research tissue donation to LDB under NDRI's Protocol (#704541; NDRI Tissue Procurement Program). also evaluate brain tissue for microglial activation and QA, and interrogate postmortem tissue for Borrelia using immunoflouresence (IFA) and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) [ , ]. 2Materials and methods Autopsy tissue: Autopsy tissue was obtained from the Lyme Disease Biobank (LDB) through their partnership with the National Disease Research Interchange (NDRI). University of Pennsylvania (IRB#5 FWA00004028) approved the authorization/consent forms for research tissue donation to LDB under NDRI's Protocol (#704541; NDRI Tissue Procurement Program). Medical records from healthcare providers, hospitals, and the mother's description of illness were redacted. Brain tissue (141 g) was received, fixed in formalin, and portions were embedded into paraffin blocks. Cassettes of fixed tissue from other organs (detailed below) were also received. From each sample, a small piece was removed and stored in PBS/0.02 % sodium azide at 4 °C, and the remainder was embedded in paraffin. A total of 23 tissues were processed. DNA isolation: Genomic DNA from the tissue samples was extracted using QIAamp DNA FFPE kit (Qiagen, 56404). Initially, slides were deparaffinized using a Leica Autostainer X, and tissue sections were scraped into a 1.5 ml microcentrifuge tube using sterile blades. For each preparation, tissue sections with a thickness of 30–50 μm and a surface area of up to 250 mm 2 or piece of tissue weighing <25 mg was added to a tube. Tissue sections were resuspended in a mixture containing 180 μl of buffer ATL and 20 μl of proteinase K as previously described [ ]. PCR and primers: After decontaminating the workspace, initial PCR was performed using either Q5 Hot start High-Fidelity DNA polymerase (NEB, M0493L) or Taq DNA polymerase (Qiagen, 201203), and 5 μl of isolated DNA. Primers are listed below. Microglial staining: Sections were stained with ionized calcium-binding adaptor molecule 1 (Iba1) and CD68 double immunohistochemistry with a pale Verhoeff counterstain to facilitate delineation of gray and white matter as described previously [ ]. Immunofluorescence (IFA): Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissues from the following (precentral gyrus, cingulate gyrus, rostral hippocampus, superior and middle temporal gyri, inferior parietal lobule, caudal basal ganglia, thalamus with mamillary body, midbrain, pons, medulla, cerebellar cortex, cerebellar dentate nucleus, dura mater, pancreas, lung, testis, lymph node, spleen, heart, liver, kidney, adrenal gland, and skeletal muscle) were sectioned, in a dedicated room where no Borrelia experiments are conducted, at 5 μm in thickness and stained for B. burgdorferi as previously described [ ] with slight modifications in antibody incubation times. After blocking, tissue sections were also incubated overnight at room temperature with primary rabbit anti-rBipA immune serum (a kind gift from Dr. Job E. Lopez) [ ] at a dilution of 1:300. The next day, tissue sections were washed with Triton-X (TX-100) and PBS/fish skin gelatin (FSG) buffer washes. Slides were then incubated with secondary antibody goat anti-rabbit IgG conjugated to Alexa-Fluor 594 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, R37117 ) diluted 1:1000 in blocking buffer, and incubated for 2 hrs. Slides were washed after incubation with primary antibody and counterstained with DAPI (Millipore Sigma# CAS 28718-90-3) for 10 min to stain nuclei. Uninfected non-human primate (NHP) heart and pancreas tissues were used as controls ( ). Thalamus with mamillary body and pons were stained for QA based on microglial activation in these regions. A similar protocol as described above was followed. Tissues were subjected to pH-9 antigen retrieval after deparaffinization, followed by overnight incubation with primary anti-Quinolinic acid rabbit polyclonal antibody (Immusmol, IS1010) diluted in blocking buffer at 1:1000 dilution. After washes, tissues were then incubated for 2 hours with the secondary antibody goat anti-rabbit IgG conjugated to AlexaFluor 594 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, R37117 ) diluted 1:1000 in blocking buffer. Slides were washed and counterstained with DAPI, and Prolong™Gold Anti-fade mountant (ThermoFisher) was applied. Slides were coverslipped before visualization. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH): Heart and pancreas tissue were fixed, embedded in methacrylate and sectioned as described previously [ ]. FISH hybridization mix contained a Borrelia genus-specific oligonucleotide probe (reBorr0) labeled with Cy3, a panbacterial probe (EUB338) labeled with Cy5, and a nonsense Probe (NOS338) labeled with FITC, to exclude unspecific binding [ , , ], and the nucleic acid stain DAPI. Sections were hybridized as described [ ]. To control for probe specificity, positive control Borrelia burgdorferi (0 MM) and negative controls Treponema pallidum (2MM) and Treponema denticola were included in each FISH experiment (see ). For microscopy, an epifluorescence microscope (Axio Imager Z2; Carl Zeiss, Jena, Germany) equipped with narrow-band filter sets (AHF; Analysentechnik,Tübingen, Germany) was used.
