GnRH neurons play an essential role in the formation and integration of the neuronal network [ ]. The retrograde endocannabinoid signaling pathway plays a critical role in regulating stress and anxiety [ ]. Malfunction of the dopamine system in the prefrontal cortex contributes to the cognitive and negative symptoms of schizophrenia [ , ]. Previous studies showed that apelin system is related to emotional behavior [ , ] and depression due to its involvement in the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis [ ].The higher level of cytokine caused by MIA can trigger the misguidance of neurons, which could also alter axon guidance processes [ ]. To isolate prenatal effects on enhancers, we identified 1,720 overlapping differential enhancer peaks between the two prenatal comparisons (Mock-Mock vs. MIA-Mock and Mock-MIA vs. MIA-MIA) (Fig. ). We annotated them to genes (Fig. ) using existing HiC [ ] data first, then the rest of the peaks with their closest genes. In addition to the KEGG terms discovered from the individual comparisons (glutamatergic synapse, retrograde endocannabinoid signaling, and dopaminergic synapse), we also found KEGG terms such as GABAergic synapse and MAPK signaling that are related to neurodevelopmental disorders. Previous studies have provided evidence of significant alterations in the developmental shift of GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) in the offspring’s brain following MIA [ ]. The MAPK signaling pathway is also implicated in the frontal cortex of schizophrenia subjects [ ]. Interestingly, KEGG terms such as nicotine addiction and morphine addiction are also present. Studies suggest that pups exposed to maternal immune activation have higher motivation for cocaine self-administration [ ]. Taken together, MIA during the prenatal stage alters enhancer and promoter activities and induces transcriptomic changes in genes involved in neurotransmission, synaptic development, and disease risk. These findings support a model in which MIA disrupts core neurobiological processes relevant to neuropsychiatric and addiction disorders. Finally, to examine the level of background within differential analyses, we also conducted differential analysis of two additional control groups (Supplementary Fig. ): Mock-Mock_1: Offspring born to control mother and raised by their birth mother, together with stepsiblings born to a different control mother. Mock-Mock_2: Offspring born to control mother but raised by control surrogate mother, together with stepsiblings born to the control surrogate mother. Between groups Mock-Mock_1 and Mock-Mock_2, we identified 648 differential enhancers, 156 differential promoters, and 350 differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (FDR < 0.05, |log₂FC| > 0.5) (Supplementary Fig. ). These numbers of differential enhancers, promoters, and DEGs are notably lower than those obtained between groups involving prenatal effects. Although we identified autism [ ] related gene Smc1a (−log₁₀(FDR) = 7.95) among the DEGs, only 18 genes overlapped between differential-enhancer/promoter-associated genes and DEGs (Supplementary Fig. ). No enriched KEGG terms were identified with these genes. Overall, the background signal in the differential analysis does not affect our conclusions. Epigenomic and transcriptomic alterations caused by postnatal effects of MIA To study the postnatal effects of MIA, we compared Mock-MIA with Mock-Mock and also MIA-Mock with MIA-MIA. The differences revealed by these two comparisons indicate whether fostering by a MIA mother induces epigenomic and transcriptomic alterations in offspring. We identified 5134 differential enhancers, 335 differential promoters, and 2723 DEGs between Mock-MIA and Mock-Mock (|log₂FC| > 0.5, FDR < 0.05) (Fig. ). We also identified 5174 differential enhancers, 254 differential promoters, and 1557 DEGs between MIA-Mock and MIA-MIA (|log₂FC| > 0.5, FDR < 0.05) (Fig. ). The DEGs between Mock-MIA and Mock-Mock include Kctd16 (−log₁₀(FDR) = 20.04), Tecr (−log₁₀(FDR) = 17.12), Igsf9b (−log₁₀(FDR) = 17.82), and Tm2d3 (−log₁₀(FDR) = 15.53) (Supplementary Fig. ). The significant DEGs identified between MIA-Mock and MIA-MIA include Kidins220 [ , ] (−log₁₀(FDR) = 10.35), Pcdhgc5 [ ] (−log₁₀(FDR) = 10.05), and Arfgef3 [ ] (−log₁₀(FDR) = 9.00) (Supplementary Fig. ). Next, we prioritized genes associated with both epigenomic and transcriptomic changes. We identified 477 genes in the comparison of Mock-MIA vs. Mock-Mock. We identified 299 genes in the comparison of MIA-Mock vs. MIA-MIA (Fig. ). The first group of 477 genes is enriched for KEGG terms related to several neurodegenerative diseases, including spinocerebellar ataxia and Alzheimer’s disease. Additionally, we identified KEGG terms (FDR < 0.05) related to neurodevelopment similar to the ones associated with prenatal effects, such as glutamatergic synapse, cAMP signaling pathway, retrograde endocannabinoid signaling, and tight

= 10.05), and Arfgef3 [ ] (−log₁₀(FDR) = 9.00) (Supplementary Fig. ). Next, we prioritized genes associated with both epigenomic and transcriptomic changes. We identified 477 genes in the comparison of Mock-MIA vs. Mock-Mock. We identified 299 genes in the comparison of MIA-Mock vs. MIA-MIA (Fig. ). The first group of 477 genes is enriched for KEGG terms related to several neurodegenerative diseases, including spinocerebellar ataxia and Alzheimer’s disease. Additionally, we identified KEGG terms (FDR < 0.05) related to neurodevelopment similar to the ones associated with prenatal effects, such as glutamatergic synapse, cAMP signaling pathway, retrograde endocannabinoid signaling, and tight junction [ , ] (Fig. ). The second group of 299 genes enriches a number of KEGG terms that also relate to synaptic signaling, addiction-related pathways and neurodegenerative diseases including GABAergic and glutamatergic synapses, nicotine addiction, and Alzheimer’s disease (Fig. ). These findings suggest that postnatal MIA exposure alters molecular programs involved in synaptic plasticity and neurobehavioral regulation, potentially linking immune experience during early life to long-term risk for both neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric conditions. We identified 1708 overlapping differential enhancer peaks between the two comparisons (Mock-MIA vs. Mock-Mock and MIA-Mock vs. MIA-MIA). These represent enhancers that are the most related to postnatal effects of MIA. We generated enriched KEGG terms with the annotated genes from these peaks (Fig. ). We found enriched neurotransmission and neuromodulation pathways such as cAMP signaling pathway, GABAergic synapse, glutamatergic synapse, MAPK signaling pathway and dopaminergic synapse, and also terms related to addiction, including nicotine addiction, morphine addiction, and amphetamine addiction. The WNT pathway is recognized as a significant contributor to embryonic development and to conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease and metabolic disorders [ ]. Compared to prenatal effects, postnatal effects are associated with a broader set of KEGG terms related to neurodegenerative pathways. Finally, we examined the impact of maternal and peer separations [ ] that are potentially involved in cross-fostering and our postnatal analysis as a background. Between groups Mock-Mock_1 and Mock-Mock_3 (offspring born to control mother and raised by their birth mother, without any cross-fostering manipulation), we identified 469 differential enhancers, 108 differential promoters, and 1693 DEGs (|log₂FC| > 0.5, FDR < 0.05) (Supplementary Fig. , Supplementary Data ). Between groups Mock-Mock_2 and Mock-Mock_3, we identified 348 differential enhancers, 648 differential promoters, and 1222 DEGs (Supplementary Data ) under the same criteria. We found 45 and 57 overlapping genes between differential enhancer/promoter and DEGs for Mock-Mock_1 vs. Mock-Mock_3 and Mock-Mock_2 vs. Mock-Mock_3, respectively (Supplementary Fig. ). The 57 overlapping genes for Mock-Mock_2 versus Mock-Mock_3 exhibit enriched KEGG pathways including GnRH related pathway, glutamatergic synapse and cAMP signaling pathway (Supplementary Fig. ). We discovered Egr2 among the DEGs for Mock-Mock_1 vs. Mock-Mock_3. Egr2 has been linked to peripheral neuropathy phenotypes in previous studies [ ] (Supplementary Fig. ). Additionally, Prmt7 was found in the DEGs list for Mock-Mock_2 vs. Mock-Mock_3 and is associated with syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder [ ] (Supplementary Fig. ). Although all Mock-Mock groups were untreated controls, comparisons involving Mock-Mock3 showed over 1200 DEGs, while Mock-Mock1 vs. Mock-Mock2 differed by only approximately 350 DEGs. The background signal should only affect our differential analysis minimally. Overlap between prenatal and postnatal effects at the epigenomic level There is substantial overlap in genes impacted by prenatal and postnatal effects. We identified 599 differential-enhancer-linked genes shared between prenatal and postnatal effects, while 268 and 276 were unique differential-enhancer-linked genes involved in the prenatal and postnatal effects, respectively. Although KEGG enrichment analysis of the unique gene sets did not yield significant results, we performed Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment to identify distinct biological processes associated with prenatal and postnatal effects (Fig. ). The 268 prenatal-specific enhancer-linked genes were enriched for developmental terms such as telencephalon development, forebrain development, and central nervous system development (Fig. ). In contrast, the 276 postnatal-specific enhancer-linked genes were enriched for processes related to synaptic signaling, axonogenesis, and neuron differentiation (Fig. ). These findings highlight stage-specific regulatory effects of MIA on brain development. K-means clustering of enhancer peaks We conducted K-means clustering for enhancer peaks to group enhancer features into clusters that potentially generate biological insights [ , ]. Consensus H3K27ac peaks from the four tested conditions (Mock-Mock, MIA-Mock, Mock-MIA, and MIA-MIA) were grouped into four clusters based on H3K27ac peak intensity patterns (Supplementary Fig. ). Clusters I and II highlight differences among the four groups. Mock-Mock serves as the baseline, as it was not exposed to MIA in utero or raised by MIA mothers. In cluster I, Mock-Mock exhibits the lowest signal, while MIA-Mock and Mock-MIA are comparable, and MIA-MIA shows the highest signal. Cluster I is enriched for pathways such as adrenergic signaling in cardiomyocytes, which is linked to neurotransmitter signaling [ ]. Additionally, pathways such as neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction and amphetamine addiction are also enriched. The enriched transcription factor MEF2D has

into four clusters based on H3K27ac peak intensity patterns (Supplementary Fig. ). Clusters I and II highlight differences among the four groups. Mock-Mock serves as the baseline, as it was not exposed to MIA in utero or raised by MIA mothers. In cluster I, Mock-Mock exhibits the lowest signal, while MIA-Mock and Mock-MIA are comparable, and MIA-MIA shows the highest signal. Cluster I is enriched for pathways such as adrenergic signaling in cardiomyocytes, which is linked to neurotransmitter signaling [ ]. Additionally, pathways such as neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction and amphetamine addiction are also enriched. The enriched transcription factor MEF2D has also been associated with MIA [ ]. In cluster II, Mock-Mock exhibits the highest level, while MIA-Mock, Mock-MIA, and MIA-MIA show lower levels of signal. This suggests that the enhancer-associated genes in this cluster may be downregulated following exposure to MIA. The enriched pathways include glutamatergic synapses, adrenergic signaling in cardiomyocytes, axon guidance, and dopaminergic synapses, all of which are known to be related to neurotransmission or neurodevelopment. The enriched transcription factors FOSL1 and FOSL2 have been associated with the establishment of the maternal-fetal interface [ ]. WGCNA analysis reveals key transcriptomic changes To identify gene co-expression patterns associated with MIA, we performed weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) that clusters genes into modules based on expression similarity and correlates them with experimental conditions [ ] (Supplementary Fig. ). We present gene co-expression modules correlated with experimental groups (Supplementary Fig. ). Among the significant modules, MEblack exhibited strong associations in MIA-Mock vs. Mock-Mock and MIA-MIA vs. Mock-MIA, indicating its relevance to prenatal MIA effects. KEGG enrichment analysis identified pathways involved in dopaminergic synapse, neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction, and cAMP signaling (Supplementary Fig. ). Gene network analysis highlighted Penk [ ] and Tac1 [ ], associated with neuropeptide signaling(Supplementary Fig. ). Although MEturquoise and MEpink also demonstrated statistical significance, their biological relevance is less clear. MEturquoise exhibits positive module-trait correlations in MIA-Mock and Mock-MIA but negative correlations in Mock-Mock and MIA-MIA, suggesting complex postnatal influences. Despite its enrichment in neurodegenerative pathways, the implication of MEturquoise in prenatal MIA effects remains unclear. Similarly, MEpink, while statistically significant, lacks enriched KEGG terms, limiting its functional interpretation. Key transcriptional regulations and regulated genes in MIA offspring We integrated transcriptomic data with H3K27ac data to identify key transcription factors (Fig. ) and their regulated genes using the Taiji pipeline [ , ]. Taiji combines diverse genomic modalities to construct transcriptional regulatory networks and predict regulatory interactions between transcription factors (TFs) and genes, using the personalized PageRank algorithm. To assess prenatal MIA effects, we compared Mock-Mock and MIA-Mock groups (Fig. ) and identified key transcription factors including SOX, RELA, BCL6, and EGR2. The SOX transcription factor family plays a crucial role in the development of the central nervous system. Specifically, SOX5 is identified as one of the four key regulators that primarily regulate dysregulated genes in schizophrenia within neurons. SOX5 is genetically associated with both schizophrenia and neurodevelopmental disorders (NDD), and serves as a crucial neurodevelopmental regulatory factor [ ]. The human gene corresponding to the transcription factor RELA is related to the development of schizophrenia [ ]. BCL6 has been linked to Alzheimer’s disease [ ]. EGR2 transcription factor has been found to be linked to schizophrenia and bipolar disorder [ ]. Some of these findings on prenatal effects (i.e. RELA, BCL6, and EGR2) are also confirmed by comparing Mock-MIA and MIA-MIA (Fig. ). Additionally, we identified RREB1, a transcription factor essential for neuronal survival in the mammalian brain [ ] and POU6F2, which regulates myelination and neurogenesis and is linked to bipolar disorder through DNA methylation [ ]. We also analyzed the transcription factor involvement in the postnatal effects of MIA. In the comparison of Mock-MIA vs. Mock-Mock, key transcription factors identified include TCF3, SOX3, POU6F2 and BCL6 (Fig. ). The methylation pattern observed at the Tcf3 gene is associated with T-cell maturation within the blood of schizophrenia patients [ ]. With MIA-Mock vs. MIA-MIA (Fig. ), we identified SOX5, POU6F2, RREB1 and EGR2 which were mentioned above. Several TFs, including SOX5, BCL6, EGR2, RHOX11 and PRRX2, were consistently identified across both prenatal and postnatal comparisons. Across all comparisons, KEGG terms included cAMP signaling, axon guidance, MAPK signaling, glutamatergic synapse, and addiction-related pathways such as morphine and nicotine addiction (Fig. ). These pathways reflect common involvement in neurotransmission, intracellular signaling and behavior regulation. Altogether, these findings indicate a conserved regulatory core associated with MIA exposure. To distinguish MIA-specific effects from baseline variation, we analyzed transcriptional regulators captured by comparisons of several control groups that do not involve MIA mothers (Supplementary Fig. ). While TFs such as PRRX2, TCF3, and KLF family members are active, overlap with MIA-associated TFs is limited and key regulators like SOX5 and EGR2 are absent. KEGG enrichment of regulated genes (Supplementary

guidance, MAPK signaling, glutamatergic synapse, and addiction-related pathways such as morphine and nicotine addiction (Fig. ). These pathways reflect common involvement in neurotransmission, intracellular signaling and behavior regulation. Altogether, these findings indicate a conserved regulatory core associated with MIA exposure. To distinguish MIA-specific effects from baseline variation, we analyzed transcriptional regulators captured by comparisons of several control groups that do not involve MIA mothers (Supplementary Fig. ). While TFs such as PRRX2, TCF3, and KLF family members are active, overlap with MIA-associated TFs is limited and key regulators like SOX5 and EGR2 are absent. KEGG enrichment of regulated genes (Supplementary Fig. ) reveals broader and less consistent patterns compared to the ones involving MIA treatment. This confirms that the regulatory changes involving MIA treatment are distinct from stochastic variations. MIA effects association with neuropsychiatric disorders The genome-wide association studies (GWAS) employ statistical methods to establish links between genotypes and phenotypes. This is achieved by examining various genetic variants among individuals with similar genetic backgrounds but different phenotypes [ ]. Recent estimates suggested that over 90% of GWAS regions discovered so far are not in gene bodies but potentially on regulatory elements including promoters and enhancers [ ]. A total of 115 GWAS datasets focused on neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative diseases have become available since 2007 [ ]. A previous study confirmed the linkage between maternal immune activation and neuropsychiatric diseases such as schizophrenia and autism spectrum disorder [ , ]. Thus, we examined the potential association between differential enhancers and promoters discovered in this study and the human disease traits discovered by GWAS. We first utilized the genome annotation tool UCSC LiftOver to convert the differential enhancer and promoter regions from the mouse genome mm10 to the human genome hg38. The UCSC LiftOver tool has been used in many previous studies for cross-species mapping of enhancer and promoter regions [ , ]. Since our focus is on evolutionarily conserved regulatory regions, UCSC LiftOver is a reliable tool. By utilizing summary statistics from GWAS with LD score regression [ ], we then evaluated the overlap between differential enhancers and promoters discovered in our study and GWAS regions associated with specific traits (Fig. ). We evaluated both differential enhancers (Fig. ) and differential promoters (Fig. ) among various experimental groups. We computed the enrichment associated with schizophrenia, other neuropsychiatric disorders, and other non-psychiatric-related diseases using linkage disequilibrium (LD) score regression [ – ]. Differential enhancer regions generally exhibit higher enrichment (-log(P) value) compared to the differential promoter regions (Fig. ). This suggests that the regulatory elements within enhancers may play a more prominent role in the genetic susceptibility to psychiatric disorders compared to promoters. When compared to control traits such as ulcerative colitis, type 2 diabetes, epilepsy, and celiac disease, neuropsychiatric disease traits including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, depression, neuroticism, and ADHD show notably higher enrichment. In both prenatal and postnatal comparison groups, the enrichment for psychiatric disorders including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, depression, and neuroticism exhibits -log(P) values significantly above the threshold of P < 0.05. The high -log(P) values observed for psychiatric diseases indicate a stronger genetic association with differential epigenomic features, highlighting the important contributions of both prenatal and postnatal MIA exposure to psychiatric disorders. Discussion Our findings reveal that MIA during pregnancy induces widespread and persistent epigenomic and transcriptomic alterations in the frontal cortex of adult offspring, with distinct contributions from both prenatal and postnatal factors. By using a cross-fostering design, we disentangled the prenatal and postnatal origins of these changes and demonstrated that MIA exerts long-lasting regulatory effects on genes and pathways involved in neurotransmission, neurodevelopment, and psychiatric disease risk. Notably, enhancer and promoter modifications, as well as DEGs, were enriched in synaptic signaling pathways – particularly those involving glutamatergic, GABAergic, and dopaminergic transmission – highlighting core molecular mechanisms potentially disrupted in disorders such as schizophrenia, autism, and depression. These data provide compelling evidence that MIA not only reprograms early developmental trajectories through epigenetic mechanisms but also leaves a molecular footprint that may underlie behavioral phenotypes and increased vulnerability to neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases later in life. The relative contributions of prenatal and postnatal environments to brain development remain an area of active investigation. Studies suggest that prenatal exposures exert long-term effects through hormonal signaling, immune activation, and epigenetic reprogramming during critical gestational windows [ , ], whereas postnatal experiences are thought to shape synaptic refinement and circuit-level plasticity through sensory input and maternal care [ , ]. In influenza-based MIA models, maternal immune activation leads to elevated cytokine production, including IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IL-17a, IFN-α, and TNF-α, which can alter placental signaling, disrupt fetal neurogenesis, and impact long-term cortical structure and behavior [ – ]. Postnatal effects may result from persistent maternal immune dysregulation affecting lactation or maternal care [ , ]. However, the biological continuity between these periods

long-term effects through hormonal signaling, immune activation, and epigenetic reprogramming during critical gestational windows [ , ], whereas postnatal experiences are thought to shape synaptic refinement and circuit-level plasticity through sensory input and maternal care [ , ]. In influenza-based MIA models, maternal immune activation leads to elevated cytokine production, including IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IL-17a, IFN-α, and TNF-α, which can alter placental signaling, disrupt fetal neurogenesis, and impact long-term cortical structure and behavior [ – ]. Postnatal effects may result from persistent maternal immune dysregulation affecting lactation or maternal care [ , ]. However, the biological continuity between these periods complicates interpretation, and direct comparisons are often confounded by shared maternal or environmental effects [ ]. By applying the cross-fostering design, our model reduces these confounds, enabling clearer attribution of observed effects to the timing of maternal immune challenge. It is worth noting that the presence of cross-fostered groups within the same cage potentially leads to some level of microbiota homogenization [ ] that may affect the observed transcriptional and epigenetic changes due to MIA. Our results highlighted significant genes across comparison groups. For prenatal comparison, we discovered DEGs including Adam22 (−log₁₀(FDR) = 17.64), Ogt (−log₁₀(FDR) = 14.87), Nfrkb (−log₁₀(FDR) = 14.40), Igsf9b (−log₁₀(FDR) = 16.70), Plxna4 (−log₁₀(FDR) = 17.36), and Arhgef2 (−log₁₀(FDR) = 16.43). The Adam family, especially Adam22 , plays an important role in peripheral myelination [ ]. Ogt is involved in the embryonic development and the regulation of gene expression within the nervous system [ ]. Nfrkb or NF-κB is a central regulator of inflammation and immune response [ ]. Variants in Igsf9b are associated with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder [ ]. The Plxna4 gene has been linked to Alzheimer disease in humans through GWAS study [ ]. Arhgef2 mutations have been implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders [ ]. For postnatal comparison, we discovered DEGs including Kctd16 (−log₁₀(FDR) = 20.04), Tecr (−log₁₀(FDR) = 17.12), Igsf9b (−log₁₀(FDR) = 17.82), and Tm2d3 (−log₁₀(FDR) = 15.53). The upregulation of Kctd16 is consistent with previous findings from MIA studies [ ]. Tm2d3 has been linked to late-onset Alzheimer’s disease (AD) through an exome-wide association study [ ]. We also identified Kidins220 [ , ] (−log₁₀(FDR) = 10.35), Pcdhgc5 [ ] (−log₁₀(FDR) = 10.05), and Arfgef3 [ ] (−log₁₀(FDR) = 9.00), from postnatal comparison, all of which are associated with schizophrenia and potentially other neurodevelopmental disorders. Our results suggest that the prenatal and postnatal effects of MIA have substantial overlap in terms of the genes being affected at the epigenomic level. We identified 599 enhancer-associated genes shared between prenatal and postnatal changes, representing a substantial fraction of each group (867 for prenatal, 875 for postnatal). These shared genes were enriched in synaptic signaling pathways related to glutamatergic, dopaminergic, and GABAergic transmission. The overlap between prenatal and postnatal effects suggests the persistence of a core regulatory program across different developmental stages. On the other hand, prenatal-specific enhancers are enriched for gene ontology terms related to forebrain and telencephalon development, while postnatal-specific enhancers are linked to axonogenesis and synapse organization. These patterns reflect distinct neurodevelopmental programs, with prenatal regulation driving early brain patterning and progenitor expansion, and postnatal regulation supporting synaptic refinement and network integration [ , ]. This stage specificity may arise from dynamic shifts in enhancer activity aligned with developmental priorities. Transcription factor (TF) motif analysis further supported this view. TFs such as SOX5, BCL6, EGR2, RHOX11, and PRRX2 were active across both developmental stages. Previous studies indicate that some of these TFs, including SOX5, BCL6 and EGR2 are altered in frontal cortex samples from both schizophrenia subjects and adult MIA mice [ , , , ]. The recurrence of these key neurodevelopmental TFs aligns with the shared enhancer–gene associations, indicating a common upstream regulatory architecture. To evaluate the relevance of these regulatory elements to human disease, we performed cross-species LD score regression, mapping mouse differential enhancer/promoter regions to the human genome and integrating GWAS summary statistics. We observed strong enrichment of prenatal enhancer regions for neuropsychiatric traits, including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and depression. Postnatal-related differential enhancer regions exhibited similarly high enrichment. While LD score enrichment does not establish causality, it provides evidence that MIA-related regulatory elements overlap with genetic risk loci for neuropsychiatric diseases. Our analysis also revealed enrichment of addiction-related pathways in both prenatal and postnatal effects of MIA, including those involved in morphine and nicotine addiction, suggesting that MIA may alter regulatory programs linked to substance use vulnerability. Previous studies have reported conflicting behavioral outcomes. For example, a study of prenatal LPS exposure showed no effect on cocaine self-administration [ ], suggesting that MIA alone may not enhance vulnerability to addiction. In contrast, another study demonstrated that while MIA increased the likelihood of acquiring cocaine self-administration, it did not influence the amount of cocaine intake once the behavior was established

neuropsychiatric diseases. Our analysis also revealed enrichment of addiction-related pathways in both prenatal and postnatal effects of MIA, including those involved in morphine and nicotine addiction, suggesting that MIA may alter regulatory programs linked to substance use vulnerability. Previous studies have reported conflicting behavioral outcomes. For example, a study of prenatal LPS exposure showed no effect on cocaine self-administration [ ], suggesting that MIA alone may not enhance vulnerability to addiction. In contrast, another study demonstrated that while MIA increased the likelihood of acquiring cocaine self-administration, it did not influence the amount of cocaine intake once the behavior was established [ ]. Moreover, when combined with adolescent alcohol exposure, MIA has been shown to increase alcohol intake and disrupt corticostriatal oscillations [ ]. These findings suggest that MIA may not directly induce addictive behaviors, but instead prime neural circuits involved in reward and reinforcement, thereby increasing sensitivity to later environmental challenges. Beyond pathways associated with reward processing, we also observed enrichment of broader GO categories such as brain development, nervous system development, and synaptic signaling, indicating that MIA impacts fundamental neurodevelopmental and synaptic organization processes. The transcriptional and epigenetic alterations identified in glutamatergic, GABAergic, and dopaminergic systems could directly affect neuronal excitability and circuit function, though the extent to which these molecular changes translate into behavioral outcomes remains unknown. Alternatively, they may reflect a primed state that increases vulnerability to subsequent stressors or environmental exposures [ , ]. Previous evidence suggests that maternal immune activation can reconfigure neuroimmune and synaptic systems, creating long-lasting sensitivity that remains latent until later challenges emerge [ , – ]. Early-life stress (ELS) and maternal immune activation share several convergent biological themes including the effects on hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal (HPA) axis pathways and dopaminergic circuits [ , – ]. Studies also show ELS related pathways including impaired cellular maintenance, metabolic dysfunction, and long-lasting glial or neuronal alterations [ – ]. We did not observe direct enrichment of HPA axis pathways, which are frequently implicated in ELS models [ , ], although we detected effects of MIA on neuronal alterations and dopaminergic circuits. In addition to these neuronal regulatory mechanisms, non-neuronal cells also play a central role in mediating and amplifying immune-driven effects on brain development [ ]. Although this study focused on NeuN + neuronal nuclei to capture gene regulatory changes linked to neuronal function, glial populations constitute an equally important component of the brain’s response to immune challenge. Microglia and astrocytes regulate synaptic development, cytokine signaling, and stress reactivity, and their dysfunction has been implicated in MIA-related and psychiatric phenotypes [ , , ]. Integrating glial-specific transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling in future work will be critical for resolving the full cellular spectrum of MIA-induced alterations. Maternal immune activation can lead to diverse outcomes among exposed offspring. Some develop strong behavioral or molecular alterations, while others remain unaffected or show adaptive responses [ , ]. This variation likely reflects differences in genetic background, immune activation strength and timing, and postnatal conditions [ ]. Maternal factors also shape offspring response: adequate micronutrient levels (vitamin D, iron, zinc), balanced omega-3 fatty acids, and effective antioxidant or anti-inflammatory systems promote resilience, whereas hypoferremia, gestational diabetes, stress, and microbiome imbalance increase risk [ , ]. Our study did not assess maternal health or nutrition, but these variables may influence offspring outcomes and should be considered in future work. Although resilience after MIA has been reported, studies directly examining resilience to depression-like effects are limited. Insights from depression and stress research suggest that stable HPA-axis control, efficient immune resolution, intact synaptic plasticity, and supportive environments can buffer against depressive outcomes [ , , ]. Future studies should explore these protective mechanisms within MIA models. Taken together, our study underscores the enduring impact of MIA on the epigenomic landscape of the developing brain, with both prenatal and postnatal stages contributing to long-term regulatory alterations in pathways critical for neuropsychiatric disease risk. By integrating transcriptomic, epigenomic, and cross-species analyses, we provide mechanistic insights into how early-life immune challenges shape brain function and vulnerability to psychiatric and substance use disorders. Our work defines the epigenomic framework linking MIA to altered gene regulation and highlights biological pathways for future mechanistic investigation. Finally, these findings highlight the importance of temporal context in neurodevelopmental risk, suggesting that interventions aimed at mitigating the effects of MIA may need to consider both gestational and early postnatal windows. chunks.content: Introduction Aortic diseases such as aortic aneurysm (AA), aortic dissection (AD), and atherosclerosis are the leading causes of morbidity and mortality worldwide. AA, as one of the serious life-threatening vascular diseases, can involve almost any portion of the aorta, with abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) being more common than thoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA). Combined, these pathologies cause over 25,000 U.S. deaths annually [ ]. AD, although less common (estimated incidence: 2.9–3.5/100,000 person-years), has a devastating short-term (30-day) mortality rate of up to 10 %–35 % despite optimal management [ ]. Aortic atherosclerosis is frequently a precursor for other vascular pathologies, affecting a large proportion of the elderly population and contributing significantly to cardiovascular disease burden [ ]. Present clinical approaches to the diagnosis of aortic disease are largely based on anatomic imaging modalities such as computed tomography (CT) angiography, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and ultrasound [ ]. These provide excellent structural detail but are of limited use for early disease detection, predicting biological activity, or even forecasting progression [ ]. Treatments are still unsatisfactory, and medications only tend to control risks (e.g., blood pressure control in AD) rather than target the underlying pathology of the disease. Surgery is still considered the gold standard treatment modality for severe disease, but it has a high risk of complications and might not be appropriate in every patient [ ]. In this clinical context, metabolomics has been proven to be an efficient approach for addressing unmet clinical needs in aortic diseases. As the comprehensive study of small-molecule metabolites, metabolomics offers a functional readout of cellular activity, integrating genetic, epigenetic, and environmental influences [ ]. Unlike other omics approaches, metabolomics reflects the downstream effects of all regulatory mechanisms and is therefore closer to the disease phenotype [ ]. Given that the metabolome is dynamic and sensitive to pathophysiologic changes, it could enable earlier identification of a disease process before structural changes become apparent [ ]. Most importantly, metabolites are bioactive molecules that directly participate in disease pathogenesis, making them both biomarkers and therapeutic targets. Technologically, advances in mass spectrometry (MS) and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) have significantly enhanced metabolomic analyses, increasing sensitivity and specificity [ ]. These advances have facilitated the application of metabolomics to vascular biology, revealing previously unrecognized metabolic perturbations in aortic diseases ( ) [ ], ]. Beyond simply cataloging metabolic alterations, this review argues that metabolomics illuminates convergent metabolic axes – most notably mitochondrial dysfunction and the diet-gut-vascular interplay. We posit that these axes represent tractable translational targets rather than passive biomarkers. Ultimately, we propose that a strategic pivot toward modulating the gut-vascular axis could enable next-generation therapeutic interventions, moving clinical management beyond its current reliance on hemodynamic control. Within this framework, we critically evaluate current metabolomics research, summarize disease-specific metabolic signatures, and explore their utility as diagnostic biomarkers. Finally, we address the biological and technical barriers to translation, particularly those related to multi-omics integration, to provide a roadmap for advancing precision medicine in aortic diseases. Metabolomics methodologies: technical framework Analytical platforms Parallel advances in analytical chemistry and bioinformatics have propelled the rapid evolution of metabolomics ( ) [ ]. The primary aim of metabolomics is to comprehensively characterize the metabolome in complex biological matrices such as serum, plasma, urine, and tissues. However, the chemical diversity and wide dynamic range of metabolite concentrations present considerable analytical challenges. To address this, sophisticated instrumental platforms are required, among which MS and NMR spectroscopy are the most widely adopted ( ). Liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) has become the leading platform in metabolomics due to its high sensitivity, broad dynamic range, and capacity to detect thousands of metabolites in a single run [ ]. It has an affinity toward polar and semi-polar metabolites, including amino acids, organic acids, nucleotides, and complex lipids. Coupling different chromatographic modes to high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) has also significantly expanded the coverage of the metabolome [ ]. Recently, combining ion mobility spectrometry (IMS) with multidimensional separation methods has greatly enhanced the ability to resolve and identify metabolites and offers unique benefits when applied to the study of complex specimens like the aorta. Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) is still one of the most robust and reproducible platforms for metabolomics analysis, especially for volatile and thermally stable compounds. Many metabolites require chemical derivatization to increase volatility, but GC-MS provides high chromatographic separation efficiency and can be used to analyze organic acids, fatty acids, sugars, and steroids [ ]. Furthermore, GC-MS has a standardized electron ionization mode for very accurate metabolite identification via large spectral libraries, providing advantages over more variable ionization methods used with LC-MS [ ]. NMR provides an extremely reproducible, quantitative method for metabolomics that requires little sample processing. The sensitivity is lower than that of MS-based methods, but NMR is suitable for detecting abundant metabolites in biofluids, preserving molecular structure,

volatile and thermally stable compounds. Many metabolites require chemical derivatization to increase volatility, but GC-MS provides high chromatographic separation efficiency and can be used to analyze organic acids, fatty acids, sugars, and steroids [ ]. Furthermore, GC-MS has a standardized electron ionization mode for very accurate metabolite identification via large spectral libraries, providing advantages over more variable ionization methods used with LC-MS [ ]. NMR provides an extremely reproducible, quantitative method for metabolomics that requires little sample processing. The sensitivity is lower than that of MS-based methods, but NMR is suitable for detecting abundant metabolites in biofluids, preserving molecular structure, and enabling de novo compound identification [ ], ]. The technique is nondestructive, with good quantitative accuracy, making it ideal for use in a clinical setting or as part of long-term studies. For aortic disease, NMR is routinely used to determine lipoprotein sub-classification and to monitor global changes in patients’ serum/plasma metabolism [ ]. Every approach has its strengths: LC-MS covers a wide range of metabolites but is sensitive only to some; GC-MS can provide highly reproducible analyses of selected metabolite types; and NMR offers reliable structure identification and absolute quantification. The combination of data from different platforms may provide a more holistic picture of perturbed metabolism in aortic disease, though it also poses significant bioinformatic challenges [ ]. Untargeted and targeted metabolomics In general, there are two main types of metabolomics approaches for studying aortic diseases: untargeted and targeted methods, which differ in how they function during analysis. Untargeted metabolomics is a discovery-driven approach to analyzing the full complement of metabolites in a given sample without prior selection. This hypothesis-generating approach enables us to obtain an unbiased view of altered metabolism, making it especially useful for discovering new pathophysiological mechanisms and unsuspected metabolic signatures in disease [ ]. Untargeted metabolomics studies identified disease-specific perturbations in metabolic profiles, including abnormal phospholipid metabolism and deregulated amino acid pathways in AAA and AD [ ], ]. The main drawback with this approach, however, is the annotation problem: in most cases, less than one-third of all detected features are reliably identifiable, which leaves the majority of metabolites unknown. In contrast, targeted metabolomics is hypothesis-driven, aiming to accurately quantify a priori-defined subset of metabolites relevant to specific pathways or putative disease mechanisms. Targeted metabolomics offers greater sensitivity, dynamic range, and quantitative accuracy, making it suitable for biomarker validation and pathway-focused studies [ ]. The most widely used platform in targeted metabolomics is multiple reaction monitoring (MRM) with triple-quadrupole mass spectrometry (TQMS), which allows the selective isolation and detection of precursor-product ion pairs for each metabolite, providing high selectivity and robustness [ ]. Recent advances in TQMS instrumentation, including improved ionization efficiencies and faster scan rates, enable simultaneous quantification of up to hundreds of metabolites. In aortic disease research, targeted metabolomics has played a key role in validating candidate biomarkers, including succinate in aortic aneurysm and dissection (AAD), and in validating metabolic alterations hypothesized in the first untargeted screening assays [ ]. As we will see below, when combined in series, these two methods provide an effective workflow: untargeted metabolomics generates new hypotheses and reveals global metabolic changes, whereas targeted metabolomics offers strong evidence for specific metabolites and pathways through quantification. Thus, such an integrated approach would be critical for gaining further mechanistic insight and for translating findings from metabolism into the clinical management of aortopathies. Data processing and analysis Raw metabolomics data require extensive preprocessing and rigorous statistical analysis to extract biologically meaningful information – steps essential to ensuring data quality, reproducibility, and interpretability [ ]. The first step is signal processing, which aims to maximize the number of true metabolites while minimizing technical noise. For MS data, this involves peak finding, peak alignment, deconvolution of coeluting ions, and integration of ion intensities; conversely, preprocessing for NMR spectra generally requires phase correction, baseline correction, and chemical shift calibration to standardize spectra across samples. To ensure data quality, QC samples, typically pooled from all the biological samples, are run at regular intervals for monitoring data stability. The relative standard deviation (RSD) of metabolite abundance values in QC samples is widely used to evaluate technical precision, with RSD<30 % usually deemed sufficient for untargeted profiling. Data gaps (e.g., low abundance undetected or instrument noise) are also an important issue. Imputing missing data is usually done by replacing it with a small non-zero value, using k-nearest neighbors, or machine-learning-based methods such as random forests [ ]. Normalization is then performed to minimize the non-biological variance introduced during sample preparation and analysis, while preserving biological differences. Popularly used approaches are the total-ion-current normalization, probabilistic quotient normalization, and internal-standard normalization [ ]. The metabolomics standards initiative has defined four levels of identification confidence, with Level 1 (identified compound), requiring agreement on at least two orthogonal properties (e.g., Level 1 (retention time, mass spectrum) with authentic standard); Level 2 (putatively annotated compound), where spectral characteristics match with spectral databases; Level 3 (putatively characterized compound class), where only the chemical class is known; and Level 4 (unknown compound), for unknown or unclassified metabolites. The analysis and understanding of metabolomics results depend on the use of bioinformatic resources to annotate metabolites, map them to pathways, and link them to other multi-omics data. Databases such as HMDB [ ], METLIN [ ], MassBank [ ], mzCloud [ ], and LIPID MAPS [ ] help identify metabolites and place them in the context of pathways. In aortic disease metabolomics, disease-specific metabolites are typically detected using a combination of targeted and untargeted approaches. Targeted workflows enable high-confidence (Level 1) identification against authentic standards using optimized procedures, whereas untargeted methods identify new modifications but with lower annotation confidence (Level 2–3). After identification, pathway annotation provides mechanistic insight by assigning metabolites to biochemical networks. Bioinformatics tools, e.g., MetaboAnalyst [ ], KEGG [ ], and MetExplore [ ] facilitate the statistical assessment of pathway perturbations and the visualization of network-level alterations, thereby providing context for placing this metabolic reprogramming within the larger picture of aortic disease pathobiology. Metabolic reprogramming in aortic pathogenesis Amino acid metabolism The metabolism of amino acids is one of the most severely affected processes in aortopathies and varies significantly across amino acid groups. Comprehensive metabolomics profiling has revealed marked disruptions in amino acid pathways that not only serve as potential biomarkers but also contribute directly to aortic pathophysiology. Sulfur-containing amino acids Methionine (Met) and cysteine (Cys), two sulfur-containing amino acids (SCAAs), are linked through SCAAs metabolism, which is an important hub in vascular biology that can produce either harmful or beneficial mediators, especially homocysteine (Hcy) and H 2 S. These pathways have a significant impact on the redox state of the cell and the ECM, as well as on inflammation pathways, suggesting their role in aortic disease. The clinical importance of this pathway is demonstrated by the fact that hyperhomocysteinemia (HHcy) has been recognized as a significant risk factor for cardiovascular and cerebrovascular disease in its own right, and that high plasma Hcy levels have been repeatedly implicated in the development and progression of AAD [ ], [ ], [ ], [ ], [ ], [ ]. Mechanistically, Hcy induces endothelial dysfunction through S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH) accumulation (an inhibitor of methyltransferases) and reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation via sulfhydryl auto-oxidation. Also, it disrupts aortic wall integrity by interfering with fibrillin-1 assembly in the ECM and activating MMP-2/9, thereby accelerating the destruction of elastic fibers [ ], ]. In contrast, the end product of the transsulfuration pathway (H 2 S) is generally considered vasoprotective, with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and cytoprotective properties. Enzymatic degradation of Hcy into H 2 S (primarily catalyzed by CSE) was considered a favorable detoxifying route, and pharmacological H 2 S donors might be able to counteract the pathological processes initiated by HHcy. However, a recent study by Bechelli et al. challenges this paradigm and shows that treatment with sodium thiosulfate (STS), an H 2 S-donor of clinical interest, dose-dependently exacerbated elastase-induced AAA in mice ( ) [ ]. These observations underscore that H 2 S plays a context-dependent role in vascular biology. Its overall effect will depend, amongst other things, on the disease model (hypertensive or normotensive), the cell of origin, the enzyme producer (CSE vs. CBS vs. 3-MST), the local concentration, and the disease phase (e.g., early inflammation vs. late remodeling). This interorgan network, in which intestinal citrulline is converted to arginine by the kidney, illustrates the systemic regulation of vascular health. Gln is one of the most important precursors of citrulline and can prevent experimental AAA by inhibiting VSMC apoptosis, suppressing M1 macrophage activation, and ameliorating oxidative stress and ECM degradation, reinforcing the therapeutic potential for targeting this larger metabolic network ( ). Glutamine and glutamate Gln is the most abundant circulating amino acid. It is mainly synthesized via skeletal muscle glutamine synthetase (GS), which employs circulating glutamate (Glu) secreted by organs such as the liver. In contrast, the liver produces Glu by deaminating Gln with glutaminase-2 (GLS2). The systemic glutamine homeostasis appears to exert a paradoxical effect on vascular remodeling, potentially altering our understanding of a high glutamine/glutamate ratio (GGR) as generally cardiometabolically protective [ ], [ ], [ ]. Although traditionally considered a good metabolic marker, recently we have shown that if this rise results from dysfunctional hepatic GLS2, then it signals pathology. In particular, defective hepatic glutaminolysis results in high plasma GGR yet paradoxically promotes atherogenesis by dysregulating extracellular matrix remodeling ( ) [ ]. This contradiction requires reviewing the actual role of Gln in AA, which shares some features with atherosclerosis but also differs from it. In particular, regarding aneurysmal formation, Gln supplementation could be protective by reducing oxidative stress, inhibiting VSMC apoptosis, and inhibiting MMP activity. Moreover, Gln metabolism modulates innate immunity, favoring a M2 anti-inflammatory macrophage phenotype, which may prevent destructive inflammation of the aortic wall [ ]. An important open issue concerns whether such local beneficial effects in the aneurysm microenvironment could offset, or be independent of, the system-wide deleterious impact observed in the setting of a high-GGR, GLS2-deficient condition. The fate of Glu itself is similarly important, particularly in its flux into proline synthesis for collagen maintenance. One path that may be particularly relevant to therapy is the enzyme-catalyzed conversion of glutamate to proline, a prerequisite substrate for collagen synthesis [ ]. Deficiency of mitochondrial NAD + thus forms an enzymatic bottleneck in this glutamate-to-proline pathway, eventually decreasing collagen III synthesis. This deficiency leads to degradation of the aorta’s extracellular matrix, thereby causing TAA and AAA [ ]. This suggests that increasing the rate of Glu entry into the proline pathway could be considered, possibly independently of the systemic GGR, as a valid approach to strengthen aorta wall strength. Branched-chain amino acids In addition to being the building blocks of proteins, Branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs, leucine, isoleucine, and valine) emerge as important signal molecules and biomarkers in cardiovascular metabolic disease states. The catabolism of these AAs is tightly coupled to mitochondrial function, and aberrant flux of BCAAs has been associated with a variety of cardiovascular diseases [ ], ]. Evidence is mounting that abnormal BCAAs metabolism plays a role in the development of AAD [ ], ]. Defective BCAA catabolism is not only an indicator but also an active promoter of VSMC dedifferentiation and media degeneration. As for endothelial cells (ECs), elevated BCAAs contribute to dysfunction by increasing ROS and peroxynitrite production [ ]. In addition, in VSMCs, the accumulation of BCAAs is due to the suppression of catabolic enzymes, which overactivates the mTOR signaling cascade. This metabolic-signaling axis leads to a pathogenic cascade of mitochondrial damage and inflammation and to a pathological shift towards a synthetic rather than a contractile phenotype, which is directly involved in the onset of AD [ ]. Such mechanistic understanding offers treatment possibilities, such as drug-based manipulation of the branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase kinase (BCKDK) to augment BCAAs catabolism, and/or inhibition of mTOR, which has proven effective at slowing the disease process ( ) [ ]. However, the upstream drivers of such a catabolic deficit are unclear, and translating these treatments should be approached with caution, given the widespread contribution of these pathways to whole-body metabolism. Mitochondrial dysfunction signatures TCA cycle metabolic reprogramming Beyond its established role in producing cellular energy, the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle also serves as an important node in intracellular signal transduction, with certain intermediates being crucial determinants of either protective or destructive events within the aorta. The protective effects of α-ketoglutarate (α-KG) are well substantiated for AAA. NR1D1 represses the TCA cycle enzyme aconitase-2 (ACO2), leading to mitochondrial dysfunction [ ]. Supplementation with α-KG, the direct downstream product of ACO2, rescues the defect and prevents AAA development [ ], ]. On the other hand, the accumulation of succinate (through oxoglutarate dehydrogenase, OGDH), or of citrate (ANK transporter deficiency), is a pro-inflammatory trigger. Mechanistically, succinate promotes mitochondrial ROS via the p38α-CREB-OGDH pathway in AAD [ ], and citrate accumulates to drive epigenetic reprogramming through histone acetylation, promoting a maladaptive VSMC phenotype [ ]. Hence, TCA cycle dysfunction in aortic disease is not characterized by a homogeneous inhibition; rather, it appears to be more of a reprogramming, shifting the ratios of some crucial intermediates ( ). Electron transport chain dysfunction Mitochondrial dysfunction, especially impairment of the electron transport chain (ETC) and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS), has become an important underlying process in the pathogenesis of many aortic diseases, such as AAD and atherosclerosis. In VSMCs, impaired OXPHOS, frequently triggered by nicotinamide phosphoribosyl transferase (NAMPT) deficiency, promotes cell senescence, DNA damage, and a significant shift from a contractile to a synthetic phenotype, which favors AAD development [ ]. Likewise, an integrative transcriptomic analysis of human ascending aortas showed that VSMCs undergo a dynamic phenotypic switch during AD, controlled by the activator protein-1 (AP-1) transcriptional factor complex [ ]. Pharmacologic enhancement of OXPHOS by coenzyme Q10 or inhibition of AP-1 blocked this phenotypic switch and attenuated aortic degeneration, significantly enhancing survival in a murine AD model. This identifies the TNF-OXPHOS-AP-1 axis as an important regulatory loop promoting AD pathogenesis. Similarly, macrophage ETC dysfunction resulting from oxidized LDL binding to CD36 diverts the cell’s metabolism away from producing ATP towards the generation of superoxide. This reprogrammed metabolism promotes NF-κB activation and supports chronic vascular inflammation, thereby driving accelerated plaque development [ ]. Together, ETC dysfunction thus represents an emerging common pathway in aortic disease involving all major vascular cells ( ). Dysregulated lipid metabolism and mitochondrial injury Apart from amino acid metabolism, the TCA cycle, and the ETC, dramatic changes in lipid metabolism represent another hallmark of aortic diseases, including adaptive changes in energy expenditure and dysregulated lipid signaling. Unlike the homogeneous view of metabolic suppression, context-specific activation of FAO in individual cells could even drive pathophysiology. For example, in aortic adventitial fibroblasts (AAF), upregulation of FAO machinery (carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A, CPT1A) increases ATP generation to support cell growth and the overproduction of ECM. This metabolic switch promotes vascular scarring, suggesting that elevated mitochondrial FAO, if harnessed by stromal cells, can be a deleterious response [ ]. In addition to bioenergetics, the accumulation of certain lipid species has a direct lipotoxic and inflammatory effect. Hypertriglyceridemia promotes AAA development and rupture by mechanically inhibiting lysyl oxidase (LOX) maturation and activity, thereby causing loss of structural integrity of the aortic wall [ ]. Ceramides, which are sphingolipids, have been identified as key mediators of vascular inflammation. These accumulate due to reduced catabolism or increased production, triggering inflammatory pathways and aggregating with leukocytes [ ]. Moreover, circulating ceramides act as endogenous ligands for G-protein-coupled receptors in ECs and macrophages, directly activating the NLRP3 inflammasome to maintain chronic vascular inflammation [ ]. Another axis of mitochondrial injury involves the dysregulation of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs). In atheroprone areas, the enzymatic metabolism of PUFAs to a pro-oxidant diol causes loss of protein-cholesterol associations in mitochondria, inhibition of Complex I, excess ROS, mitochondrial membrane depolarization, and activation of atheroprone transcriptional programs [ ]. This oxidative injury is also enhanced by lipid peroxidation; extracellular vesicles (EVs) rich in oxidized phospholipids promote iron accumulation and macrophage migration, thus aggravating MMP expression and the degradation of elastic fibers [ ]. In summary, dysregulated lipid metabolism drives aortic pathology through a dual mechanism: enhanced FAO, which fuels fibrosis, and toxic lipid accumulation, triggering mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammation ( ). Gut microbiota-derived metabolites In addition to intrinsic defects in mitochondrial and cellular metabolism, extrinsic factors significantly dictate the aortic wall’s metabolic status. Prominent among these are microbiota-derived metabolites, which systemically reprogram host immune responses and vascular metabolism [ ], ]. Trimethylamine N-oxide Trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) illustrates a mechanism by which gut microbes may broadly influence cardiometabolic disease. Dietary substrates containing trimethylamine (TMA) groups (e.g., choline and L-carnitine, abundant in red meat and dairy) are first metabolized by gut bacteria into TMA. This intermediate is subsequently taken up and oxidized in the liver by flavin monooxygenase 3 (FMO3) to form TMAO [ ], [ ], [ ]. Clinically, increased circulating TMAO is strongly linked to the presence and progression of aortic diseases [ ], [ ], [ ]. Mechanistically, TMAO contributes to aorta wall injury via several pathways. Primarily, it elicits a robust inflammatory response by activating the NLRP3 inflammasome, a mechanism that involves suppression of the SIRT3-SOD2 pathway, leading to increased mitochondrial ROS levels [ ]. Concurrently, and perhaps more critically, TMAO directly inflicts proteotoxic endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress on VSMCs. It robustly activates the PERK-eIF2α-ATF4/5-CHOP branch of the unfolded protein response (UPR), ultimately driving VSMC apoptosis and structural vessel degeneration ( ) [ ]. Short-chain fatty acids In contrast to TMAO, short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) – principally acetate, propionate, and butyrate – represent a class of microbiota-derived metabolites that generally exert vasoprotective effects [ ]. Produced through bacterial fermentation of dietary fiber, SCFAs act via dual mechanisms: as endogenous histone deacetylases (HDACs) inhibitors, that modulate epigenetic landscapes, and as ligands for specific G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs, particularly GPR41, GPR43, and GPR109A) that transduce anti-inflammatory [ ], ]. Pre-clinical studies highlight the therapeutic relevance of the SCFA-GPCR axis in vascular disease. For instance, propionate supplementation attenuates hypertension and vascular damage by expanding regulatory T cell (Treg) populations and suppressing vascular inflammation. [ ]. In the context of AAA, propionate expands the Treg pool within the colonic lamina propria to the site of aortic inflammation to exert suppressive effects [ ]. Similarly, butyrate ameliorated atherosclerotic inflammation by modulating macrophage polarization via a novel GPR43/HDAC-miRNA regulatory axis [ ]. In AD, butyrate uniquely halts disease progression by preserving the contractile, differentiated phenotype of VSMCs in a GPR41-dependent manner ( ) [ ]. Secondary bile acids Secondary bile acids (BAs, e.g., deoxycholic acid, lithocholic acid, ursodeoxycholic acid [UDCA]) are generated by the gut microbiota through the deconjugation and dehydroxylation of primary BAs [ ]. These microbially modified metabolites potently activate host receptors, most prominently the farnesoid X receptor (FXR) and the membrane-bound TGR5, thereby controlling several inflammatory pathways [ ]. Dysregulated BAs are increasingly implicated in cardiovascular diseases [ ]. The hydrophilic BAs, particularly UDCA and its taurine-conjugated form, tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA), are increasingly recognized as vasoprotective agents. UDCA counteracts oxidative stress and inhibits VSMC apoptosis, a key event in AAD pathogenesis, by strongly upregulating the antioxidant transcription factor NRF2 [ ]. Notably, UDCA serum levels are clinically reduced in AAD patients; its replenishment exerts a protective effect on AAD via the intestinal FXR/ceramide synthase two axis, revealing a gut-specific signaling pathway [ ]. Furthermore, functioning as a chemical chaperone, TUDCA suppresses angiotensin II-induced AAD development by reducing ER stress in vascular cells, providing a counter-regulatory mechanism against TMAO-driven vascular injury ( ) [ ]. Tryptophan-derived metabolites Tryptophan (Trp) metabolism represents a critical pathway co-regulated by the host and microbes. Dietary Trp is metabolized by intestinal bacteria into indole and its derivatives, such as indole-3-propionic acid (IPA), indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), and indole-3-aldehyde (I3A) [ ]. These bacterial metabolites enter the circulation and activate the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR), a ligand-activated transcription factor essential for vascular homeostasis [ ]. Simultaneously, host cells metabolize Trp through the kynurenine pathway, which is regulated by indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase (IDO) and produces distinct bioactive metabolites, like 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid (3-HAA) [ ]. The balance between these bacterial (indole) and host (kynurenine) Trp metabolism dictates aortic health. Regarding bacteria-produced indole metabolites, increasing evidence indicates a protective role for these metabolites in several inflammatory diseases [ ]. Clinically, IPA is markedly downregulated in patients with CAD, with its circulating levels inversely correlating with atherosclerosis prevalence and severity; experimentally, IPA alleviates plaque burden by promoting macrophage reverse cholesterol transport [ ]. Conversely, host-derived 3-HAA promotes angiotensin II-induced AAA formation by inducing oxidative stress and matrix degradation [ ]. Crucially, high-fat diets can increase intestinal IDO activity, shifting Trp metabolism toward detrimental kynurenine production, whereas IDO inhibition or indole supplementation restores the balance and attenuates vascular inflammation ( ) [ ]. Although strong correlations exist between intestinal metabolites (especially TMAO and SCFAs) and aortic disease in many studies, it should be emphasized that most of this clinical evidence is observational. The field currently lacks large-scale human interventional studies demonstrating direct reversal of disease by modulating those metabolites. In addition, profound compositional dissimilarities between the murine and human gut microbiome create a significant “translational gap,” challenging the direct extrapolation from the pre-clinical setting, which is often very homogeneous, to the heterogeneous environment of the human gut. Metabolite-directed therapeutic targets Metabolism is profoundly reprogrammed in aortic disease; changes in the abundance of individual metabolites can serve as a readout of disease progression or as a therapeutic intervention point. We draw together such data from multiple disease states to identify commonalities and differences that might inform the metabolic basis of AAA, TAA, AD, and atherosclerosis. For brevity, we present selected examples of metabolite changes along with the corresponding quality of evidence for associated markers, associated pathophysiological roles, and/or potential therapeutic targets in . This conceptual framework emphasizes that there is no distinction between developing a therapy and identifying a biomarker, thereby setting the stage for an in-depth discussion of treatment options. Targeting metabolic enzymes The discovery and characterization of dysregulated metabolism in aortic disease have revealed an attractive landscape for enzymetargeted therapies; evidence presented in metabolomics methodologies: technical framework has highlighted dramatic changes to central pathways, including glycolysis, the TCA cycle, amino acid metabolism, and microbiota-associated metabolism, that maintains pathological vascular remodeling. Thus, targeting these key enzymes in these pathways presents an attractive opportunity to reverse disease-driving metabolic programs. The glycolytic enzyme pyruvate kinase muscle isozyme 2 (PKM2) appears to be a pleiotropic regulator in many cells that promotes the progression of aortic disease. In VSMCs, deficiency of the E3 ubiquitin ligase March2 attenuates PKM2 dimer-to-tetramer conversion, exacerbating glucose metabolic reprogramming and promoting histone H3K18 lactylation, which in turn facilitates a p53-mediated apoptotic transcriptional program in AD. Administration of TEPP-46, a specific PKM2 activator that promotes its tetramerization, markedly alleviates AAD pathology [ ]. Beyond VSMCs, PKM2 expression is elevated in infiltrating T lymphocytes within vascular lesions. T-cell-specific PKM2 deficiency significantly reduces the incidence of elastase-induced AAA and attenuates macrophage infiltration into the vascular adventitia. Mechanistically, PKM2 activation in T cells promotes AAA progression via EVs, leading to redox imbalance and stimulating macrophage migration [ ]. Targeting the TCA cycle also holds therapeutic promise. The enzyme ACO2 is transcriptionally repressed by NR1D1, contributing to mitochondrial dysfunction during AAA formation. NR1D1 deficiency restores ACO2 expression and mitochondrial function in early stages of disease. Consistent with a protective role, supplementation with α-KG, a direct product of ACO2 activity, prevents and treats AAA in mice by suppressing oxidative stress and macrophage infiltration [ ]. In contrast, succinate-producing TCA enzyme OGDH promotes AAD via a p38α-CREB-OGDH axis, amplifying mitochondrial ROS in macrophages, introducing another actionable node [ ]. Enzymes involved in the regulation of amino acid metabolism also provide other therapeutic targets. Arginase is a manganese-dependent enzyme that catalyses the hydrolysis of L-arginine into ornithine and urea. It has two isoforms (ARG1 and ARG2) that play distinct roles in vascular pathophysiology [ ]. ARG1 increases the stability of atheromatous plaques by down-regulating inflammatory cytokines secretion and inducing smooth muscle cell proliferation, although ARG2 controls Parkin-mediated p32 degradation and thus Ca 2+ -dependent eNOS activation in ECs [ ], ]. Another key enzyme, IDO, catalyzes the rate-limiting step in the kynurenine pathway of Trp catabolism. The Trp metabolite 3-HAA activates NF-κB signaling and upregulates MMP2 expression in VSMCs, suggesting that inhibition of IDO or downstream kynurenine pathway metabolites could mitigate AAA development [ ]. Furthermore, targeting BCAAs catabolism, for instance by inhibiting BCKDK to boost BCAAs oxidation, represents a promising strategy to attenuate mTOR hyperactivation and VSMC dysfunction in AD [ ]. Beyond central carbon metabolism, enzymes involved in mitochondrial FAO and microbiota-host co-metabolism present novel targets. Impairment of CPT-I, the rate-limiting enzyme in fatty acid β-oxidation, leads to toxic lipid accumulation and exacerbates bioenergetic deficit. Restoring CPT-I activity via PPAR-β/δ agonism has been shown to ameliorate endothelial dysfunction [ ]. Impairment of CPT-I, the rate-limiting enzyme in fatty acid β-oxidation, leads to toxic lipid accumulation and exacerbates bioenergetic deficit. Restoring CPT-I activity via PPAR-β/δ agonism has been shown to ameliorate endothelial dysfunction [ ]. Similarly, targeting the gut microbial enzymes involved in TMA production, such as microbial cutC/D lyases, offers an innovative approach to reduce circulating TMAO levels and attenuate its pro-apoptotic and inflammatory effects on the aortic wall [ ], ]. A second class of drug targets is epigenetic enzymes, which communicate with or are regulated by metabolism and thereby respond more directly to epimutations caused by metabolites. HDACs, including SIRT1 and HDAC4, regulate the expression of metabolic enzymes in VSMCs and inflammatory cells. Recently, it has been shown that intracellular citrate accumulation – driven by the loss of the citrate transporter ANK – increases histone acetylation on H3K23, H3K27, and H4K5. This metabolite-mediated epigenetic change drives the development of a pro-inflammatory VSMC phenotype. It accelerates aneurysmal progression, suggesting that targeting the citrate-ACLY axis and/or individual HDACs may be a therapeutic strategy [ ]. Inhibiting these metabolic enzymes has several potential advantages, such as selectivity of action and a relatively mature pharmacological discovery process; however, important hurdles remain, such as the possibility of off-target activity due to the widespread expression of many metabolic enzymes and the requirement for tissue-specific delivery approaches in order to avoid global disruption of metabolism. The future success of these approaches may depend on creating cell-type-specific delivery and multiple enzymes targeting to address the interdependent nature of metabolic dysfunction seen in aortic disease. Diet-microbiota-metabolite axis interventions Traditional pharmacologic interventions are mostly focused on controlling blood pressure (i.e., antihypertensives), but do not halt or reverse the metabolic inflammation that is driving the aortic wall disintegration in the first place. Direct modulation of these global metabolic pathways can be challenging and lead to unwanted side effects; therefore, strategies that alter the larger diet-gut-vascular axis are of growing interest as next-generation therapies. This strategy is designed to remodel the host’s metabolic microenvironment – an important driver for aortic disease – via dietary modification, supplementation with beneficial microbial metabolites, or direct microbial community engineering to address the underlying cause of pathology that is not addressed by current standards of care regimens. Diet represents an obvious starting point to reduce harmful microbiota-derived metabolites, as in the case of restricting consumption of TMA precursor nutrients, such as choline or L-carnitine that are present abundantly in red meats and dairy products; L-carnitine can be transformed into TMA by gut microflora and then oxidized into TMAO in the liver, a compound highly associated with vascular inflammation, ER stress, and AA development. Dietary restriction of L-carnitine might thus also dampen the vascular damage induced by TMAO. In addition, 3,3-dimethyl-1-butanol (DMB), a choline analogue and microbial TMA lyase inhibitor, decreases TMAO production and prevents atherosclerosis and aneurysm development in pre-clinical models, underscoring its potential as an active food component for the prevention of other metabolic risk factors beyond dyslipidemia [ ], ]. Besides inhibiting deleterious metabolites, another simple method to treat blood vessels is to selectively deliver beneficial bacterial products (postbiotics). SCFAs, such as acetate, propionate, or butyrate, have pleiotropic protective effects. While acetate supplementation has been demonstrated to decrease BP in hypertensive models [ ], as with the traditional treatment goal of controlling hemodynamic, it also has wider-ranging beneficial effects. For example, propionate increases regulatory T-cell numbers and reduces AAA development [ ], whereas butyrate prevents atherosclerosis by altering macrophage polarization via a GPR43/HDAC-miRNA axis [ ]. Likewise, IPA, a Trp-derived bacterial metabolite, promotes cholesterol efflux from macrophages through the miR-142-5p/ABCA1 pathway [ ]. Taken together, these findings suggest that manipulating the gut metabolome offers vascular protection through anti-inflammatory and anti-remodeling mechanisms, complementing conventional antihypertensive therapies. A more global method of remodeling the gut metabolome, fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT), attempts to restore an otherwise healthy microbiome. In studies using atherosclerosis-prone mouse models, it has been shown that transferring microbiota from wild-type to CTRP9 knockout mice reduces disease severity, whereas transferring CTRP9-KO microbiota aggravates lesions in wild-type recipient mice [ ]. Preliminary human studies are beginning to investigate the potential viability of FMT; e.g., one recent randomized trial on hypertensive subjects found a temporary lowering of blood pressure after FMT, proving initial safety, although not long-term [ ]. Despite being in the research phase of aortic disease, FMT shows promise to restore desirable microbiota functionality and global metabolite profiles.
