More than half of the total information sources (57%) utilized data from the DUMA program, including almost 70% of information sources from NSW, WA, Queensland, and SA ( ). Information on the determinants of health Information on specific health determinants varied considerably ( ). Each information source included details of between one and 22 determinants of interest. Most sources provided information on individual characteristics of detainees such as gender, age, and Indigenous status, but very few provided information on the country of birth (n = 8) or ethnicity of detainees (n = 8). No information sources were identified that included information on the refugee or migration status of detainees. Some socioeconomic determinants were reported frequently, such as employment status (n = 60), educational attainment (n = 48), housing (n = 51), and previous history of imprisonment (n = 47). No sources reported information related to food security, and very few reported income (n = 2) or the residential neighborhood of people in police custody facilities (n = 3). Health behaviors commonly associated with criminal behavior (the focus of most DUMA-derived literature) were reported most frequently: 126 information sources reported illicit substance use and 80 reported alcohol use. Sexual practices were reported in 22 information sources, almost exclusively (n = 21) in the context of reporting the number of people in police custody facilities engaged in sex work or exchanging sex for drugs. Sources reporting on diet (n = 19) and exercise patterns (n = 15) did so in the context of discussing the quality of food and access or lack of access to exercise spaces in police custody facilities. Very few (n = 7) information sources reported tobacco use. Relatively few information sources reported on psychological distress (n = 27) or isolation (n = 12) of people in police custody facilities. Of the environmental determinants reported, most were about access to health services while in police custody facilities (n = 27), followed by the duration of time spent in these facilities (n = 22). When assessing the co-occurrence of health determinants ( ), clusters of determinants were aligned with the key areas of the DUMA program, including individual characteristics (age, gender, Indigenous status), socioeconomic factors (level of education, employment status, housing and previous imprisonment), and alcohol and other drug use. When comparing the co-occurrence of determinants between information sources that utilized DUMA data ( ) and sources that used other data ( ) differences were observed. First, information sources that utilized DUMA data did not report on the environmental conditions in police custody facilities. Second, the environmental conditions of police custody facilities were a common key focus in non-DUMA information sources. Third, non-DUMA sources had more commonly reported psychosocial and structural safety determinants of health, such as the presence of psychological distress or exposure to violence. Information on health conditions In total, 85 information sources included quantitative or qualitative descriptions of illnesses or diseases in people in police custody (65 grey literature and 20 academic publications). Information sources that included data on health conditions most frequently reported those belonging to Chapter 6 of the ICD-11, which includes mental health, behavioral or neurodevelopmental disorders ( ), including drug dependence. This finding was consistent across both academic and grey literature information sources (see respective tabs of ). Nearly all information sources (n = 84) that contained health condition data, included information on at least one mental health, behavioral or neurodevelopmental condition. Other frequently described conditions were from Chapter 22 “Injury, poisoning or certain other consequences of external causes” and Chapter 23 “External causes of morbidity or mortality”. No information sources described people in police custody facilities with conditions from 10 chapters of ICD-11 ( ). Information on causes of death In total, 41 information sources discussed deaths in police custody. Of these, 39 included specific causes of death which could be mapped to ICD-11. Of the sources about deaths in police custody, 30 used data directly from the NDICP. Very few sources (n = 8) reported on deaths in police custody where specific causes of death were mentioned and where the deaths or injuries occurred in police facilities [ , , – ]. This was in part due to most sources reporting data from NDICP, which includes in their definition of police custody those being pursued, apprehended, or transported to custodial facilities, and does not disaggregate cause of death data by those held in police custodial facilities. Therefore, information on causes of death for individuals in police custody frequently included deaths due to gunshot wounds or motor vehicle accidents during pursuit or apprehension of suspects. Aside from the yearly NDICP reports, some sources did not differentiate causes of death that occurred while in police

occurred in police facilities [ , , – ]. This was in part due to most sources reporting data from NDICP, which includes in their definition of police custody those being pursued, apprehended, or transported to custodial facilities, and does not disaggregate cause of death data by those held in police custodial facilities. Therefore, information on causes of death for individuals in police custody frequently included deaths due to gunshot wounds or motor vehicle accidents during pursuit or apprehension of suspects. Aside from the yearly NDICP reports, some sources did not differentiate causes of death that occurred while in police custody compared to after recent contact with police [ , ], or causes of death of people in police custody facilities rather than other custodial settings [ , ]. For sources that discussed deaths occurring in police custody facilities, causes of death were wide ranging and included death from injuries (either self-inflicted, or due to assault), ischemic heart disease, respiratory failure, hanging, drug withdrawal or overdose, pneumonia, unexpected death in epilepsy, sepsis, and brain hemorrhage [ , , – ]. Discussion The aim of this scoping review was to identify and describe the available information on the health and determinants of health of individuals in police custody in Australia. We reviewed 172 information sources that met our inclusion criteria and identified four key findings. First, the available information is dominated by grey literature publications and more than half of all publications used data from a single source – the DUMA program. Having more than half of all information sources on this topic from this single source raises several issues. The DUMA program is not intended to be a representative sample of people in police custody facilities in Australia, especially given it does not collect data from every state and territory. In the latest yearly report published in 2022, data was collected from five metropolitan sites (Adelaide, Bankstown, Brisbane, Perth and Surry Hills) and, on average, 20% of potentially eligible individuals were deemed unfit for participation in the study [ ]. This determination is made by the police officer in charge based on the “level of risk” a detainee may pose to an interviewer [ ]. In addition, in more recent years, the DUMA program has excluded juvenile detainees. Importantly, except where a specific health addendum questionnaire was added, the DUMA program only provided indirect evidence on the health of people in police custody facilities related to select socioeconomic determinants of health, substance use, and self-reported substance dependence. The lack of peer-reviewed, academic literature further highlights a lack of rigorous and targeted information on the health of people in police custody facilities in Australia and raises the possibility that researchers face barriers accessing participants in this setting [ ]. We were only able to identify 31 academic sources published over a 25-year period. Second, there is limited breadth of information available on the determinants of health and health status of people in police custody facilities. While many information sources included basic demographics, select socioeconomic determinants, and alcohol and illicit drug use data, there was sparse reporting of other important determinants of health such as tobacco use, diet, exercise, stress, and exposure to violence. Information sources including data on health conditions most commonly focused on a single aspect of health – mental health. We identified almost twice as many sources that included information on mental health conditions than for all other health conditions combined. In addition, we identified no general health needs analyses or health surveys that aimed to capture the burden of disease among police detainees. One source from the Australian Capital Territory audited the activities and duties of police custody forensic physicians, which may have provided an indirect indication on the most common health conditions in this population, but unfortunately did not disclose the diagnoses of patients seen by the service [ ]. The information gaps identified reflect priorities on data collection and reporting rather than an absence of health issues. Surveillance systems have historically prioritized substance use and demographic profiling over comprehensive health assessments, resulting in a literature base that disproportionately reports on mental health while neglecting physical health, psychosocial factors, and environmental conditions. Third is the limited systematic reporting of patterns of deaths in custody. While individual investigations into deaths and coroners’ reports were not included in our review, we identified 41 information sources that discussed deaths in police custody facilities. However, 30 of these only used data from the NDICP, where the specific causes of deaths for those that died while in police facility cells could not be disaggregated from those that died while being pursued or arrested by police. Many more people die in Australia each year while being pursued or arrested by police than those that die in police custody facilities [ ]. Where deaths

reporting of patterns of deaths in custody. While individual investigations into deaths and coroners’ reports were not included in our review, we identified 41 information sources that discussed deaths in police custody facilities. However, 30 of these only used data from the NDICP, where the specific causes of deaths for those that died while in police facility cells could not be disaggregated from those that died while being pursued or arrested by police. Many more people die in Australia each year while being pursued or arrested by police than those that die in police custody facilities [ ]. Where deaths in custodial facilities rather than during pursuit or arrest is the primary interest, the utility of the yearly aggregate data reported through the NDICP becomes extremely limited. Our findings contrast with the literature and information available from other high-income, Western countries, where large studies have assessed the health needs of police detainees. For example, in the Netherlands, multiple studies have compared the medical complaints and presentations of police detainees with the general population [ , ]. These studies have identified that compared to the general population, police detainees are more likely to be clinically underweight, have chronic pulmonary problems, chronic joint inflammation, hypertension, and serious heart conditions [ ]. In the UK, police detainees were found to have high rates of existing physical illnesses, undiagnosed and untreated acute conditions, in addition to higher rates of psychiatric illness than the general population [ , ]. In France, one study reported that somatic diagnoses were even higher than psychiatric diagnoses in their police custody population [ ]. Implications This review has implications for guiding further research and advocacy. First, we recommend the expansion of academic research into the health and determinants of health of people in police custody, beyond its current scope of mental health and substance dependence. General health needs analyses of this population, like those completed in the UK, Netherlands and France would provide important data for evaluating the services responsible for detainee health and informing quality improvements. Second, we recommend the adoption of a systematic approach for data collection and public reporting on the health of police detainees. The establishment of a minimum data set for health screening, and implementation of health surveillance would increase transparency, and enable evidence-based policy development to improve health outcomes among detainees. Third, we recommend the further operationalization of Australia’s Optional Protocol to the Convention Against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (OPCAT) obligations. Although Australia ratified OPCAT in 2017, it remains in breach of its obligations, with three jurisdictions (Victoria, New South Wales, and Queensland) not yet represented by the National Preventative Mechanism (NPM) as of 2025 [ ]. OPCAT related inspections and reports have already started to improve transparency into the conditions in police custody in the Australian Capital Territory and external Australian Territories [ , , , ]. We recommend the expansion of these inspections to all police custody facilities, and the consistent publication of inspection reports. Limitations This review has several limitations. First, due to resource limitations, data charting was completed by a single author and double checked by a second author, as opposed to the preferred method of double blinded data extraction with reconciliation. This may have increased the risk of data charting errors. Second, the scope of this review was limited to exclude coroner reports and investigations into single deaths in custody. Accordingly, the findings related to deaths in police custody facilities and their cause of death should be interpreted cautiously. This is especially important given many information sources we identified did not disaggregate deaths that occurred in police custody facilities from deaths during other interactions with police. Instead, other sources which exclusively focus on summarizing the findings from coroner reports on deaths in custody in Australia, should be consulted for further information on this topic [ , , ]. Third, we chose to investigate a discrete list of determinants of health, based on the AIHW framework, to limit this scope of work to an achievable size. For example, determinants relevant to detainees’ families (such as a history of childhood trauma, family history of incarceration, marital status, or having dependent children) and environmental determinants (such as access to natural light, or privacy in showering and bathroom facilities) were not included in this review. Fourth, we acknowledge that the exclusion of information sources that did not include primary data means some important perspectives and insights into the health of people in police custody may have been missed. For example, during screening we encountered several articles from the criminology, sociology, and legal fields, that explored systemic racism and structural issues within the criminal legal system. Fifth, we limited our analysis to information sources published from 2000. While this decision improved the feasibility of the review, the

Fourth, we acknowledge that the exclusion of information sources that did not include primary data means some important perspectives and insights into the health of people in police custody may have been missed. For example, during screening we encountered several articles from the criminology, sociology, and legal fields, that explored systemic racism and structural issues within the criminal legal system. Fifth, we limited our analysis to information sources published from 2000. While this decision improved the feasibility of the review, the shortened timeframe may have meant that our study missed important insights from earlier information sources. Conclusion This comprehensive review mapped the currently available information on the health and determinants of health of people in police custody in Australia, and found that it is fragmented, predominantly derived from a single program, and focused on mental health and substance use. To better direct health service design, monitoring, and evaluation, we call for more transparent publication of health data of people in police custody facilities, particularly where key information is lacking, such as for physical health conditions. Increased transparency and information generation will be critical for providing an environment conducive to promoting rather than undermining the health of people in police custody facilities. chunks.content: Research in context Evidence before this study We searched major databases, including PubMed, EMBASE, SCOPUS, Google Scholar, and the Cochrane Library using the MeSH terms “multiple sclerosis” OR “neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders” OR “NMOSD” OR “MOG antibody disease” OR “demyelinating diseases” AND “registry” (last search: 27 August 2025). The search yielded 2780 articles. After removal of duplicates and exclusion of publications not focused on registries, 398 articles were relevant to registries of multiple sclerosis and other demyelinating disorders. Several established registries were identified, including NARCOMS (USA), MSBase (global), OFSEP (France), the Big MS Data Network, and national registries from Denmark, Sweden, Switzerland, Germany, Norway, Italy, Poland, Canada, China, Argentina and Iran, as well as the UK MS Register, Australian MS Longitudinal Study, Spanish REEM, and Czech ReMuS. Regional collaborations such as MENACTRIMS in the Middle East and North Africa also contribute valuable data. Collectively, these registries have provided high-quality real-world evidence on epidemiology, natural history, treatment outcomes, and long-term prognosis of multiple sclerosis and related demyelinating disorders. In contrast, studies from India have been limited to single-centre cohorts of patients with multiple sclerosis, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, or MOG antibody associated disease and there is no large prospective data from a nationwide multicentric registry of patients. Added value of this study The Indian Multiple Sclerosis and Allied Demyelinating Disorders Registry and Research Network (IMSRN) is a, multicentric, prospective registry for demyelinating disorders in India. It systematically captures demographic, clinical, imaging, laboratory, treatment, and outcome data across a diverse population that has been underrepresented in global research. IMSRN thus provides a prospective dataset from South-East Asia, enabling comparisons with international registries and offering insights into regional disease patterns, diagnostic practices, and therapeutic approaches. Implications of all the available evidence Collectively, evidence from global registries demonstrates how systematic, prospective data collection can clarify the natural history of demyelinating disorders, evaluate long-term treatment outcomes, and guide treatment decisions. Until now, this evidence has largely come from Europe, North America, and other high-income regions. The IMSRN fills a gap by providing prospective data from India, a country with unique ethnic, environmental, and socioeconomic contexts. When integrated with existing international networks, these data will enable meaningful cross-population comparisons, highlight regional variations in disease burden and treatment access, and support the development of equitable and contextually relevant health policies. Introduction Multiple sclerosis (MS), neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders (NMOSD), myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody associated disease (MOGAD), acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) etc., are some of the key central nervous system (CNS) demyelinating disorders. These conditions show substantial heterogeneity in clinical presentation, disease course, and treatment response, making region-specific epidemiological and real-world data essential for guiding diagnosis and management. To date, only limited studies from India have described the clinical features, disease course, and treatment patterns in these patients, and most have been restricted by small sample sizes and short follow-up. , , , , Consequently, there remains a critical gap in evidence, underscoring the need for large-scale, nationwide data with longitudinal follow-up to more accurately define disease characteristics, guide clinical management, and add to the existing world literature. The Indian Multiple Sclerosis And Allied Demyelinating Disorders Registry and Research Network (IMSRN) is a database for MS and allied demyelinating disorders ( https://imsrn.icmr.org.in/ ). The registry was initiated in August 2021 and prospectively collects standardised longitudinal data from 22 collaborating centres across the country, including demographics, clinical phenotypes, relapse details, treatments, laboratory evaluation, biobanking, pregnancy outcomes, and imaging to characterise long-term disease behaviour and outcomes. The present study describes the demographic, clinical, laboratory, treatment characteristics, and follow-up data of patients enrolled in the IMSRN and summarises the relative distribution and key features of major disease phenotypes (MS, NMOSD, MOGAD, and others) recruited until 25 October 2025, thereby providing an overview of real-world data in this cohort. Methods The IMSRN is a hospital-based registry that currently includes 22 sites. The sites were selected based upon region, patient volume and presence of a neurologist with a special interest in these disorders. These are tertiary referral institutes situated in the northern, southern, western, and eastern parts of India. Patients of all ages, including both paediatric and adult patients, were eligible for inclusion in the registry. Following informed consent, patients with CNS demyelinating disorders are recruited into the registry. An outline of the registry, data collection methods and follow up has been published previously. The current study is a prospective, observational registry-based analysis of patients recruited between 16 August 2021 and 25 October 2025. The diagnosis of MS was made according to the 2017 revisions of the McDonald criteria. NMOSD was diagnosed using the 2015 International Panel for NMO Diagnosis (IPND) criteria. MOGAD was diagnosed according to the International MOGAD Panel proposed criteria ; for patients enrolled before the publication of these criteria, the diagnosis was based on compatible clinical and radiological features

disorders are recruited into the registry. An outline of the registry, data collection methods and follow up has been published previously. The current study is a prospective, observational registry-based analysis of patients recruited between 16 August 2021 and 25 October 2025. The diagnosis of MS was made according to the 2017 revisions of the McDonald criteria. NMOSD was diagnosed using the 2015 International Panel for NMO Diagnosis (IPND) criteria. MOGAD was diagnosed according to the International MOGAD Panel proposed criteria ; for patients enrolled before the publication of these criteria, the diagnosis was based on compatible clinical and radiological features in conjunction with MOG-IgG seropositivity. ADEM was diagnosed according to the International Pediatric Multiple Sclerosis Study Group (IPMSSG) criteria. Across all participating sites, AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG testing was performed using a fixed cell-based assay (Euroimmun) in accredited laboratories with external quality assurance. Antibody testing data were recorded from serum samples in the registry. Patients who did not meet the diagnostic criteria for NMOSD (seropositive and seronegative), MS, or MOGAD were categorised under “other” demyelinating disorders. The “other” group includes double seronegative myelitis, double seronegative optic neuritis, double seronegative longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (LETM), seronegative LETM with other CNS involvement, double seronegative opticospinal syndrome, double seronegative brainstem demyelination, tumefactive demyelinating lesions (TDL), and other unclassified CNS demyelinating disorders. Details of patients’ demographics, family history, clinical disease history, including disease onset, relapses, investigative work-up done, medication use (current and previous), assessment on various scales, disability status, and imaging details are recorded both in a print version of the case record form and online on the IMSRN database portal. Gender is self-reported using a structured questionnaire with response options of male, female, and others. Socioeconomic status was evaluated using Kuppuswamy scale. The details are filled as per the standard operating procedure manual outlining all definitions of variables. The anonymised imaging is uploaded in a DICOM format on an OSIRIX enabled database portal ( https://www.osirix-viewer.com/ ), and details on predefined variables of imaging are entered on the database. The clinical diagnosis as recorded is based on the decision of the treating neurologist judged by the clinical features, imaging, and laboratory details using standard diagnostic criteria. Follow-up data is collected every six months or earlier as indicated. Each patient is enquired about the clinical status, medication-related issues, any relapse or disease worsening, pregnancy, and assessment on various scales, some being mandatory and others optional for a six-month or 12-month follow-up. Follow-up details on imaging, if done in the interim, are also recorded. The study is monitored by a task force committee of the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), which periodically reviews the progress of the registry ( ). Statistical analysis Descriptive statistics were performed and are presented as mean ± SD or median (interquartile range) for continuous variables, and as count with percentages for categorical variables. Group comparisons were performed using the Student's t test or Mann–Whitney U test for continuous variables, and the chi-square test for categorical variables. Shapiro–Wilk test was used to assess the normality of continuous variables. Temporal trend analyses were performed by stratifying patients into four symptom onset-year cohorts: before 2010, 2010–2014, 2015–2019, and after 2019. Diagnostic delay was assessed by calculating the duration (in days) between first symptom onset and confirmed diagnosis for each cohort, using Kaplan–Meier curves. DMT utilisation patterns were evaluated across the same cohorts by computing the proportion of patients receiving each DMT. These analyses were descriptive in nature. Longitudinal follow-up data were analysed in patients with MS to assess disease stability using EDSS scores, and within-patient changes between baseline and 12- and 24-month follow-up were evaluated using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. All statistical analyses were performed using STATA version 14, with a two-sided alpha level of <0.05 considered statistically significant. Ethics statement The project has been approved by institutional ethics committee of the national coordinating centre at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) New Delhi vide reference number IEC-62/07.02.2020, 232 RP-08/2020 and ethics committees of all collaborating institutes. Following informed consent, patients with CNS demyelinating disorders are recruited into the registry. Role of funding source The study is sponsored by the ICMR vide Grant number 5/4-5/192/NeuroTF/2019-NCD-1. It had no role in study design, collection, analysis, interpretation of data, writing of the report and in the decision to submit the paper for publication. The various clinical phenotypes are described in . These include radiologically isolated syndrome (RIS), clinically isolated syndrome (CIS), MS, NMOSD, MOGAD, ADEM, chronic relapsing inflammatory optic neuritis (CRION), chronic lymphocytic inflammation with pontine perivascular enhancement responsive to steroids (CLIPPERS), glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) astrocytopathy, and others category. The latter includes double seronegative myelitis, double seronegative optic neuritis, double seronegative LETM, double seronegative LETM with other CNS involvement, double seronegative opticospinal syndrome, double seronegative brainstem demyelination, TDL, and other unclassified CNS demyelinating disorders. Few patients with inflammatory CNS disorders were also recruited in the early phase of the registry. The various key demographic variables are outlined in and . The mean (SD), median (range) age of the cohort at recruitment is 34.62 (12.16) and 33 (3.0–85.0) years, respectively ( ). 300 patients (6.11%) were aged <18 years. There are 3251 female participants and 1725 male participants, with an overall female-to-male ratio of 1.9:1. NMOSD has the highest female-to-male ratio of 3.58:1, and MOGAD is equally distributed between two sexes ( ). Majority were urban residents and in the higher economic strata, especially among the MS cohort. Only 36.71% patients were involved in regular exercise. Majority of patients had never smoked, vaped, consumed tobacco or taken alcohol. Most were non-vegetarian and consumed a mixed diet. Among available data 61.19% patients were married and 2647 patients reported having children. Family history of neuroimmunological illness was observed in 1.65% of patients and was highest in the MS population (2.23%). Comorbidities included asthma (3.11%), hypertension (7.83%), diabetes (6.77%), epilepsy (2.50%), psychiatric comorbidity (2.57%), cardiac illness (0.69%) and stroke (0.59%). Past history of infection reported were measles (7.66%), mumps (3.76%), any immunological illness (1.5%), and COVID-19 (13.2%). Many of the patients were not aware of their childhood vaccination status. Where vaccination history was certain, it was reported in majority ( ). A limited number of patients (292; 6.16%) were taking alternative medication. The disease characteristics are outlined in and . The mean (SD) age of disease onset in the current cohort is 29.12 (11.80) years ( ). The median (IQR) duration of disease at the time of recruitment was 2.79 (0.51–7.22) years ( ) and was the longest for MS; 4.91 (1.82–9.51) years ( ). The median (IQR) duration between disease onset and diagnosis (calculated in days and from time of onset of symptoms to a formal diagnosis given to the patient) was 85 (20–588) days and was highest in patients with MS followed by CRION, and shorter for ADEM, MOGAD and NMOSD ( ). Overall, the two commonly involved systems at presentation were optic nerves and spinal cord across all major disease phenotypes other than ADEM where supratentorial involvement was the most common. Multifocal presentation at onset was observed in 622 patients. The median (IQR) relapse rate was 2 (2–4) and similar across all groups and the most common region of involvement in relapses was spinal cord followed by the visual pathway ( ). The median (IQR) EDSS of the overall cohort was 2 (1–4.5) respectively, and was higher for NMOSD and ADEM. There was a clear reduction in the time from symptom onset to diagnosis across successive onset-year cohorts for all disease groups ( ). Among patients with onset prior to 2010, the median (IQR) onset-to-diagnosis duration was longest for all phenotypes. This progressively decreased for those with onset between 2010 and 2014. The most pronounced decline was observed after 2019. Laboratory characteristics are outlined in the and . Among available data, antinuclear antibody (ANA) was positive in 351 (11.65%) patients, extractable nuclear antigen (ENA) profile was positive in 86 (9.41%), and the majority were seronegative for any concomitant antibody. Among the NMOSD cohort, aquaporin-4 IgG was positive in 69.8%. Among 4217 patients who underwent the test, MOG IgG was positive in 16.29% patients. It was positive in all patients diagnosed with MOGAD, and two patients with MS. One NMOSD patient was double seropositive for AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG; given that testing was performed using fixed cell-based assays as part of routine clinical care, this may represent a rare double positivity or a potential false-positive MOG-IgG result. In the seronegative NMOSD group, all patient tested negative for both AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG. In the ADEM group, most patients underwent AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG testing,

It was positive in all patients diagnosed with MOGAD, and two patients with MS. One NMOSD patient was double seropositive for AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG; given that testing was performed using fixed cell-based assays as part of routine clinical care, this may represent a rare double positivity or a potential false-positive MOG-IgG result. In the seronegative NMOSD group, all patient tested negative for both AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG. In the ADEM group, most patients underwent AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG testing, with all tested patients being negative. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was tested in 3317 (74.12%) patients, and the details are outlined in and . Highest prevalence of positive OCB (oligoclonal band) test was present in patients with MS, although it was observed across the spectrum ( ). A total of 8709 MRI scans have been contributed to the central database from participating centres. Imaging frequency is determined according to each site's study protocol. Both baseline and follow-up scans were uploaded via a secure portal, and all images were anonymised and coded sequentially for each patient based on the order of MRI acquisition. The various current and previous DMTs are outlined in and . Among 3768 patients where data was available, Rituximab was the most common DMT in use or previously prescribed, followed by dimethyl fumarate (DMF). Azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil were the most common oral immunosuppressants in use among patients with non-MS phenotypes. Some of the patients were also on maintenance prednisolone as indicated at the time of recruitment. Among patients with MS, oral dimethyl fumarate and rituximab were the most commonly prescribed agents. Among NMOSD and MOGAD as well, rituximab was the most common drug in use. A very small number of patients were on interferons, reflecting the decline in use of these medications. A progressive trend across successive onset-year cohorts for MS patients reflected a change in the prescribing patterns and patient preferences ( ). Data of 4560 follow-ups is available across various time points (6–54 months), collected every six months. Data for the disease course was available for 4423 patients. The majority of patients were stable (63.05%) or had improved (29.93%), and a small proportion (7.02%) worsened ( and ). “Improved” was defined as a decrease in EDSS by ≥ 0.5 points along with the patient's subjective improvement in functional status (self-care or ambulation); “Stable” was defined as no meaningful change in EDSS and clinical status; and “Worsening” was defined as an increase in EDSS by ≥ 0.5 points along with subjective worsening in functional status. Most patients (91.53%) continued on previous DMTs, and in a few, it was either stopped, switched or temporarily withheld due to various reasons. Among available data (n = 3613), 2566 (71%) patients were in clinical no evidence of disease activity (NEDA) based on the absence of relapses and any disability worsening. Infections were observed in 160 (3.79%) patients in the cohort as per available data (n = 4226) at last follow-up. Among MS patients, the highest infection rate was observed at 24 months ( ). Among 64 MS patients who developed infections while on disease-modifying therapies (DMTs), most were receiving rituximab (32.25%; n = 20), followed by dimethyl fumarate (18.75%; n = 11). A smaller proportion of infections occurred in patients on interferon beta 1a (3.12%; n = 2), azathioprine (1.56%; n = 1), teriflunomide (1.56%; n = 1), and natalizumab (1.56%; n = 1). Relapse proportion in MS patients remained low across follow-up visits ( ). EDSS status among MS patients showed overall stability, with a greater proportion demonstrating improvement than worsening at each follow-up ( ). EDSS score in PPMS and SPMS showed no significant difference while in RRMS, improvement in disability was observed in disability assessment at 12 and 24 months ( ). We compared some key characteristics of patients with MS versus NMOSD and MOGAD ( ). Mean age at onset differed significantly across groups, being highest in NMOSD (30.85 [SD 12.61] years), followed by MOGAD (28.50 [14.57] years) and MS (27.87 [9.35] years; p < 0.001). The median duration between onset and diagnosis was longest in MS compared with NMOSD and MOGAD with a much higher female predominance in NMOSD. CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands were more frequent in MS, optic pathway involvement was more frequent in MOGAD and median EDSS was higher in NMOSD. Many international MS registries have been collecting data prospectively, including NARCOMS (USA), the Swedish MS registry, the Danish MS registry, Italian MS registry, OFSEP (France), UK MS Register, MSBase, German, Polish, Swiss, MENACTRIMS, Norwegian MS registries and the newly established Big MS database. , , The majority of published data are available for MS. We compared key demographic and clinical indicators with the IMSRN

compared with NMOSD and MOGAD with a much higher female predominance in NMOSD. CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands were more frequent in MS, optic pathway involvement was more frequent in MOGAD and median EDSS was higher in NMOSD. Many international MS registries have been collecting data prospectively, including NARCOMS (USA), the Swedish MS registry, the Danish MS registry, Italian MS registry, OFSEP (France), UK MS Register, MSBase, German, Polish, Swiss, MENACTRIMS, Norwegian MS registries and the newly established Big MS database. , , The majority of published data are available for MS. We compared key demographic and clinical indicators with the IMSRN MS cohort ( ). The predominant disease phenotype across registries is RRMS (IMSRN: 82.6%; Danish: 78%; Swedish: 62%; Italian: 71%; MSBase: 81.5%), with a similar female predominance (IMSRN F:M ratio 2:1; range 2–4:1 across registries). Age at onset was slightly younger in the IMSRN cohort (median 27.9 years) compared with Danish (35.6 years), Swedish (34.4 years), Italian (32.5 years), and MSBase (31.4 years) cohorts. Disease duration was shorter in IMSRN (median 5.48 years for MS) relative to long-standing registries (e.g., UK 14.5 years, MSBase 12.4 years), reflecting the relatively recent establishment of the registry. Time from onset to diagnosis was comparable or shorter in IMSRN (median 0.55 years) versus some European cohorts (e.g., MSBase 1.73 years). Follow-up duration was also shorter in IMSRN when compared with established registries with >10 years of follow-up. Overall, demographic patterns, clinical characteristics, and disease phenotypes in IMSRN are comparable to international registries, while the shorter follow-up reflects early-phase registry maturity. Discussion IMSRN is an Indian multicentric registry to prospectively collect information about various facets of the common CNS demyelinating disorders, including demographics, clinical profile, laboratory data, imaging and follow-up. Registries are important in understanding large demographic datasets, real-world disease behaviour, long-term outcomes and therapeutic responses. , , , It provides an opportunity for observing the similarities and differences between disease characteristics worldwide. The incidence, prevalence, possible risk factors and disease behaviour of these disorders may vary across the globe. MS, the most common among the primary demyelinating disorders, is also reflected in the present registry with proportionately much higher numbers, although the exact incidence and prevalence are not well known from India. As per the last Atlas of MS, even though the disease has increased over time, a gap regarding understanding the incidence and prevalence of MS continues to exist. , , The higher relative frequency of NMOSD and MOGAD observed in our cohort is consistent with prior epidemiological data from Asia. Although MS remains the most prevalent demyelinating disorder across Asian populations, large population-based studies have shown that the relative proportion of NMOSD is higher in Asia than in Western countries. In East Asia, NMOSD has a higher prevalence (4/100,000) than in predominantly Caucasian populations (1–1.5/100,000), and MOGAD constitutes a substantial proportion of cases previously classified as antibody-negative NMOSD or isolated optic neuritis, including cohorts from Japan, China, Sri Lanka, and India. Population-based data from Singapore show prevalence rates of MS (6.6/100,000), AQP4-positive NMOSD (3.8/100,000), and MOGAD (1.3/100,000), indicating that NMOSD and MOGAD together approach the prevalence of MS, in contrast to Western populations. The female predominance and age of onset in the present cohort are consistent with published data worldwide. In our NMOSD cohort, the male-to-female ratio was 1:3.58. Consistent with prior Asian data, this represents a less extreme female predominance than the 9:1 ratio typically reported in Western AQP4-positive NMOSD, with Asian population-based studies reporting female:male ratios ranging from 2:1 to 6:1 in Japan, Korea, China, and Taiwan, and even lower ratios in some South Asian cohorts. We observed longer delays in diagnosis of MS compared to other disorders. This observation has also been reported in the past and is likely multifactorial with patient, physician and investigative delays being responsible. , , , In a large survey conducted for the MS Atlas of MSIF (Multiple Sclerosis International Federation), at least one major barrier for diagnostic delay was reported by majority of coordinators from 107 countries. Since NMOSD and MOGAD present with more severe and acute symptoms, and serological tests have improved sensitivity of diagnosis, the diagnostic time delay is probably shorter. However, a marked improvement in diagnostic timelines across successive onset-year cohorts for all disease groups was observed in the IMSRN registry, with steadily reducing delays after 2010 likely reflecting greater clinical awareness, availability of more trained professionals, earlier and wider availability of MRI and antibody testing, more efficient referral pathways, and simplification of diagnostic criteria; collectively enabling faster diagnosis and treatment initiation. A study on optic neuritis, however, reported that cost was an impediment to timely diagnosis and management. MS may present with mild symptoms, which may be non-specific, and patients may visit non-neurologists for symptomatic relief, leading to a delay in diagnosis, although revision of diagnostic criteria has possibly

cohorts for all disease groups was observed in the IMSRN registry, with steadily reducing delays after 2010 likely reflecting greater clinical awareness, availability of more trained professionals, earlier and wider availability of MRI and antibody testing, more efficient referral pathways, and simplification of diagnostic criteria; collectively enabling faster diagnosis and treatment initiation. A study on optic neuritis, however, reported that cost was an impediment to timely diagnosis and management. MS may present with mild symptoms, which may be non-specific, and patients may visit non-neurologists for symptomatic relief, leading to a delay in diagnosis, although revision of diagnostic criteria has possibly led to an earlier diagnosis by experts. , A recent extensive report discusses the various facets of timely evaluation, diagnosis and management for patients with MS, NMOSD and MOGAD. There is an unmet need for improving this gap, which is likely to be improved with public awareness, education, training of health care professionals, and improvement of resources. , , A higher socioeconomic status (SE), education level, and lifestyle may affect the incidence and prevalence of MS, although the exact mechanisms are not certain. , This is also reflected in the higher prevalence of MS in developed countries, as was observed in the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2016 study, suggesting a strong relationship between MS and socio-demographic index (SDI). The IMSRN data also reflected a higher SE status in the MS cohort. We used a specific SE scale to assess socioeconomic status, which has its inherent limitations. , The increasing burden of MS globally may be a reflection of changing epidemiology and lifestyle, which seem relevant to India as well. Socioeconomic status may also drive inequitable care, limited access to treatments, increase in comorbidities, and suboptimal patient outcomes. , , , A recent study also observed a relationship between higher mortality and low socioeconomic status amongst patients with MS. Differences in educational level and socioeconomic status across residential settings may influence healthcare-seeking behaviour and referral patterns and could therefore act as potential confounders in this registry-based analysis. Employment status was assessed in adults 18 years and above. Exact observations are limited due to a significant number of subjects being homemakers or still pursuing education and not in formal employment. A large number of patients were employed, but a proportion were previously employed for which we didn't collect further information about specific reasons that led to unemployment. Many factors may influence employment in these disorders, including disease type, severity, disability, fatigue, coping mechanisms, psychosocial causes and silent disability, etc. , , , , Comorbidities could exist among patients with demyelinating disorders as observed in the present study. These could affect diagnostic delays, cognition, mortality, and quality of life. , A recent study found significant psychiatric comorbidities in patients with NMOSD, and another study suggested the influence of comorbidity on both the occurrence and outcome of optic neuritis among patients with NMOSD and MOGAD. Population and longitudinal studies suggest direct and indirect association of MS with the presence of disorders like cancer, ischaemic heart disease, but an uncertainty on stroke. The observed pattern is likely multifactorial, potentially reflecting underlying genetic susceptibility, while also being influenced by conventional risk factors such as smoking and hypertension, together with the growing burden of non-communicable diseases; although the occurrence of MS in the young population weakens the conventional risk factor theory, as observed in the present study, with only a small proportion of patients having them. The majority of patients had mild disability, although there was a range of disability depending upon the disease severity, duration and type of illness. Although follow-up is not too long in the present cohort, the majority of patients remained stable. Early diagnosis, DMT exposure and timely transition to more effective agents likely contribute to the reduction of cumulative disability presently when compared to historical cohorts. Among the available data of current DMT use in the population, both immunomodulators and immunosuppressive therapy use were observed across the spectrum of drugs available. Rituximab was the most commonly used DMT, followed by dimethyl fumarate, azathioprine and mycophenolate mofetil. , Although currently used for treatment of non-MS phenotypes, azathioprine and other immunosuppressive medications have been used to treat MS due to the high cost of DMTs. , With the availability of low-cost generic formulations of medications like dimethyl fumarate and teriflunomide, access to treatment has significantly improved over the past few years, even though cost may still be a limiting factor for treatment for patients. Our analysis of first-line DMT use trends in MS over time demonstrates a clear shift from interferon-based therapies toward oral agents, particularly dimethyl fumarate, which has seen a marked rise in use since 2015. A parallel increase in rituximab use is also observed, reflecting its growing acceptance as a cost-effective and highly efficacious therapy. Overall, it reflects a trend

of DMTs. , With the availability of low-cost generic formulations of medications like dimethyl fumarate and teriflunomide, access to treatment has significantly improved over the past few years, even though cost may still be a limiting factor for treatment for patients. Our analysis of first-line DMT use trends in MS over time demonstrates a clear shift from interferon-based therapies toward oral agents, particularly dimethyl fumarate, which has seen a marked rise in use since 2015. A parallel increase in rituximab use is also observed, reflecting its growing acceptance as a cost-effective and highly efficacious therapy. Overall, it reflects a trend towards more accessible and convenient therapies driven by the introduction of affordable generics and biosimilars in the country. Other highly effective medications, including natalizumab, ocrelizumab, and ofatumumab, were used in a limited number of patients. Ocrelizumab has recently been approved for use in India and expands the availability of anti-CD20 medications. Complement inhibitors are currently unavailable for the treatment of NMOSD. Cost is a major limiting factor for treatment with these medications. Rituximab is cost-effective, has a long interdosing interval and an acceptable safety profile, making it a frequent choice of medication for MS patients, both for induction or switching therapy in India and also in other countries. , Cheaper Rituximab biosimilars have been available in the country for the past few years, providing an effective and more affordable treatment option. Due to its worldwide use and efficacy, rituximab has now also been included in the essential medication list of the WHO for the treatment of MS in 2024. Strengths of this study is the prospective and standardised data collection with longitudinal follow-up and country-wide representation, enabling to build the first large database of these disorders. Limitations of the registry are the missing data on some elements. There may be some variability in data collection, although we have ensured standardised data collection method is followed by all sites. As this is a hospital-based, referral centre registry and not a population-based cohort, true incidence and prevalence may not be reliably estimated. Treatment strategies and availability of therapies have also evolved over the study period, which may have influenced observed treatment patterns and outcomes. Further analysis from the IMSRN registry will help understand specific disease phenotypes, pregnancy outcomes, imaging patterns and biomarkers. The IMSRN also aims to expand its long-term goal towards population-based estimates of incidence, prevalence and disease characteristics, as well as patient-reported-outcomes to enable more detailed longitudinal, phenotype-specific, and treatment-outcome analyses. In conclusion, data collected from IMSRN presents a unique opportunity to study disease characteristics and longitudinal follow-up of a wide spectrum of CNS demyelinating disorders, including MS, NMOSD and MOGAD. The comparison of Indian data to that reported from other countries , , , suggests that the core elements do seem to be quite similar and presents an opportunity to understand potential disease characteristics that could be related to various factors. Further analysis of the IMSRN database on individual disorders and multiple facets will enhance our understanding and foster patient care. documents.title: Lyme Disease Diagnosis Management

chunks.content: Introduction Lyme disease represents the most widespread vector-borne disease within the Northern Hemisphere and is predominantly attributed to the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi, which is transmitted to humans through the bites of infected Ixodes ticks. Notwithstanding its acknowledgment more than forty years prior, Lyme disease persists as an escalating public health challenge, especially within the geographical boundaries of North America and Europe. , The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimates that approximately 476,000 individuals in the United States receive a clinical diagnosis and subsequent treatment for Lyme disease on an annual basis, while in Europe, over 65,000 cases are recorded each year. From a clinical standpoint, Lyme disease manifests in a phased manner, initiating with localized infections such as erythema migrans and potentially advancing to disseminated manifestations that encompass Lyme arthritis, carditis, and neuroborreliosis in the absence of timely intervention. , Although antibiotic therapy proves effective when administered without delay, any postponement in diagnosis and subsequent treatment may result in persistent symptoms that fall under the classification of post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome (PTLDS). , The absence of a sanctioned vaccine intended for human application constitutes a significant limitation in contemporary preventive methodologies, especially in areas where the disease is endemic. , VLA15 represents an innovative recombinant protein subunit vaccine currently in co-development by Valneva and Pfizer. This vaccine is engineered to target six predominant OspA serotypes (1 through 6), which encompass the most prevalent Borrelia species responsible for Lyme disease within both North America and Europe. , Preclinical investigations conducted utilizing animal models have suggested that VLA15 elicits robust antibody responses, and it can be a suitable candidate that may afford protection against multiple Borrelia species. , Clinical trials of phase I and II carried out in Europe and the United States have substantiated that the vaccine is not only well-tolerated but also immunogenic across a broad spectrum of ages, encompassing children as young as 5 years. , These trials documented significant anti-OspA antibody titers and reported no serious vaccine-related adverse events. In light of these findings, a large-scale phase III trial, designated VALOR (Vaccine Against Lyme for Outdoor Recreationists), was initiated in 2022 to evaluate the efficacy of VLA15 among individuals residing in endemic regions. Although the actual effectiveness in real-world contexts remains under scrutiny, the formulation and development of VLA15 signify considerable progress in vaccine technology and aim to address the shortcomings of previous methodologies. Given the escalating global incidence of Lyme disease, the broadened geographic distribution of tick vectors influenced by climate change, , and the growing public demand for effective preventive strategies, VLA15 emerges as the most promising candidate for a human Lyme disease vaccine currently under development. This meta-analysis endeavors to meticulously examine and amalgamate all extant published data pertaining to the safety and immune response elicited by the VLA15 Lyme disease vaccine. Through a systematic evaluation of data derived from both preclinical and clinical investigations, this manuscript aspires to deliver a comprehensive appraisal of the feasibility of VLA15 as a prophylactic vaccine for Lyme borreliosis. In light of the escalating global prevalence of Lyme disease, the absence of an authorized human vaccine, and the inadequacies of existing preventive measures, VLA15 may signify a promising contender in addressing a substantial and burgeoning public health issue. Methods This meta-analysis was conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) criteria and registered with PROSPERO 2025 CRD420251058818. Accessible at https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251058818 . Data sources and search strategy A thorough literature search was executed across a range of electronic databases, encompassing PubMed (MEDLINE), ScienceDirect, EMBASE, Scopus, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, from the inception until May 2025. The search terminology employed included: “VLA15,” “OspA-based,” and “Lyme disease.” Two independent and impartial reviewers (T.N.A and A.T), devoid of any conflicts of interest, undertook the search process. Furthermore, ClinicalTrials.gov was examined to uncover pertinent published or unpublished clinical trials. To ensure the comprehensiveness of the search, manual exploration was also conducted on the reference lists of all included studies, in addition to relevant meta-analyses and review articles, with the aim of identifying potentially eligible studies. Study selection The studies eligible for inclusion were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated the VLA15 (OspA-based) vaccine in healthy adults, children, or populations at heightened risk (e.g., individuals residing in Lyme endemic regions). The included studies were mandated to compare the VLA15 vaccine against a placebo or no vaccination. Studies were excluded if they were uncontrolled trials, review articles synthesizing other trials, or studies not involving the direct administration of the VLA15 vaccine. Preclinical studies involving animal subjects or in vitro experiments, as well as observational designs, such as case-control, cohort (whether retrospective or prospective), and cross-sectional studies, were also excluded. Non-original articles, encompassing commentaries, letters to the editor, and case reports, were likewise excluded. Data

The included studies were mandated to compare the VLA15 vaccine against a placebo or no vaccination. Studies were excluded if they were uncontrolled trials, review articles synthesizing other trials, or studies not involving the direct administration of the VLA15 vaccine. Preclinical studies involving animal subjects or in vitro experiments, as well as observational designs, such as case-control, cohort (whether retrospective or prospective), and cross-sectional studies, were also excluded. Non-original articles, encompassing commentaries, letters to the editor, and case reports, were likewise excluded. Data extraction and assessment of study quality Subsequent to the exportation of the acquired articles to EndNote reference management software, duplicate studies were eliminated. The remaining articles were independently scrutinized by the reviewers based on their titles and abstracts. A full-text assessment was subsequently conducted to evaluate eligibility in accordance with the predefined inclusion criteria. A third reviewer (A.T) was consulted to address any disagreements that arose during the selection process. Data from the included RCTs were extracted into a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet. Baseline characteristics gathered included: mean age (± standard deviation), vaccine dosage (high vs low), gender distribution, baseline body mass index (BMI), and ethnic origin (classified as White, Black, or Mixed). Outcomes Safety outcomes Injection site pain Redness Swelling Tenderness Nausea Headache Fatigue Myalgia Arthralgia Fever Unsolicited adverse event Immunogenicity outcomes IgG antibody response Geometric mean titer (GMT) values Seroconversion rates (SRR) The methodological quality and risk of bias of the incorporated RCTs were appraised independently by two reviewers utilizing the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (ROB 2) tool. The results were subsequently compared, and any discrepancies were reconciled through consensus among the review team. Meta-analysis Statistical analysis was conducted employing Review Manager software (version 5.4; Copenhagen: The Nordic Cochrane Centre, The Cochrane Collaboration, 2014). Forest plots were generated for the results’ visual display. Effect sizes for dichotomous outcomes were represented as risk ratios (RR) accompanied by corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs), utilizing a random-effects model to accommodate potential heterogeneity. The evaluation of statistical heterogeneity across studies was performed through the I ² statistic, where an I ² value surpassing 50% was interpreted as a sign of significant heterogeneity. Results Study selection In this study, a total of 430 records were initially identified through database searches in PubMed (95), Cochrane Library (40), Scopus (80), and clinical trial registers (215). After removing 25 duplicate records, 190 records were screened for relevance based on titles and abstracts, leading to the exclusion of 160 records. Full-text retrieval was sought for 30 reports, but 2 could not be retrieved. The remaining 28 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, of which 25 were excluded due to reasons such as wrong population ( n = 5), inappropriate study design ( n = 10), incorrect comparator ( n = 6), and insufficient outcome data ( n = 4). Ultimately, three studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in both the qualitative and quantitative synthesis. PRISMA Flowchart illustrates these findings in . Baseline characteristics The baseline characteristics were drawn from three studies: Laura, Nicole (a and b), and Sikand. A total of 5907 participants were included in the review, randomizing 4500 to the VLA15 vaccine arm, while 1407 participants to the placebo/control arm across the analysis. The baseline table ( ) provides information on several key parameters, including the total number of participants, gender distribution (male, female, and females of childbearing potential), and racial composition (White, Asian, Black African, American Indian/Alaska Native, and Other). Additional variables reported included age at screening, body height, body weight, body mass index (BMI), and baseline serostatus for Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato. Quality assessment The risk of bias was evaluated using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool 2.0 (ROB 2), independently by two authors (M.S.K and T.N.A). The randomization process, deviations from planned interventions, missing outcome data, outcome assessment, and selection of the reported result are the five areas in which it evaluates the risk of bias in RCTs. The study’s risk of bias is assessed across domains, categorized as low, some concerns, or high ( ). A total of 191 in the experimental (VLA-15) arm experienced fever, compared to 27 in the control arm. The pooled RR for fever was 2.65 (95% CI: 1.77–3.96; p < 0.0001), suggesting that the VLA-15 vaccine significantly increased the risk of fever compared to the control. The test for overall effect showed a highly significant result ( Z = 4.74; p < 0.00001), indicating that fever was significantly more likely in individuals receiving VLA15 than those receiving placebo. Importantly, there was no heterogeneity between

The pooled RR for fever was 2.65 (95% CI: 1.77–3.96; p < 0.0001), suggesting that the VLA-15 vaccine significantly increased the risk of fever compared to the control. The test for overall effect showed a highly significant result ( Z = 4.74; p < 0.00001), indicating that fever was significantly more likely in individuals receiving VLA15 than those receiving placebo. Importantly, there was no heterogeneity between studies ( I ² = 0%, χ² = 2.97, df = 3, p = 0.40), which strengthens the reliability of this finding ( ) assesses the risk of headache after receiving the VLA-15 vaccine. Here, 565 in the experimental group reported headaches, while 218 in the control group experienced headaches. The pooled RR for headache was 1.40 (95% CI: 1.21–1.62; p < 0.0001), indicating a significantly higher risk of headache among vaccinated participants compared to those in the control group. This finding was statistically significant ( Z = 4.96, p < 0.00001), establishing headache as a significant adverse event associated with VLA15. Moreover, there was no heterogeneity across the studies ( I ² = 0%, χ² = 2.82, df = 6, p = 0.83), suggesting the results are consistent and reliable ( ). Risk of fatigue and arthralgia among users of VLA-15 vaccine versus control evaluates the risk of fatigue as an adverse effect of the VLA-15 vaccine. A total of 575 patients in the VLA-15 arm experienced fatigue, compared to 224 (15.6%) in the control arm. The pooled RR for fatigue was 1.33 (95% CI: 1.15–1.55; p = 0.0001), indicating that vaccination with VLA-15 was associated with a higher risk of fatigue relative to placebo. The test for overall effect was highly significant ( Z = 3.84; p = 0.0001), demonstrating a clear association between VLA-15 administration and increased fatigue incidence. Notably, there was no significant heterogeneity across studies ( I ² = 0%, χ² = 5.82, df = 6, p = 0.44), supporting the consistency of this finding. These results suggest that fatigue is a frequent and statistically significant adverse event associated with the VLA-15 vaccine. Subgroup analyses by dosage showed no significant differences ( p = 0.77 for subgroup differences), with the 30μg dose showing the strongest effect (RR 1.47, 95% CI 1.18–1.84; ). revealed a statistically significant increase in arthralgia risk with the VLA-15 vaccine, demonstrating an overall RR of 2.50 (95% CI: 1.67–3.76; Z = 4.43, p < 0.00001) with no observed heterogeneity (Tau² = 0.00; I ² = 0%, p = 0.46). Subgroup analyses by dose showed a clear dose-response relationship: the 135 μg dose group exhibited a particularly elevated risk (RR = 4.20, 95% CI: 1.42–12.39; Z = 2.60, p = 0.009; Tau² = 0.13, I ² = 11%) and the 180 μg dose group showed similarly increased risk (RR = 2.48, 95% CI: 1.32–4.69; Z = 2.81, p = 0.005; Tau² = 0.06, I ² = 16%). While lower doses showed nonsignificant effects (30 μg: RR = 2.14, 95% CI: 0.83–5.48, Z = 1.58, p = 0.11; 90 μg: RR = 0.86, 95% CI: 0.10–7.04, Z = 0.15, p = 0.89), the test for subgroup differences confirmed no significant variation between dose groups (χ² = 1.99, p = 0.58, I ² = 0%) ( ). Risk of tenderness and nausea among users of VLA-15 vaccine versus control evaluates an increased risk of tenderness associated with the VLA-15 vaccine (RR = 2.55, 95% CI: 2.20–2.96; Z = 12.34, p < 0.00001), with excellent consistency across studies (Tau² = 0.00; I ² = 0%, p = 0.70). Subgroup analyses revealed a consistent dose-response relationship, with all dosage groups showing statistically significant effects. The test for subgroup differences showed no significant variation between dose groups (χ² = 0.09, p = 0.95, I ² = 0%), indicating the increased risk was consistent across all tested dosages. These robust findings, supported by extremely low p -values and minimal heterogeneity, clearly establish that the experimental intervention significantly elevates tenderness risk regardless of dose level ( ). revealed no statistically significant difference between the VLA-15 vaccine and control groups (RR = 1.34, 95% CI: 0.94–1.90; Z = 1.64, p = 0.10), with excellent consistency across studies (Tau² = 0.00; I ² = 0%, p = 0.49). Subgroup analyses by dose showed similarly non-significant results. The test for subgroup differences confirmed no significant variation between dose groups (χ² = 0.10, p = 0.95, I ² = 0%). These consistent findings, supported by non-significant p -values and minimal heterogeneity across all analyses, indicate that the experimental intervention does not significantly affect nausea risk at any tested dose level.
