documents.title: NICE NG136 Hypertension in adults diagnosis and management

chunks.content: Introduction Stroke has a major impact on people’s lives, with often devastating personal, social and economic consequences for the individual and their family. The cost of stroke in the European Union (EU) in 2015 was estimated at €45 billion, accounting for a total mortality rate of 17% within the EU, making it the second most common cause of death [ ]. Increased disability and mortality rates result from recurrent strokes, yet despite this, an assessment of the availability of secondary prevention measures after stroke or transient ischaemic attack (TIA) across Europe has shown significant gaps in specialist care, monitoring and treatment programmes [ ]. The European Stroke Action Plan (ESAP) for the years 2018–2030 outlined targets for the development of stroke care [ ]. The report outlined six domains in their action plan, one of which is secondary prevention and organised follow-up. The 5-year risk of recurrent stroke is estimated at 9.5% with recurrent stroke often resulting in more debilitating outcomes [ ]. Management of risk factors such as smoking, hyperlipidaemia, obesity, diabetes, atrial fibrillation, sedentary lifestyle, raised body mass index and hypertension, have the potential to reduce recurrent events by up to 80% [ , ]. Of these, researchers have demonstrated hypertension to be the most important modifiable risk factor in stroke [ ]. In recurrent stroke the risk increases by about one-third for every 10 mmHg increase in systolic blood pressure [ ]. In a survey of secondary prevention of stroke in Europe, satisfactory levels of blood pressure (BP) control are achieved in less than 60% of countries [ ]. Figures from Ireland were included in this data. However, there were limitations to this study. Authors didn’t have access to primary registry data and many of the responses were estimated, allowing for the possibility of unintentional biases. A recent paper published in the Lancet showed that Ireland, Finland and Spain have the lowest rate of awareness, treatment and control of BP in their populations, based on an analysis of national representative surveys in 12 high-income countries [ ]. Reasons for sub-optimal BP control are multi-faceted and include patient factors (adherence) [ , ], physician factors (including therapeutic inertia) [ ], lifestyle issues and treatment resistant hypertension [ ]. However, a recent study considering pseudo-resistance in high-risk cardiovascular patients suggests that treatment resistant hypertension may be less prevalent than expected, with half of the patients in this study prescribed sub-optimal doses of their anti-hypertensive medications [ ]. Blood pressure guidelines for the prevention of stroke have been the subject of much discussion with differences emerging between specialist groups. The recent American Heart Association (AHA) guidelines have adopted a target of < 130/80 mmHg for the secondary prevention of stroke [ ]. The European Society of Cardiology/ European Society of Hypertension (ESC/ ESH) changed their guidance from < 140/90 mmHg [ ] to < 130/80 mmHg in their most recent guidelines published in 2018 [ ]. Recent hypertension guidelines from the National Institute of Health and Care Excellence (NICE) have not committed to the lower target and instead have set a target of < 140/90 mmHg for adults under 80 years [ , ]. The Irish health care system does not have universal registration with a GP or mandatory coding of diseases. Almost half of the population is registered through the Primary Care Reimbursement Service (PCRS) and registered to one single general practitioner [ ]. The remainder are described as private patients and able to see any general practitioner. All patients over the age of 70 years, under six, and those below defined income levels [less than €304 (£270) gross per week for a single person; €441 (£395) gross per week for a couple] are registered with the PCRS [ ]. Of those registered with the PCRS- three quarters receive free primary healthcare and medications (those with the lowest income), the remaining quarter have free access to primary care only [ ]. We based all prevalence analysis on patients who are registered with the PCRS as we can be certain these patients are registered with a single practice. The primary aim of this study was to describe the prevalence of sub-optimal blood pressure control in a cross-sectional cohort of patients with a previous stroke/ TIA in primary care. Secondly, we wished to examine the characteristics of this cohort- looking for associations that could predict poor blood pressure control and thirdly we wished to assess anti-hypertensive drug dosing schedules in these patients. To our knowledge, this is the first study examining these issues in primary care. To our knowledge, this is the first study examining these issues in primary care. Methods General practices in the University of Limerick, Education and Research Network [ ] were invited to participate via email. Out of the 14 practices that responded, ten practices were selected as they were within 2 h travel from the university, had the capacity to host the researcher and used electronic health care records. The 10 practices that participated included a variety of practice sizes (small, medium, large) and types (urban, rural, mixed, teaching and non-teaching) (Table ). This was a convenience sample but the participating practices were purposefully selected to be representative of Irish General Practice [ ]. Data collection was conducted in July and August 2019 according to a prespecified data extraction protocol designed by RD ( ). Data collection was supported in practices by DMC, who received a summer student research scholarship, and was supervised by RD. This work fulfilled for the GP, the Irish Medical Council requirement to conduct an annual audit. Eligible patients were identified as those patients who were coded for stroke or TIA or those who were not coded but had a hospital diagnosed stroke or TIA in their discharge summaries from specialists. These events were classed as either ischaemic stroke, haemorrhagic stroke, TIA or unknown. If patients had more than one of these events, they were classed based on their most severe event. Disease coding typically categorised the type of each stroke, where this was not available or ambiguity existed, hospital discharge summaries and consultant reports were examined to clarify the diagnosis. All practices used electronic health care records, but used a variety of software systems; Socrates®, Health One™ or Helix Practice Manager. Search methods differed between the systems, some using specific diagnostic searches and others disease coding, each using the analysis function inbuilt in that system. In Socrates®, the International Classification of Disease-10 (ICD-10) [ ] codes G45, and I60-I64 were used, along with the International Classification of Primary Care-2 (ICPC-2) [ ] specific codes K89 (Transient cerebral ischaemia), K90 (Stroke/cerebrovascular accident), and K91 (Cerebrovascular disease) to facilitate case identification. In Health One® and Helix Practice Manager they searched using keywords, such as “stroke, cerebrovascular accident, CVA, infarct, cerebral bleed, subarachnoid haemorrhage, TIA, Transient Ischemic attack” in the patient’s past history section if coding of disease was not used in that practice. Sub-optimal BP control was assessed by comparing the last office BP on file with the ESH/ESC 2013 [ ] and NICE guideline (NG136) [ ] recommendation of BP < 140/90 mmHg for the secondary prevention of stroke. Only patients who were actively attending the general practitioner were included. European guidelines are more applicable to the Irish context and at the time of the study Irish GPs would have been more familiar with the 2013 ESH/ESC guideline [ ] or the NICE guidelines [ ]. In the absence of an up to date Irish guideline, the most recent published in 2010 [ ], Irish GPs are more likely to follow European and NICE guidelines [ ] and therefore we used BP < 140/90 mmHg as the target. To help describe the characteristics of these patients we recorded, if available, demographics, stroke subtype, blood pressure, kidney function, lipid profile and drug data. Co-morbidities of diabetes and chronic kidney disease (CKD) were also recorded. Patients were described as having diabetes if they had ICPC codes T89 (Diabetes insulin dependent) or T90 (Diabetes non-insulin dependent), ICD codes E10 (Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus), E11 ( Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus), patient’s active diagnosis contained diabetes keyword, or were taking insulin or oral hypoglycaemic agents. Patients were described as having CKD if an estimated Glomerular Filtration Rate (eGFR) less than 60mls/ min/ 1.73m 2 was recorded in the last two renal function tests [ ]. Anti-hypertensive medications were recorded as defined by the British National Formulary (BNF) 2019 [ ], and included the following drug groups: diuretics, angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, calcium channel blockers, angiotensin II type 1 receptor blockers, adrenergic beta antagonists and doxazosin. The use of ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) was examined, especially in those with sub-optimal BP control to identify cases of white coat hypertension (a normal 24-h ABPM, with an elevated manual office BP reading). Day time average readings > 134/84 mmHg signified sub-optimal BP control [ ]. Optimal anti-hypertensive medication dosing use was determined by benchmarking prescribed anti-hypertensive drug doses, for each individual prescribed drug, against the World Health Organisation-Defined Daily Dosing (WHO-DDD) schedule. We used this as a surrogate for investigating the adequacy

The use of ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) was examined, especially in those with sub-optimal BP control to identify cases of white coat hypertension (a normal 24-h ABPM, with an elevated manual office BP reading). Day time average readings > 134/84 mmHg signified sub-optimal BP control [ ]. Optimal anti-hypertensive medication dosing use was determined by benchmarking prescribed anti-hypertensive drug doses, for each individual prescribed drug, against the World Health Organisation-Defined Daily Dosing (WHO-DDD) schedule. We used this as a surrogate for investigating the adequacy of dosing. The WHO-DDD is the assumed average maintenance dose per day for a drug, used for its main indication in adults [ ]. Egan et al. adopted a slightly different approach, examining the number of patients who were receiving for each medication, diuretics apart, at least half the maximum dose [ ]. We present both approaches here. Patients were deemed to be adequately dosed when all prescribed drugs were at or above these thresholds. Graphical summaries were created for all patient characteristics to identify any anomalies or potential outliers. Summary statistics were generated that were appropriate for the explanatory variable in question (i.e. mean, standard deviation and medians). Independent t-tests were used to compare the mean of the various quantitative variables between the groups, controlled (< 140/90 mmHg) and uncontrolled (≥140/90 mmHg) and a two-sample comparison of proportions (chi-square test) to similarly compare factors. Chi-squared tests were also used to test whether a significant difference was found between the expected frequencies in different categories in controlled (< 140/90 mmHg) versus uncontrolled (≥140/90 mmHg) patients. Binary logistic regression was used to model the association between the (log) odds of BP control (< 140/90 mmHg) and explanatory variables of interest. All statistical analysis took place in SPSS- version 26 [ ]. Results Ten practices participated (Table ) with 328 patients identified as having a previous stroke or TIA. When office BP readings were compared with the ESH/ ESC 2013 [ ] and NICE (NG136) [ ] guidelines (< 140/90 mmHg), we found that 116 (35.9%) patients had sub-optimal BP control. Patient characteristics are described in Table . 62.2% of the population ( n = 328) studied are male with 37.8% female. Stroke subtype included 29.3% ischaemic stroke, 9.8% haemorrhagic stroke and 41.2% TIA, with 19.8% unknown or not recorded. 87.8% were registered with PCRS for free GP services. Multimorbidity is a common feature within this cohort of patients, 15.5% had diabetes, 22.6% had CKD and 4.9% had both diabetes and CKD. Independent t-tests were used to compare the mean of the various quantitative variables (age, parameters of renal function, ambulatory blood pressure, lipids) between the two groups, controlled (< 140/90 mmHg) and uncontrolled (≥140/90 mmHg). A two-sample comparison of proportions (or chi-square test) to compare factors (gender, PCRS status, co-morbidity and sub-optimal BP control (≥140/90 mmHg) was also performed. No statistically significant differences between the groups were demonstrated. Chi-squared tests were also used to test whether a significant difference was found between the expected frequencies and the observed frequencies in different categories in controlled (< 140/90 mmHg) versus uncontrolled patients (≥140/90 mmHg), and no significant differences were observed in sex, stroke subtype, GMS status and comorbidities. Binary logistic regression was used to model the association between the (log) odds of BP control and explanatory variables of interest. No predictors of sub-optimal BP were identified. Detailed data on drug-dosing was available for 252 patients prescribed antihypertensive medications (Table ). For those with BP ≥140/90 mmHg, 44 (47.3%) patients and 22 (23.7%) patients were inadequately dosed, in each of their medications, according to WHO-DDD guidelines [ ] and Egan et al. guidelines [ ] respectively. Of the 116 patients that had uncontrolled BP ≥140/90 mmHg, 23 patients were not taking any anti-hypertensive medication and 31 were taking a single agent. Results of ABPM were available for 64 (55.2%) of the 116 patients with sub-optimal BP control. Of those who had ABPM ( n = 64), nine patients demonstrated white coat hypertension, the remaining 55 had sub-optimal BP control, with average day time readings > 134/84 mmHg [ , ]. Discussion Summary of main findings Blood pressure control was sub-optimal in approximately one-third (35.4%) of patients according to ESH/ESC 2013 and NICE (NG136) guidelines, where BP < 140/90 mmHg is deemed satisfactory. Anti-hypertensive medication dosing appears sub-optimal in close to half of these patients when compared with WHO-DDD criteria. Comparison with existing literature Of those identified with a previous stroke or TIA, 63.1% had blood pressure controlled to < 140/90 mmHg. This compares well with results from a study in Norwegian general practice finding that 47% of patients, 1 year post stroke, had BP controlled to < 140/90 mmHg [ ]. However, there is

findings Blood pressure control was sub-optimal in approximately one-third (35.4%) of patients according to ESH/ESC 2013 and NICE (NG136) guidelines, where BP < 140/90 mmHg is deemed satisfactory. Anti-hypertensive medication dosing appears sub-optimal in close to half of these patients when compared with WHO-DDD criteria. Comparison with existing literature Of those identified with a previous stroke or TIA, 63.1% had blood pressure controlled to < 140/90 mmHg. This compares well with results from a study in Norwegian general practice finding that 47% of patients, 1 year post stroke, had BP controlled to < 140/90 mmHg [ ]. However, there is a paucity of research examining blood pressure control and secondary prevention of stroke in the primary care setting. Due to an aging population, the number of people with stroke is set to rise by 58% between 2007 and 2021 [ ]. This projected rise in the number of strokes will have a significant impact on health care spending. The cost of stroke has been estimated at €557 million per annum in Ireland [ ], €4.11 billion (£3.6 billion) per annum in the UK [ ] and €45 billion per annum within the EU [ ]. Consequently, with rising health care costs, it is imperative that prevention measures reducing the incidence of stroke or further strokes, are adopted. For clinicians, deciding which is the most appropriate target for blood pressure control in this group of patients is difficult. Having two or three differing guidelines, each recommending different targets can cause confusion regarding the most appropriate clinical management. The United Kingdom, National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE- Clinical Guideline NG136) [ ] has recently reviewed the evidence and decided that the current target of < 140/90 mmHg shall be maintained for all adults under 80 years [ ], and will not follow the AHA guidelines to reduce blood pressure targets to < 130/80 mmHg, as evidenced by the SPRINT trial [ ]. NICE stated that the methodology used to measure BP in SPRINT is simply not achievable in clinical care settings at this stage [ ]. The current ESC/ESH guideline [ ] has changed its recommendation from a target BP of < 140/90 mmHg [ ] (as used in our study) to < 130/80 mmHg. However, it recommends caution with lower targets, especially in those patients over 65 years where the target is 130–140/80 mmHg, if tolerated. Caution must be exercised with all patients, as reducing systolic blood pressure to < 120 mmHg may provide benefit for some persons, but problems for others [ ]. Achieving blood pressure targets in this complex co-morbid group of patients – with a mean age of 73 years, and in whom a quarter have CKD - can be difficult. There are occasions in practice when meeting blood pressure guidelines is not appropriate and higher blood pressure readings are acceptable– those with concurrent unstable coronary artery disease, those with previous anti-hypertensive based acute kidney injury or cerebral hypo-perfusion. A further group worth mentioning are those with extreme variability in blood pressure readings (mixed high and low) or those with isolated systolic hypertension and a large pulse pressure. These groups cannot often tolerate focused blood pressure reduction programs and treating physicians do not pursue further after trial of treatment, as this can impact seriously on their quality of life. We accept this may be a reality for some patients. Interestingly, of those with uncontrolled BP ≥140/90 mmHg ( n = 116), 22 patients did not have any anti-hypertensive medications prescribed and a further 31 patients had only a single agent prescribed. Current ESC/ESH guidelines advise that two anti-hypertensive agents are required to ensure BP control in most instances, and these should be commenced initially as a fixed dose combination therapy [ ]. Of the 93 patients prescribed one or more antihypertensives, 47.3% ( n = 44) of these did not meet the recommended dose in all their anti-hypertensive drugs when measured against the WHO-DDD guidelines (Table ). The WHO-DDD is a stringent measure of the adequacy of dosing, we accept this. However to counter balance we also analysed drug dosing from a methodology used by Egan et al. [ ]. Here, where the threshold for dosing adequacy is much lower, almost a quarter of patients are still inadequately dosed when BP remains > 140/90 mmHg. It is acknowledged that a patient with a clear indication for drug treatment may sometimes not be prescribed the drug due to factors like liver or kidney failure, weight, patient receiving end of life care, and/or previous adverse response to the drug in question. It can be accepted that in some instances, not receiving a drug treatment does not necessarily suggest poor medical treatment or therapeutic nihilism. However, as Gil-Guillen et al. suggest, physician inertia to escalate drug-dosing in hypertension can

adequacy is much lower, almost a quarter of patients are still inadequately dosed when BP remains > 140/90 mmHg. It is acknowledged that a patient with a clear indication for drug treatment may sometimes not be prescribed the drug due to factors like liver or kidney failure, weight, patient receiving end of life care, and/or previous adverse response to the drug in question. It can be accepted that in some instances, not receiving a drug treatment does not necessarily suggest poor medical treatment or therapeutic nihilism. However, as Gil-Guillen et al. suggest, physician inertia to escalate drug-dosing in hypertension can be a significant problem up to 70% of the time [ ]. The ESC/ESH guidelines support the use of ABPM when investigating high office blood pressure readings [ ]. It is an important tool when investigating white coat hypertension. It also provides important information on night time BP control which is an independent predictor of death and negative cardiovascular outcomes [ ]. Nevertheless, providing ABPM in general practice can be costly and is not suitable for all patients e.g. those with pulse irregularity such as atrial fibrillation, those who are easily confused or those who find it too uncomfortable to wear. Results from this study show that ABPM could be utilised to a greater extent as just over half the cohort have ever had ABPM. Reimbursement for the use of ABPM by primary care practitioners in Ireland, is available since 2018 for all PCRS registered patients. It is anticipated that this will lead to an increase use of ABPM as a tool for diagnosis and monitoring into the future. Strengths and limitations We believe this is the first estimate of blood pressure control in a cohort of patients post stroke/TIA in primary care with specific consideration of anti-hypertensive drug dosing. A further strength of this study was that all data was collected at the level of the patient’s file in their own general practice. Limitations of this study include the use of 10 general practices from the same geographical area. The cross-sectional design took in to account BP readings from one point in time only and did not take in to consideration out of office BP monitoring or indeed the other factors that may influence recurrent stroke (smoking, hyperlipidaemia, obesity, diabetes, atrial fibrillation and sedentary lifestyle). As this was a retrospective study, there was no common protocol for the measuring and recording of office BP. It is also accepted that the WHO-DDD is a surrogate marker for assessing the adequacy of drug-dosing. Implications for research and practice The results of this study have provided important information on blood pressure control in patients who have had a previous stroke or TIA. Recent stroke audits have focused primarily on acute hospital care [ , , ]. There is a paucity of research in primary care. Community care and long term follow up in primary care has been underfunded and under-resourced, despite recommendations from recent stroke audits to health authorities to address this deficit [ ]. Gaps in secondary prevention could be tackled through EU-wide policies, development of national and regional guidelines and strategies, and direct intervention-based reimbursement [ ]. A new contract for general practice services in Ireland has been negotiated recently [ ]. This aims to provide essential resources and funding to build the capacity for chronic disease management in primary care. Care for people who have had a cerebrovascular event (stroke or TIA) is addressed as part of this plan. Providing funding for chronic disease management is a recent advancement in primary care in Ireland. It has been available for the care of people with Type 2 Diabetes who are registered with PCRS since 2017. It has benefited these patients by improving and standardising the recording of clinical information and has also shown an improvement in the achievement of clinical targets [ ]. There is clear evidence that reducing blood pressure to below 140/90 mmHg benefits those who have had a previous stroke or TIA [ ]. This BP level should be the desired initial target for patients and their doctors before considering further reductions. Further research is needed to explore how GPs might be supported to optimise the management of BP. This may involve an examination of prescriber inertia to increase anti-hypertensive drug doses, supporting the use of out-of-office readings to confirm sub-optimal control and enhance BP management, and patient strategies to encourage adherence to drug therapy and the adoption of a healthy lifestyle. These challenges may be met by introducing novel approaches for BP control in primary care, such as home care and self-care approaches [ ]. Conclusion Blood pressure control appears sub-optimal in at least one-third of patients with a previous stroke or TIA. Half of these patients could respond to anti-hypertensive dose escalation. Further work is

This may involve an examination of prescriber inertia to increase anti-hypertensive drug doses, supporting the use of out-of-office readings to confirm sub-optimal control and enhance BP management, and patient strategies to encourage adherence to drug therapy and the adoption of a healthy lifestyle. These challenges may be met by introducing novel approaches for BP control in primary care, such as home care and self-care approaches [ ]. Conclusion Blood pressure control appears sub-optimal in at least one-third of patients with a previous stroke or TIA. Half of these patients could respond to anti-hypertensive dose escalation. Further work is required to see how best to manage blood pressure in patients with a previous stroke or TIA in Primary Care, as the majority of consultations for hypertension take place in this setting.

documents.title: NICE NG106 Chronic heart failure in adults

chunks.content: Based on population and reported mean incident rates, more than 2 million people are diagnosed with heart failure (HF) each year in Europe, and many more present with similar common signs and symptoms, requiring investigation and exclusion of HF. Demand for diagnostic services is outstripping supply and the problem is set to grow as crude HF incidence rises due to aging populations. Natriuretic peptides have a vital role to play as a triage tool in primary care, limiting the number of patients requiring onward referral for echocardiogram and specialist review, protecting resources for those most in need. The current single threshold of NT‐proBNP <125 pg/mL to rule out HF recommended in European and American Guidelines , has excellent negative predictive value but poor specificity, particularly in the elderly where HF burden is greatest. Community presentation with HF symptoms and elevated NT‐proBNP represents a sentinel event, after which hospitalisations and mortality rise sharply, and delayed HF diagnosis is a global issue. In the United Kingdom, nearly 80% of HF diagnoses were reported to occur during emergency admissions, highlighting persistent delays despite long‐established national guidelines. In the United States, low rates of NP and echocardiographic testing are reported, leading to diagnostic delays and increasing proportions of hospital diagnoses. Women, socially deprived groups, and those with multiple comorbidities experience the greatest delays. Low‐ and middle‐income countries bear an even higher burden, with delayed diagnosis contributing to higher mortality rates. Late diagnosis is consistently linked to worse outcomes, and those diagnosed during hospitalisation have higher mortality rates than those diagnosed earlier in primary care. , , Age‐related variation in natriuretic peptide levels has long been recognized and confirmed by early population‐based studies. In 2010, an international multicentre study demonstrated that age‐specific NT‐proBNP thresholds outperformed a single fixed threshold for the detection of systolic dysfunction in primary care. Large population studies show that NT‐proBNP values rise steeply with age and >75% of healthy individuals >80 years exceeded the 125 pg/mL NT‐proBNP threshold. The 2023 HFA‐ESC Consensus Statement on NT‐proBNP testing recommended the introduction of age‐related thresholds with HF considered ‘likely’ in the outpatient setting if NT‐proBNP ≥125 pg/mL for those aged <50 years, ≥250 pg/mL between 50 and 75 years, and ≥500 pg/mL over 75 years. However, these cut‐points were determined from the 95 th percentile of the Generation Scotland cohort rather than from a prospective clinical study. As NT‐proBNP falls with increasing BMI, the statement also suggested lowering NT‐proBNP age‐adjusted thresholds by 25%, 30% and 40% for BMI ranges 30–35 kg/m², 35–40 kg/m², and >40 kg/m². In the current issue of ESC HF, Taylor et al report the diagnostic accuracy of the ESC‐HFA age‐related NT‐proBNP thresholds in a retrospective cohort. The study employed English primary care data between 2004 and 2018 from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) and linked to inpatient Hospital Episode Statistics (HES). The CPRD archives hold data from around 15% of general practices in the UK and the large cohort undergoing NT‐proBNP testing ( n = 155 347) enabled the assessment of age‐adjusted thresholds overall, in both sexes, and by body mass index (BMI). Patients entered the cohort on the date of their NT‐proBNP test and exited the cohort on the date of their HF diagnosis or after 6 months, whichever occurred first. HF diagnosis was obtained from diagnostic codes entered in primary care or during hospital admission or in cases where echocardiography findings were consistent with HF. The current ESC single threshold of ≥125 pg/mL showed a sensitivity of 95% and specificity of only 50%. Age‐adjusted thresholds for <50 years, 50–74 years, and ≥75 years had increased specificity (78%, 68% and 64%) but reduced sensitivity (84%, 89%, 84%) meaning some lower‐risk HF cases may initially be missed in the community. The negative predictive value was 95% or above across all age categories. For all age‐adjusted thresholds, sensitivity decreased with increasing obesity category. By lowering the NT‐proBNP age‐adjusted thresholds by 25%, 30% and 40% for increasing obesity categories as suggested in the ESC‐HFA statement, the sensitivity and specificity were comparable with the test performance seen in the cohort overall. Large‐scale healthy European and U.S. cohorts show that NT‐proBNP levels are higher in women than men up to age 50, but lower in women compared with men after age 75. , Consistent with these population trends, Taylor et al found that age‐related thresholds demonstrated lower specificity in women than men under 50 years and higher specificity in women than men for those aged 75 years and older. When all age categories are analysed together, the age‐adjusted NT‐proBNP thresholds demonstrated comparable overall performance in men and women. By applying higher thresholds for older groups (e.g., ≥500 pg/mL for those aged ≥75), the natural rise of natriuretic peptides with age is accounted for, enhancing test accuracy in older populations where prevalence is highest.

lower in women compared with men after age 75. , Consistent with these population trends, Taylor et al found that age‐related thresholds demonstrated lower specificity in women than men under 50 years and higher specificity in women than men for those aged 75 years and older. When all age categories are analysed together, the age‐adjusted NT‐proBNP thresholds demonstrated comparable overall performance in men and women. By applying higher thresholds for older groups (e.g., ≥500 pg/mL for those aged ≥75), the natural rise of natriuretic peptides with age is accounted for, enhancing test accuracy in older populations where prevalence is highest. This study demonstrated that while the ESC HFA age‐adjusted NT‐proBNP thresholds preserved reasonable overall sensitivity (87%), they increased overall specificity to 70%, compared with 50% with the single 125 pg/mL threshold. The total number of patients exceeding the age‐adjusted thresholds was reduced by one‐third compared with the single threshold, with the potential to substantially reduce the demand for echocardiograms and specialist referral. The study offers large‐scale, retrospective, real‐world evidence from primary care, supporting the clinical applicability of the ESC HFA age‐adjusted NT‐proBNP thresholds. However, important limitations exist. Primary care coding can be unreliable, frequently depending on diagnoses made by non‐specialists in secondary care in the absence of echocardiography confirmation. While some coded as having HF may not have the condition, there are many other HF patients with incomplete or missing codes in GP records. The study was conducted in England, where national guidelines recommend further testing only if NT‐proBNP levels are over 400 pg/mL, potentially overlooking HF diagnoses with NT‐proBNP between 125 and 400 pg/mL. Additionally, the six‐month follow‐up window after NT‐proBNP testing—intended to capture hospital presentations or community deterioration—may be insufficient to identify all cases due to acknowledged diagnostic delays. Efficient, accurate and timely HF detection remains a significant challenge, especially in community and primary care settings. Although the current NT‐proBNP threshold of 125 pg/mL provides excellent negative predictive value, its use as a trigger for further testing to avoid missing even mild HF cases is overly cautious and generates excessive referrals, thereby inadvertently compromising patient safety by overburdening echocardiography and specialist services. As populations age, the mismatch between the numbers of elderly people with common, non‐specific symptoms and the resources required to cope with the diagnostic demand is set to grow further. Delayed HF diagnosis is a global problem that worsens mortality, prolongs untreated symptoms and drives up healthcare costs. Rapid diagnostic pathways using more specific measures—like age‐adjusted NT‐proBNP thresholds—are essential to reduce delay, decrease unnecessary admissions and enhance care for high‐risk groups. However, implementing age‐adjusted thresholds adds complexity to interpretation in primary care, whereas single thresholds are simpler to recall for general practitioners dealing with a multitude of different conditions. Nephrology once faced the same challenges with serum creatinine—an imprecise biomarker affected by age, sex and other factors. Step‐wise global consensus building eventually led to the adoption of an age‐ and sex‐adjusted eGFR as a universal reporting standard. The same could be possible for NT‐proBNP—universal, equitable and clinically meaningful results at the point of reporting. Globally billions are invested annually by combined public, charitable, pharmaceutical and device sectors in HF research, yet consensus on adjusted NP cut‐offs remains lacking after 25 years. Besides age, factors such as sex, BMI, race, ethnicity, and comorbidities affect NP levels. Prospective international studies with diverse populations and rigorous case adjudication are needed to establish optimal adjustments and implementation strategies. With millions of new HF cases and rising crude incidence in aging populations, improved detection methods are urgently needed. Most HF research targets therapeutics and devices, while diagnostic pathways struggle to meet demand, meaning that many patients will never access available therapies. Investing in detection and implementation science will enable timely treatment delivery, reduce healthcare burdens and improve patient outcomes. chunks.content: Research in context Evidence before this study We searched PubMed for articles published, in any language, between database inception and August 27, 2025, using the terms ((lung ultrasound) AND (general practice OR primary care)) AND ((community acquired pneumonia) OR (antibiotic)), yielding a total of 143 articles. Compared with chest x-ray, pathological focused lung ultrasound (FLUS) findings of a consolidation measuring >1 cm or a focal/asymmetrical B-lines pattern have shown a sensitivity of 87·8% and a specificity of 58·5% in one study in a general practice population. A practical algorithm incorporating chest x-ray to improve specificity has been proposed but may be unfeasible in many primary care settings. The effect of FLUS on antibiotic prescribing has only been evaluated once but in combination with procalcitonin point-of-care (POC) testing, in which it did not provide additional reduction in prescribing rates. Added value of this study The clinical impact of adding FLUS as a standalone POC examination on antibiotic prescribing in general practice was unexplored prior to this study. We show that our approach of adding FLUS, guided by clinical integration principles rather than a fixed diagnostic algorithm, to usual care management containing C-reactive protein POC testing, does not lead to a 15% or larger reduction in antibiotic prescribing. As this trial was not powered to detect a smaller reduction, more or larger studies are needed to detect a potential more modest effect of FLUS on antibiotics prescribing. However, FLUS was associated with fewer reconsultations for the same lower respiratory tract infection (LRTI) episode in general practice or out-of-hours primary care, possibly reflecting a reassurance effect for both GPs and patients regarding the initial diagnosis. This trial was conducted with a pragmatic design across a broad sample of general practices in Denmark, enhancing the generalisability of the findings. The near-complete follow-up and high diary completion rate further strengthen the validity of the results. Although the primary outcome did not reach statistical significance, the observed reduction in reconsultations suggests that FLUS may contribute to improved confidence in clinical decision-making. Implications of all the available evidence Current evidence does not support routine use of FLUS in all adults presenting in general practice with symptoms of acute lower respiratory tract infection where pneumonia is suspected. However, there is no evidence to suggest that FLUS poses a safety concern in this patient population. More evidence is needed to inform clinical integration strategies or diagnostic algorithms, that combine clinical assessment and FLUS findings to enhance specificity without increasing the risk of undertreatment. Introduction The threat of antimicrobial resistance is among the most pressing concerns for global public health. Antibiotic use is recognised as the main driver, and prescribing in primary healthcare, particularly in general practice, is a major contributor. Acute lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) are among the most common indications for antibiotic use in general practice, despite most being of viral origin and unlikely to benefit from antibiotic treatment. The diagnosis of pneumonia in general practice relies heavily on clinical assessment, and differentiating self-limiting viral infections from bacterial pneumonia is often challenging. , It is well known that this diagnostic uncertainty results in overuse of antibiotics. Point-of-care (POC) test strategies have been introduced to support general practitioners (GPs) in differentiating bacterial from viral infections. The C-reactive protein (CRP) POC test is the most widely used and reduces the likelihood of unnecessary antibiotic prescribing. Danish national guidelines recommend the CRP ‘speedometer’ model, in which the recommendation to prescribe antibiotics increases from CRP 20 mg/L towards values above 100 mg/L. , Within this CRP interval, the decision to prescribe antibiotics should primarily depend on clinical assessment. However, multiple CRP algorithms exist, and studies report variation in adherence. Chest x-ray is used in fewer than 10% of patients as a diagnostic aid for pneumonia in Danish general practice. Thus, imaging is not routinely used in the diagnostic work-up of patients presenting with acute LRTI in Danish general practice. Consequently, strategies to reduce diagnostic uncertainty are needed to support GPs in adopting more restrictive antibiotic prescribing, without increasing the risk of delayed antibiotic prescribing. Focused lung ultrasound (FLUS) has gained increasing attention as a POC diagnostic tool in recent years. Numerous reviews and meta-analyses support FLUS as a valuable tool for diagnosing pneumonia with high diagnostic accuracy. , , However, most evidence stems from secondary care settings and hospitalised populations. Ultrasound is now increasingly available and used in general practices for various purposes. To date, general practice research on FLUS has focused on training GPs, , , , the diagnostic accuracy and feasibility of FLUS , and its effect on antibiotic prescribing when combined with procalcitonin POC testing. The clinical impact of adding FLUS as a standalone POC modality on antibiotic prescribing in general practice remains unexplored. The aim of this randomised controlled trial was to evaluate the effect of adding

To date, general practice research on FLUS has focused on training GPs, , , , the diagnostic accuracy and feasibility of FLUS , and its effect on antibiotic prescribing when combined with procalcitonin POC testing. The clinical impact of adding FLUS as a standalone POC modality on antibiotic prescribing in general practice remains unexplored. The aim of this randomised controlled trial was to evaluate the effect of adding FLUS to usual care on antibiotic prescribing in patients with acute LRTI in whom the GP suspected pneumonia. A potential reduction in antibiotic prescribing was not intended to result in undertreatment of bacterial infections; consequently, patients’ clinical course was closely monitored as a secondary objective. Methods Study design and participants The PLUS-FLUS study was conducted as a pragmatic, randomised post-market (phase 5) superiority trial with a parallel two-group design, involving 34 GPs from 28 office-based general practice clinics across Denmark. GPs were involved as an advisory panel during the study design phase to ensure clinical relevance and feasibility. This trial is registered and statistical analysis plan available at ClinicalTrials.gov , NCT06210282 . Eligible patients were consecutively identified by the GP or assisting staff upon presentation to participating clinics. Adults (≥18 years) with acute cough (<21 days) and at least one additional symptom of acute LRTI (e.g. fever, sputum, dyspnoea, wheezing, chest discomfort), in whom the GP suspected bacterial pneumonia, were invited by the GP to participate. Patients were excluded if they: (1) had received antibiotic treatment for the current episode of acute LRTI, (2) were not listed with the GP (making medical record follow-up impossible), (3) were unable to understand or provide informed consent, or (4) declined to participate. Specialists in family medicine, working as GPs and using ultrasound weekly in practice or out-of-hours primary care, were eligible to enrol patients. Completion of a FLUS training programme with a validated assessment was required; those already trained attended a 1-h brush-up session. Accordingly, a FLUS training programme was offered before patient enrolment. Details of GP recruitment strategy, timeline of enrolment, and description of the FLUS training programme offered, are found in the . All participants gave written informed consent, patients including consent for data extraction from medical and Shared Medication Records. Patients’ sex was recorded using the unique personal identification number assigned to all Danish citizens while GPs self-reported this as free-text. Ethics The study protocol was approved by The Research Unit for General Practice in Aalborg (194-2) and the Scientific Ethics Committee of North Denmark Region (reference number: N-20230038). The study was conducted in accordance with the protocol without any adaptations. Written informed consent was obtained from all GPs and patients ahead of enrolment. Randomisation and masking Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either usual care (control) or FLUS (intervention), where GPs performed and interpreted FLUS as an additional procedure during the index consultation (day 0). Randomisation was performed using a web-based system with permuted block sizes (2, 4, 6), stratified by GP for balanced enrolment. Allocation sequences and sealed envelopes were prepared by two affiliated researchers not otherwise involved in the trial. At randomisation, the GP opened the top envelope and group allocation was revealed to both the GP and the patient. Outcome assessors and data analysts were blinded to group allocation. until database lock and primary analysis completion. Procedures All patients received usual care, reflecting current standard diagnostic assessments and clinical management in Danish general practices. Usual care was recommended to follow national guidelines, which define pneumonia as a clinical diagnosis based on symptoms (acute cough and at least one other LRTI symptom) and clinical signs such as poor general condition and/or fever. , POC CRP testing was recommended. No clear recommendations were provided regarding referral for chest x-ray. FLUS was not considered part of usual care. Randomisation took place after usual care completion and before any treatment was commenced. Patients randomised to the FLUS group received a FLUS examination in addition to usual care. GPs were instructed to follow a 14-zone FLUS scanning protocol previously applied across various settings, , including general practice in a similar patient population. The positioning of the patient during the examination was decided by the GP, either an upright or supine position or both. GPs used the ultrasound device available to them in their clinic. Types, brands, models and transducers are provided in the . GPs were trained to identify and classify FLUS pathological findings according to the European Federation of Societies for Ultrasound in Medicine and Biology (EFSUMB) coursebook, the feasibility of which had previously been tested in general practice. See the for the classification of pathological findings.

Types, brands, models and transducers are provided in the . GPs were trained to identify and classify FLUS pathological findings according to the European Federation of Societies for Ultrasound in Medicine and Biology (EFSUMB) coursebook, the feasibility of which had previously been tested in general practice. See the for the classification of pathological findings. GPs were guided to interpret FLUS findings according to the following principles: Small subpleural consolidations (2–20 mm), multiple and bilateral, with pleural irregularities and bilateral B-lines typically suggest a viral infection. In contrast, larger unilateral consolidations with air bronchogram, and in some cases pleural effusion, often indicate bacterial infection. Depending on infection severity, focal multiple B-lines might be the only detectable sign of bacterial infection, potentially indicating early or mild disease; however, their diagnostic specificity remains limited. , Nevertheless, FLUS cannot detect infections confined to the deeper lung parenchyma that do not extend to the tissue directly beneath the visceral pleura. Based on this knowledge, the clinical integration of FLUS and its implications for patient management were left to the discretion of the GPs. The FLUS training programme and 1-h brush-up session included guidance on the interpretation of pathological findings and the principles for clinical integration as described above. For each enrolled patient, the GP completed an electronic case report form in REDCap© (developed by Vanderbilt University and hosted by Aalborg University, Denmark) during or immediately after the index consultation. Information included patient baseline characteristics, symptoms, clinical findings, and any POC tests performed (e.g. CRP). The GP also registered in the case report form whether antibiotics were prescribed at the index consultation (yes/no) (primary outcome data), specifying if the prescription was immediate or wait-and-see. For patients allocated to the FLUS group, the GP documented FLUS findings. During follow-up, GPs were permitted to reassess patients at any time if deemed necessary, and no concomitant care or diagnostic procedures were restricted. All follow-up data were likewise collected using REDCap©. Patients received a validated LRTI Symptom Diary via short message service (SMS), covering the period from day 0 to day 21. The diary included items covering six dimensions: cough, dyspnoea, sputum production, general well-being, sleep disturbance and activity limitations. Patients were asked to score each of the six dimensions daily using a seven-point Likert scale (0 = no problem to 6 = as bad as it could be). The diary also contained daily questions regarding cancellation of work-related and leisure activities. On the day of the index consultation, patients were also asked to rate their satisfaction with the consultation, assessed on a five-point Likert scale (1 = very dissatisfied to 5 = very satisfied). A paper version of the diary was offered to patients who preferred not to receive the electronic format. Data on changes in medication or new prescriptions across all healthcare sectors are automatically uploaded to a Danish national digital system, the Shared Medication Record. The principal investigator (PI) collected data on all antibiotics prescribed for systemic use (Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical Classification System [ATC] code J01) from day 0–28, regardless of indication, using the patients’ Shared Medication Records. The PI collected patients' medical records on-site at general practice clinics, covering all documentation from general practice and correspondence from both primary and secondary care from day 0–60. An affiliated researcher, not otherwise involved in the trial, pseudonymised the records and concealed group allocation. The PI and a second affiliated researcher independently extracted relevant data using a pilot-tested data extraction tool. The datasets were compared, and discrepancies resolved through reassessment of the respective patient's medical record. Outcomes The primary outcome was the proportion of patients prescribed antibiotics at the index consultation (day 0), reported by the GP. The relative risk (RR) of antibiotic prescribing at the index consultation was also calculated to compare groups. Secondary outcomes and prespecified exploratory outcomes (∗) from the LRTI symptom diary were: (1) The daily total LRTI symptom score, calculated as the sum of scores for six symptoms, with values ranging from 0 to 36. The scores were presented as mean or median from day 0 to day 21. (2) The number of days with symptoms rated as a 'moderate problem' or worse (at least one symptom received a score of 3 or higher), presented as mean or median days in the period from day 0 to day 21. (3) The number of days patients signed in sick or cancelled work-related activities, presented as mean or median days in the period from day 0 to day 21. (4) The number of days patients cancelled leisure activities, presented as

(5) ∗Satisfaction with the index consultation on day 0 was measured by the proportion of patients who reported being satisfied or very satisfied (scores of 4 or 5) with the index consultation. (3) ∗The proportion of prescriptions prescribed as delayed antibiotic prescription at the index consultation. (2) ∗The proportion of patients who had any primary care contact (defined as any contact with general practice or out-of-hours services) for the LRTI episode within 28 days after the index consultation. (3) The proportion of patients admitted to the hospital within 28 days following the index consultation. (4) The proportion of patients with complications during hospitalisation (pleural infection (complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema), lung abscess, or sepsis)) within 28 days after the index consultation. (5) ∗The proportion of patients who underwent any imaging other than FLUS in secondary health care services within 28 days after the index consultation. (6) ∗The types of other imaging modalities performed within 28 days after the index consultation. (7) ∗The proportion of patients referred for suspected cancer within 60 days after the index consultation. (8) ∗The proportion of patients diagnosed with cancer within 60 days after the index consultation. (9) The number of spontaneously reported unintended events by GPs up to 60 days after the index consultation. (10) The proportion of patients who died from any cause by day 28 and day 60. Statistical analysis A sample size of 340 patients, with 170 allocated to each arm, was calculated to provide 80% power at a 5% significance level to detect an absolute reduction in antibiotic prescribing from 50% in the usual care group to 35% in the FLUS group. These assumptions were informed by previous studies on patients with LRTI in general practice. , , We assumed a maximum dropout or discontinuation rate of 10% and increased the sample size by an additional 5% to adjust for covariates in the analyses. Consequently, we aimed to include a total of 390 patients (195 in each arm). Baseline characteristics were tested for normality. Normally distributed data were presented as means with standard deviation. Non-normally distributed data were presented as medians with interquartile ranges. All patients were analysed according to the intention-to-treat principle. Mixed-effects Poisson regressions with robust variance estimation were used to estimate RRs with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Chi-square test was used for comparison of proportions. A mixed-effects repeated-measures model was used for comparing daily symptom diary scores. Generalised linear models were used to estimate outcome means. Formal interaction tests were performed on predefined subgroups. All analyses accounted for clustering by the 34 recruiting GPs to adjust for variations in usual care. To address non-normality in outcome data, bootstrap resampling with 1000 iterations was applied. No data monitoring committee was established and no interim analyses performed. All analyses were conducted using STATA 17·0 (StataCorp. 2021. Stata: Release 17. Statistical Software. College Station, TX: StataCorp LLC.) Role of funding source The funders of the study had no role in study design, data collection, data analyses, interpretation, or writing of the report. Results Between November 1, 2023, and July 10, 2024, 523 patients were assessed for eligibility and 392 were enrolled, meeting the planned sample size. Of these, 199 patients were randomly assigned to the usual care group and 193 patients to FLUS group. One patient in each group was excluded after enrolment but before analysis due to being under 18 years of age. the report. Results Between November 1, 2023, and July 10, 2024, 523 patients were assessed for eligibility and 392 were enrolled, meeting the planned sample size. Of these, 199 patients were randomly assigned to the usual care group and 193 patients to FLUS group. One patient in each group was excluded after enrolment but before analysis due to being under 18 years of age. One patient in the usual care group received FLUS at the index consultation but was included in the intention-to-treat analysis, resulting in 390 patients analysed for the primary outcome ( ). Baseline characteristics were generally similar between groups ( ), apart from a higher prevalence of asthma in the FLUS group and more non-pulmonary comorbidities in the usual care group that could influence the indication for antibiotics. The median age of patients was 58 years (IQR:44–70), and 211 of 390 (54%) were female. The most common symptoms at the index consultation were sputum production in 78% (303/390), fever (temperature ≥38·0 °C) in 54% (209/390) and dyspnoea in 52% of patients (202/390). The most frequent clinical finding reported by GPs was abnormal lung auscultation in 41% of patients (158/390), and almost all patients (99% (388/390)) underwent CRP POC testing. The median CRP value was 16 mg/L (IQR:5·8–51·0). For the primary outcome, 69 of 192 patients (36%) in the FLUS group were prescribed antibiotics at index consultation. In the usual care group, 81 of 198 patients (41%) were prescribed antibiotics, corresponding to a non-significant reduction in risk in the FLUS group, with a RR of 0·88 (95% CI: 0·68–1·14) ( ). Detailed subgroup analyses of the primary outcome for patients with CRP ≥50 mg/L, age ≥80 years, COPD or general lung disease comorbidities are presented in the . For secondary outcomes, follow-up data from Shared Medication Records and medical records were available for 387 patients. Secondary outcome results are presented in . In both groups, antibiotic prescriptions accumulated through day seven, with a higher proportion in the usual care group (99 of 195 patients, 50%) than in the FLUS group (81 of 192 patients, 42%). Still, the RR of having antibiotics prescribed up until day seven was not significantly lower in the FLUS group than in the usual care group ( ). A total of 18 patients were referred for suspected cancer within 60 days. Of these, five patients in the usual care group and one in the FLUS group were specifically referred for suspected lung cancer. The RR of patient reconsultation for the current LRTI episode in general practice or out-of-hour primary care within 28 days was significantly lower in the FLUS group (RR 0·76, CI: 0·58–0·98, p = 0·038), but no significant difference was found for reconsulting for any reason ( ). Chest x-ray was the most frequently used secondary imaging modality, performed in 19 of 192 patients (10%) in the FLUS group and 22 of 195 patients (11%) in the usual care group. Chest CT was performed in four of 192 patients (2%) in the FLUS group and six of 195 patients (3%) in the usual care group. Imaging unrelated to the lungs (e.g., other ultrasonography modalities, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), CT or x-ray (not of the chest)) was performed in five patients in the FLUS group and 13 patients in the usual care group. Of the 390 patients enrolled, 353 (91%) completed at least one day of the LRTI symptom diary: 183 in the FLUS group and 170 in the usual care group. The overall response rate was 81% with a mean of 18 (SD 5·7) days completed in the FLUS group and 17 (SD 6·5) days in the usual care group. No significant differences were observed between the two groups in LRTI symptom diary outcomes ( and ). Patient satisfaction with the index consultation was high as 91% of responding patients in both groups reported being satisfied or very satisfied (137/149 (usual care) and 145/159 (FLUS)). No unintended events within 60 days were reported. Significant pathological findings on FLUS were reported by GPs in 85 of the 192 (44%) patients randomised to the FLUS group. Among patients with pathological FLUS findings, 55 of 85 (65%) were prescribed antibiotics at the index consultation, compared with only 14 of 107 (13%) among those without pathological findings (unadjusted for confounders). The most common pathological findings in the 85 patients included focal ≥3 B-lines in 61 patients (72%), subpleural consolidation(s) (2–20 mm) in 17 (20%), pleural effusion in 11 (13%), larger consolidations in 9 (11%), interstitial syndrome in 5 (6%) and isolated visceral pleural pathology in 4 (5%). Characteristics of the 34 GPs who enrolled study participants are shown in . Fourteen GPs had no or less than one year of experience using FLUS when recruited. Twenty-nine of the GPs completed the FLUS training programme offered before patient enrolment. Results from the FLUS training programme and comparisons between participating GPs and the national population of Danish GPs are presented in the . Discussion Adding FLUS to usual care did not lead to the expected 15% reduction in antibiotic prescriptions at the index consultation. However, reconsultations related to the current LRTI episode in general practice or out-of-hours primary care were significantly reduced in the FLUS group. FLUS was not associated with any adverse effects on patient safety, symptom duration or severity or patients’ satisfaction with the consultation. However, the wide CIs observed for some secondary outcomes introduce uncertainty about the true RRs. The reduction in antibiotic prescribing found in our study with the addition of FLUS to usual care was smaller than hypothesised and modest compared with other POC testing interventions evaluated for similar purposes in general practice settings. , , Our study was powered to detect a 15% absolute reduction; therefore, it was underpowered to identify the 5% absolute reduction at the index consultation. Considering antibiotics prescribed during follow-up, the accumulated absolute reduction within the first week was 8% in the FLUS group, but this difference was also not statistically significant. At the index consultation, the antibiotic prescribing rate in the usual care group was 41%, which was lower than anticipated. This expectation had been based, among other sources, on a 2007 Danish study that reported a 56% prescribing rate in a comparable patient population. However, our findings did not indicate a stronger effect of FLUS on antibiotic prescribing within subgroups where prescribing rates were naturally higher (see the ). The effect of adding FLUS into routine diagnostic procedures on antibiotic prescribing has previously been evaluated in a prospective observational study with 148 patients in French emergency departments. Use of a 12-zone FLUS protocol led to changes in antibiotic management in 47 of 148 patients (32%), with 21 treatments initiated and 26 discontinued. Consistent with our study, this study showed no significant overall reduction in antibiotic prescribing. However, it did suggest a shift in the subset of patients to whom antibiotics were prescribed. Whether a similar pattern occurred in our study remains unclear. Nevertheless, any potential redistribution of antibiotic prescribing associated with FLUS did not translate into a clinically meaningful difference in patient outcomes, as the clinical course was comparable between groups. As previously stated, this is the first randomised trial evaluating the effect of adding FLUS alone to usual care. To date, only one previous randomised trial has assessed the combined effect of the addition of sequential procalcitonin POC testing and FLUS to usual care on antibiotic prescribing in Swiss general practices. In that three-armed trial did the addition of FLUS at a predefined procalcitonin cut-off in a small patient sample not significantly reduce antibiotic prescribing compared with procalcitonin POC testing alone added to usual care. Usual care in the Swiss study did not include CRP testing, whereas nearly all patients (99%) in our study received a CRP POC test as part of usual care. Consequently, our study did not assess the impact of FLUS in isolation, but rather its effect when added to a standard care protocol that included CRP testing. While incorporating a study arm evaluating FLUS in the absence of CRP testing might have been informative and broadened the generalizability of our findings, such an approach would not have pragmatically reflected standard care in Danish general practice. A key strength of this study is its pragmatic design, which closely mirrors routine clinical practice and the patient population typically encountered by GPs. This strengthens the study's external validity. The study was designed to minimize recall bias in the registrations by both GPs and patients. Furthermore, there was no indication of information bias in the GPs' registrations of antibiotic prescribing at the index consultation, as these data were cross-validated with entries in the Shared Medication Records by the PI for quality assurance. Comprehensive follow-up of the clinical course was achieved, with minimal loss to follow-up and a high response rate for the symptom diary. These features contributed to robust evidence regarding the impact of adding FLUS to usual care for the patient population studied. However, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, participating GPs were self-selected

recall bias in the registrations by both GPs and patients. Furthermore, there was no indication of information bias in the GPs' registrations of antibiotic prescribing at the index consultation, as these data were cross-validated with entries in the Shared Medication Records by the PI for quality assurance. Comprehensive follow-up of the clinical course was achieved, with minimal loss to follow-up and a high response rate for the symptom diary. These features contributed to robust evidence regarding the impact of adding FLUS to usual care for the patient population studied. However, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, participating GPs were self-selected and represented a subgroup (12%) of Danish GPs using POC ultrasound, potentially limiting generalisability. Therefore, our results may not fully reflect average prescribing practices among Danish GPs. Baseline prescribing rates reported in reflect practice-level data rather than individual prescribing habits, which were not available. The low baseline antibiotic prescribing and also the high uptake of CRP POC testing may potentially limit international applicability. Furthermore, participation in this trial may itself alter clinical and prescribing behaviour (Hawthorne effect), especially when GPs are unblinded to both study outcomes and allocation. Another limitation is the absence of data on symptom duration before the index consultation. Symptom duration could have affected both clinical assessment and FLUS findings, as well as the GP's subsequent management decision. This study reflects the impact of adding FLUS to usual care when GPs are guided by principles of clinical integration rather than a fixed diagnostic algorithm. Such an algorithm has, however, been proposed by Rodriguez-Contreras and colleagues. However, their algorithm would require a chest x-ray in all cases of focal or asymmetrical B-lines pattern without consolidations. Based on previous research, we anticipated that such patterns would predominate in most patients with pathological findings. , Introducing this algorithm could lead to an increased use of chest x-ray, with associated increases in costs and patient radiation exposure in a Danish clinical context. Consequently, we chose a pragmatic design in which the FLUS training programme and the brush-up session incorporated the best available knowledge on pathological findings and clinical interpretation. The results of our study probably reflect persistent uncertainties regarding the relationship between pathological FLUS findings, pathogen likelihood and disease severity progression in general practice. Whether a more conservative definition of pneumonia on FLUS (requiring consolidation) can be used in general practice, without compromising patient safety and clinical course, is unknown. As these relationships become clearer, the clinical utility of FLUS may improve. Notably, only 14 of the 107 patients in the FLUS group with no pathological FLUS findings were prescribed antibiotics. The underlying mechanism remains unclear. Possible explanations include that pathological FLUS findings aligned with pronounced symptoms supporting antibiotic use, or that a normal FLUS had a strong deterrent effect on prescribing decisions. These hypotheses fall outside the scope of this study but warrant further exploration. Patients in the FLUS group had a lower likelihood of reconsulting general practice or out-of-hours primary care for the same LRTI episode within 28 days than patients receiving usual care. Any contact initiated by either the GP or the patient that related in any way to the current LRTI episode was classified as a reconsultation. Despite the uncertainties described above, this finding suggests a possible reassurance mechanism affecting both the GP and the patient regarding the initial diagnosis. Previous research supports this interpretation , as GPs reported increased diagnostic confidence in 69 of 91 cases (76%) after performing FLUS in a similar patient population. Future research should investigate if a more modest effect on antibiotic prescribing can be detected or if there is a larger potential of adding FLUS to usual care in settings with higher antibiotic prescribing rates. Human antibiotic consumption in Denmark is relatively low compared with that in other European countries, and antibiotic prescribing rates in the usual care group were lower than anticipated. Moreover, longer-term studies are warranted to assess the safety of FLUS over time and to inform clinical referral guidelines for suspected pulmonary cancer based on FLUS findings in general practice. In our study, none of the patients referred with suspected cancer were diagnosed with cancer within the 60-day follow-up period; however, in a few cases, diagnostic clarification was still pending. FLUS is not recommended as a routine tool for all adults with suspected pneumonia based on this trial's findings. However, the study found no evidence of patient harm associated with the addition of FLUS to usual care. Future studies should carefully evaluate whether FLUS may contribute to missed diagnoses of pulmonary cancer; however, our study indicates no safety concerns related to its use in this patient population.
