Topical retinoids (tazarotene) are vitamin A derivatives that regulate keratinocyte proliferation, normalise skin differentiation, and downregulate the expression of proinflammatory genes. Topical calcineurin inhibitors (pimecrolimus, tacrolimus), while indicated and mainly used in atopic dermatitis, can be used for psoriasis, specifically for sensitive sites (face and intertriginous areas). They inhibit T‐cell activation and proinflammatory cytokine synthesis by inhibiting the calcineurin. Topical salicylic acid acts as a keratolytic agent, which reduces scaling. Salicylic acid is used mainly on thick psoriasis plaque. Topical anthralin (dithranol) and coal tar were widely used previously, but their use has decreased because of their risk of skin irritation and reversible staining of skin and clothes [ ]. A 2013 Cochrane Review update, based on 177 randomised controlled trials (including 26 trials of scalp psoriasis and 6 trials of inverse psoriasis, facial psoriasis, or both), concluded that for both body and scalp psoriasis, combined treatment with vitamin D and corticosteroids performed significantly better than either vitamin D alone or corticosteroid alone. Vitamin D generally performed better than coal tar, but findings relative to dithranol were mixed. For psoriasis of the scalp, vitamin D was significantly less effective than both potent corticosteroids and very potent corticosteroids. For both body and scalp psoriasis, potent corticosteroids were less likely than vitamin D to cause local adverse events [ ]. Since then, several new topical treatments have been tested for plaque psoriasis. Topical phosphodiesterase 4 (PDE4) inhibitors (roflumilast and crisaborole) result in downregulation of immune modulators, including tumour necrosis factor‐alpha, interferon‐gamma, interleukin‐17, and interleukin‐23. Roflumilast once daily was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2022 for plaque psoriasis, based on two phase III trials versus an inactive base vehicle [ ]. Crisaborole is FDA approved for atopic dermatitis, and was assessed against placebo for plaque psoriasis [ ]. A topical aryl hydrocarbon receptor agonist (tapinarof) modulates the expression of interleukin‐17. Tapinarof 1% cream once daily was FDA approved for plaque psoriasis in 2022, based on two phase III trials versus an inactive base vehicle [ ]. JAK inhibitors inhibit the intracellular signal pathway JAK/STAT, blocking the gene transcription of proinflammatory cytokines. Ruxolitinib cream is approved for atopic dermatitis (FDA) and vitiligo (FDA, European Medicines Agency (EMA)), and was assessed against an inactive base vehicle for plaque psoriasis [ ]. Tofacitinib ointment was compared to placebo in a phase II trial for psoriasis, but does not have any regulatory approval [ ]. Delgocitinib cream is EMA approved for moderate to severe chronic hand eczema in adults who cannot use corticosteroids [ ]. Why it is important to do this review Half of the people with psoriasis have less than 2% or 3% of their body surface area involved; a further 30% to 35% have less than 10% of their body surface area involved [ , ]. Most of these people will manage their condition exclusively with topical treatment. Robust evidence synthesis is essential so that clinicians and people with psoriasis can understand the relative efficacy and safety of available topical treatments and psoriasis. Since the publication of the updated Cochrane Review that assessed topical treatments for chronic plaque psoriasis in 2013, several trials have been carried out, including those evaluating several new treatments [ ]. Most new topical treatments are only compared to an inactive base vehicle, which makes efficacy and safety comparisons difficult. For systemic treatment of psoriasis, there are several systematic reviews with a network meta‐analysis (NMA), including a living Cochrane review, available. However, systematic reviews with NMA that compare all available topical treatments for plaque psoriasis are lacking [ ]. Objectives To evaluate the relative benefits and harms of topical pharmacological treatments in plaque psoriasis in adults and children, and rank their effectiveness and safety through a network meta‐analysis. Methods We will follow the Methodological Expectations for Cochrane Intervention Reviews (MECIR) when conducting the review, and PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA‐NMA for the reporting [ , , ]. Criteria for considering studies for this review Types of studies We will include individually‐randomised, parallel‐group trials and cross‐over trials, in which we will consider only the first phase, in order to avoid the risk of carry‐over effects in subsequent periods. We will exclude intra‐individual/split‐body studies because in this type of design, the unit of analysis is a part of the body or a lesion rather than the person. We will also exclude studies in which topical treatments were applied to selected plaque(s), such as plaque test studies [ ], since there is a significant risk of contamination between different topical treatments that the participants must apply to different lesions, as well as the risk of a carry‐over effect [ ]. We will exclude cluster‐randomised trials, as this study design may not be appropriate for generating

carry‐over effects in subsequent periods. We will exclude intra‐individual/split‐body studies because in this type of design, the unit of analysis is a part of the body or a lesion rather than the person. We will also exclude studies in which topical treatments were applied to selected plaque(s), such as plaque test studies [ ], since there is a significant risk of contamination between different topical treatments that the participants must apply to different lesions, as well as the risk of a carry‐over effect [ ]. We will exclude cluster‐randomised trials, as this study design may not be appropriate for generating evidence about individual treatment choices. Types of participants We will include trials that include participants of any age, with a clinical diagnosis of plaque psoriasis that affects any part of the body, including the scalp, folds, and face. We will exclude trials that include other types of psoriasis (guttate, generalised, or palmoplantar pustular and erythrodermic, nail psoriasis). If trials include both eligible and non‐eligible participants, we will only include those that report results separately, so we can include data from eligible participants only. Types of interventions As a living systematic review, we will continually identify new interventions, and exclude interventions that are no longer of interest (e.g. topical drugs that have been withdrawn). We will include all topical pharmacological treatments for plaque psoriasis, regardless of the base vehicle of application, including cream, lotion, gel, solution, foam, or ointment. To provide informative results for stakeholders and guideline developers, since numerous molecules have been assessed in trials but not further developed, we will only include treatments approved by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) or the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for topical psoriasis or other skin diseases (e.g. eczema, vitiligo), and we will only include these treatments at their licenced concentration(s) and application frequencies. We will include these treatments: Topical corticosteroids, classified according to the consolidated 7‐category US System into 4 categories (weak, moderate, potent, super potent) [ , ] Calcineurin inhibitors Vitamin D analogues Retinoids Salicylic acid Anthralin Coal tar Phosphodiesterase 4 (PDE4) inhibitors Aryl hydrocarbon receptor agonist Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors We will include trials comparing these treatments with each other or with a placebo, inactive base vehicle, or emollient. We will also include trials that assess a combination of these treatments as an active intervention. We will exclude trials that assess a topical treatment used in combination with systemic treatment of psoriasis (conventional, small molecules or biologic) or phototherapy. We will also exclude trials that use, as a comparator, a pharmacological topical treatment that includes the same topical treatment as the intervention, but at a different dosage, different formulation, or different frequency of application. In multi‐arm trials, we will exclude study groups that assess drugs other than those mentioned above, or at an unlicensed dosage or unusual frequency of application. Outcome measures No core outcome set for trials assessing treatments for plaque psoriasis is available. However, since 2018, core domains have been identified: skin manifestations (subdomains of primary skin manifestations, skin lesion location, palmoplantar psoriasis, and scalp psoriasis), psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis symptoms, investigator global assessment, patient global assessment, health‐related quality of life, and treatment satisfaction [ ]. We will not consider arthritis symptoms, as people with psoriatic arthritis are usually treated with systemic treatments. We chose critical and important outcomes according to core domains, and results of a consumer focus group (see ). We will exclude outcomes that measure the effect of treatments at the lesion level (rather than the participant level), because they are not clinically relevant to the way people are treated and live with psoriasis as a whole. Many different instruments are used in trials to assess severity, quality of life, or symptoms [ ]. We will not consider patient‐reported instruments that have been mixed into a single scale or score, or that measure different domains (severity, quality of life or symptoms). The Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI) score combines the assessment of the severity of lesions and the body surface area affected [ ]. PASI 90, PASI 75, and PASI 50 correspond to the percentage of participants reaching 90%, 75%, and 50% improvement, respectively, from their baseline PASI score. Critical outcomes Health‐related quality of life: measured by a validated scale, such as the Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI), Skindex, and Psoriasis Disability Index (PDI), and reported as a continuous measure [ , ]. We will prioritise the DLQI, followed by the Skindex, and then the PDI. Clear or almost‐clear disease status: proportion of participants who reach a clear or almost‐clear status, based on overall clinical disease severity (scaling, erythema, and plaque thickness), assessed by the physician. We will prioritise the Investigator's Global Assessment of Disease Severity (IGA) or the Physician Global Assessment (PGA) − reduction of two or more points and reaching

quality of life: measured by a validated scale, such as the Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI), Skindex, and Psoriasis Disability Index (PDI), and reported as a continuous measure [ , ]. We will prioritise the DLQI, followed by the Skindex, and then the PDI. Clear or almost‐clear disease status: proportion of participants who reach a clear or almost‐clear status, based on overall clinical disease severity (scaling, erythema, and plaque thickness), assessed by the physician. We will prioritise the Investigator's Global Assessment of Disease Severity (IGA) or the Physician Global Assessment (PGA) − reduction of two or more points and reaching a score of 0 (clear) or 1 (almost clear), and then the Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI) 90 [ , ]. All these measures correspond to a clear or almost‐clear status. Local adverse events: proportion of participants with local adverse events, including local irritation, burning sensation, or skin atrophy. Each participant will be counted once if they experience any such event. Each outcome will be assessed in the short term (1 to 16 weeks) and long term (over 16 weeks). Important outcomes Clinician or investigator‐assessed severity: measured as a continuous measure. We will prioritise the Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI), or a binary transformation of a continuous scale of investigator‐ or clinician‐assessed signs. In the absence of continuous measures, we will use 75% improvement in PASI (PASI 75), 90% improvement in PASI (PASI 90), or 100% improvement in PASI (PASI 100) [ ]. Participant‐assessed severity: measurement of scaling, erythema, and plaque thickness on a participant assessment scale, such as the Patient's Global Assessment of Disease Severity (PaGA) or Patient’s Global Psoriasis Assessment (PGPA). We will analyse this outcome as both a continuous and binary outcome, depending on the data available in the included studies. For the dichotomous analysis, we will report the proportion of participants achieving a score of 0 (clear) or 1 (almost clear) [ ]. Participants' symptoms (itching, stinging, burning, pain, etc): measured on a scale, such as the Psoriasis Symptom Inventory (PSI), and reported as a continuous measure [ ] Participants' Itch: reported as a continuous measure. We will prioritise the Psoriasis Symptom Inventory (PSI), then Itch Severity Scale, and then the Worst Itch Numeric Rating Scale (WI‐NRS) score [ ] Withdrawals due to adverse events: proportion of participants who withdrew due to adverse events, including local adverse events Serious adverse events: proportion of participants with serious adverse events, defined according to the International Conference of Harmonization of Technical Requirements for Registration of Pharmaceuticals for Human Use, as any event resulting in death, being life‐threatening, requiring initial or prolonged hospitalisation, or requiring intervention to prevent permanent impairment or damage [ ]. Other important outcomes Participants' satisfaction: measured on a Likert scale or another available measure. We will analyse this outcome as either a continuous or a binary outcome, depending on the data available in the included articles. Flare prevention: measured as flare or no flare during maintenance treatment (meaning continuation of treatment after remission) We will assess each outcome in the short term (1 to 16 weeks) and long term (over 16 weeks). Search methods for identification of studies We aim to identify all relevant randomised controlled trials (RCTs), regardless of language or publication status (published, unpublished). We will report adverse events reported in the included studies, rather than performing a separate search for adverse events. Electronic searches For this living systematic review, we will revise our search strategies in line with advice from the Guidance for the production and publication of Cochrane living systematic reviews, using the search strategies detailed in [ ]. We will search: the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL; current date) in the Cochrane Library; MEDLINE via PubMed (1946 to current date) Embase via embase.com (1974 to current date) We are looking for any references about the application of topical treatment to psoriasis, while combining controlled vocabulary (from MeSH or Emtree) and natural language. We used the Cochrane Highly Sensitive Search Strategy to identify randomised trials in MEDLINE (PubMed format) and the Cochrane Highly Sensitive Search Strategy used for identifying controlled trials in Embase for CENTRAL (2023 revision, embase.com format), described in the technical supplement to chapter 4 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ ] to develop our search strategy. Trials registers World Health Organization (WHO) International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP; apps.who.int/trialsearch/; current date) US National Institutes of Health Ongoing Trials Register ClinicalTrials.gov (www.clinicaltrials.gov; current date) Searching other resources Unpublished literature We will contact the principal investigator of ongoing studies and of registered studies with no associated publication or no posted data in clinical registries for information on future publication plans. Retractions and errata We will search for studies labelled as retracted publications in CENTRAL. All bibliographic databases RIS files will be imported onto

the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ ] to develop our search strategy. Trials registers World Health Organization (WHO) International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP; apps.who.int/trialsearch/; current date) US National Institutes of Health Ongoing Trials Register ClinicalTrials.gov (www.clinicaltrials.gov; current date) Searching other resources Unpublished literature We will contact the principal investigator of ongoing studies and of registered studies with no associated publication or no posted data in clinical registries for information on future publication plans. Retractions and errata We will search for studies labelled as retracted publications in CENTRAL. All bibliographic databases RIS files will be imported onto Zotero [ ], which is linked to the Retraction Watch database and can flag retracted references. Annual review of search methods for this living systematic review Searches will be run every three months from the date of the previous update and screened. Analyses will be conducted annually. Data collection and analysis Selection of studies We will select studies using Covidence [ ]. Pairs of review authors will independently examine each title and abstract to exclude irrelevant reports, and then full texts of remaining reports [ ]. In case of disagreement, we will reach consensus by discussion with a third author, when needed, after contacting the study investigators for clarification. We will provide a PRISMA flowchart to illustrate the study selection process, and list the excluded studies and their reasons for exclusion in a characteristics of excluded studies table. As this is a living systematic review, we will conduct a new search every three months and screen new search records. Data extraction and management Pairs of review authors will independently extract the data from published and unpublished reports, using a standardised form via Covidence. According to the availability of data from different sources, we will extract the data from trial registers and peer‐reviewed journal publications. In cases of discrepancies, we will prioritise data from trial registers [ , ]. Outcome data We will extract arm‐level data from each included trial; hence, the total number of participants randomised to each intervention. When only contrast‐based data are available, we will collect these. For binary outcomes (e.g. adverse events, success on an IGA scale), we will extract the number of participants experiencing the event as the numerator and the total number of participants as the denominator. For continuous outcomes (e.g. PASI, DLQI), we will extract the mean change in the outcome measure from baseline with an associated measure of variance (e.g. deviation, confidence interval), or the baseline and follow‐up mean values with associated measures of variance, or the mean baseline value and mean percentage change from baseline with an associated measure of variance. If only median values are reported, we will extract these, and where possible, convert them to mean values using appropriate statistical methods [ ]. Data on potential effect modifiers We will extract baseline demographic and clinical characteristics of participants that may act as effect modifiers: baseline severity (e.g. PASI, BSA scores), year of publication, sex, age, and location of psoriasis (scalp, genital, inverse). Risk of bias assessment in included studies Pairs of review authors will independently assess the risk of bias (RoB); a third author will be consulted in case of discrepancies. We will assess the RoB for critical outcomes using the Cochrane RoB 2 tool [ ], and the Excel tool to implement RoB (available via www.riskofbias.info/welcome/rob‐2‐0‐tool/current‐version‐of‐rob‐2). For cross‐over trials, we will only consider the first phase of the study when applying the Cochrane RoB 2 tool for RCTs. We will assess the following domains, considering the effect of interest as the effect of assignment to the interventions at baseline, regardless of whether the interventions are received as intended: Bias arising from the randomisation process; Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; Bias due to missing outcome data; Bias in measurement of the outcome; and Bias in selection of the reported result. We will determine the overall RoB judgement for each trial and each outcome according to the RoB 2 tool as follows: Low risk of bias, if the trial is considered at a low risk of bias for all domains; Some concerns, if at least one domain is assessed as having some concerns, with no high risk of bias for other domains; High risk of bias, if at least one domain is at high risk of bias, or if multiple domains are assessed as having some concerns to an extent that substantially lowers confidence in the result. We will assess the RoB for the three critical outcome results, both in the short and long term. Measures of treatment effect For continuous outcomes, such as investigator‐assessed severity measured by the PASI scale or DLQI, we will use the mean difference (MD) for studies reporting on the same scale, and the standardised mean difference (SMD) for studies reporting on multiple scales.

for other domains; High risk of bias, if at least one domain is at high risk of bias, or if multiple domains are assessed as having some concerns to an extent that substantially lowers confidence in the result. We will assess the RoB for the three critical outcome results, both in the short and long term. Measures of treatment effect For continuous outcomes, such as investigator‐assessed severity measured by the PASI scale or DLQI, we will use the mean difference (MD) for studies reporting on the same scale, and the standardised mean difference (SMD) for studies reporting on multiple scales. When authors reported several scales for the same outcome, we will select a scale according to the following predefined hierarchy: first the DLQI, followed by the Skindex, and then the PDI, in order to avoid selective inclusion of results [ ]. According to Cochrane's recommendations, and to make the results more interpretable, pooled results on the SMD scale will be back‐transformed to MD on a prioritised scale [ ]. When multiple scales are reported across studies, we will also use direct mapping from one scale to another using a method proposed by Ades and colleagues to estimate conversion factors [ ]. This approach will allow us to combine study data using an MD. For binary outcomes, such as the proportion of participants achieving clear or almost clear skin on an IGA scale and all the safety outcomes, we will use the odds ratios (ORs) as the summary measure for effect estimate. To account for the inclusion of studies with zero events in both groups, we will use penalised likelihood regression as part of a sensitivity analysis [ ]. For every treatment, we will estimate the ranking probabilities of being at each possible rank for all outcomes. We will use the surface under the cumulative ranking curve (SUCRA) to infer the treatment hierarchy [ ]. We will express SUCRA as a percentage between 0 (when it is certain a treatment is the worst) to 100% (when it is certain a treatment is the best), and will present the results in a rank‐heat plot [ , ]. Unit of analysis issues The participant will be the primary unit of analysis. We will include parallel group trials. We will exclude studies that randomise individual lesions or body parts, including split‐body designs, plaque test design and cluster design. For trials with multiple intervention groups, we will analyse comparisons in the pairwise meta‐analyses as independent two‐arm studies; when multiple arms from the same study are included in the same meta‐analysis, we will split the shared comparator group to avoid double‐counting of participants [ ]. Dealing with missing data We will contact trial authors to obtain missing outcome data from included trials dating back less than 10 years. When faced with missing data for binary outcomes, we will consider that any participant with missing outcome data did not experience clearance (for efficacy outcomes) or did not experience adverse effects (for safety outcomes), whatever the group. We will perform a sensitivity analysis with the data, ignoring the missing participants (complete case analysis). To explore the potential impact of missing data more comprehensively, we will conduct additional sensitivity analyses using the Informative Missingness Odds Ratio approach for binary outcomes, and the Informative Missingness Difference of Means approach for continuous outcomes, accounting for the uncertainty due to missing outcome and basing imputations on observed outcomes [ , ]. Reporting bias assessment We will assess reporting biases, using an adaptation of the funnel plot, by subtracting from each study‐specific effect size the mean of the meta‐analysis of the study‐specific comparison, which we will plot against the study standard error [ ]. We will employ this 'comparison‐adjusted funnel plot' for all comparisons of an active treatment against placebo, using a hierarchy of interventions based on chronological order. In the case of substantial funnel plot asymmetry for critical outcomes, we will investigate the presence of small‐study effects in the network meta‐regression [ ]. Synthesis methods We will report descriptive statistics for the overall body of evidence, including the number of interventions, number of participants, mean participant age and range, average proportion of participants by sex and gender, and proportion of studies and outcomes with different levels of risk of bias. We will also report those items separately for each intervention node and intervention comparison. For each outcome, we will conduct pairwise meta‐analysis within each intervention comparison and network meta‐analysis (NMA) across intervention comparisons. For many interventions of interest, products are available in varying concentrations and base vehicles. We will combine various formulations of topical corticosteroids into nodes based on their potency classification, using the US 7‐category classification consolidated into four levels [ ]. For other interventions, we will create nodes combining molecules used at the same concentration regardless of the base vehicle.

outcomes with different levels of risk of bias. We will also report those items separately for each intervention node and intervention comparison. For each outcome, we will conduct pairwise meta‐analysis within each intervention comparison and network meta‐analysis (NMA) across intervention comparisons. For many interventions of interest, products are available in varying concentrations and base vehicles. We will combine various formulations of topical corticosteroids into nodes based on their potency classification, using the US 7‐category classification consolidated into four levels [ ]. For other interventions, we will create nodes combining molecules used at the same concentration regardless of the base vehicle. Combination therapies (e.g. Calcipotriol 50 µg/g + betamethasone dipropionate 0.5 mg/g ointment) will be combined in the same node if the potency of both the topical corticosteroid and the concentration of the non‐steroid active ingredient are the same. Pairwise meta‐analysis We will conduct pairwise meta‐analyses for all outcomes and comparisons, provided that at least two studies are available, using a random‐effects model. We will perform random‐effects meta‐analysis, since we expect the studies to be somewhat methodologically and clinically different. When we include three or more studies in an analysis, we will use the Wald‐type method if between‐study variance (Tau 2 ) = 0 [ ], and the Hartung‐Knapp‐Sidik‐Jonkman method if Tau 2 > 0 [ ] to estimate the 95% confidence interval (CI) of the summary effect. When we include two studies, we will use the Wald‐type method [ ]. We will calculate prediction intervals (PIs) for the summary effect to capture the interval within which we expect the true intervention effect of a new study to fall. We will estimate Tau 2 using the Restricted Maximum Likelihood and its 95% CI with the Q‐profile approach [ ]. We will explore potential heterogeneity using subsequent analyses, including meta‐regression, subgroup, and sensitivity analyses. We will conduct pairwise meta‐analyses using Review Manager [ ]. Network meta‐analysis For each outcome and a connected network diagram for which the number of studies is larger than the number of intervention nodes, we will perform a random‐effects frequentist network meta‐analysis (NMA), with multi‐arm studies properly handled under the NMA model. A common within‐network Tau 2 will be assumed across intervention comparisons, which is a clinically reasonable assumption, since interventions are of the same nature. We will estimate Tau 2 and its square root Tau using the Restricted Maximum Likelihood method. We will calculate effect estimates (MD, SMD, OR) and 95% CI between each intervention. Interventions will be ranked according to their relative effectiveness and safety, separately, using the SUCRA statistic, and will be visually presented in a rank‐heat plot [ , ]. Before conducting the NMA, we will assess the transitivity assumption. If this assumption is considered reasonable, direct and indirect estimates will be synthesised into a single mixed‐effect estimate, provided that the consistency assumption holds. We will assess transitivity for each network using the following effect modifiers: risk of bias, participant age, sex (percentage of female participants), psoriasis severity, treatment duration, and year of publication. We will visually assess whether these factors are, on average, similarly distributed across the intervention comparisons, using box plots for continuous variables and bar plots for categorical variables. We will evaluate consistency in each network using both local (node‐splitting) and global (design‐by‐treatment interaction model) approaches [ , ]. If we find intransitivity or inconsistency, we will perform subgroup and meta‐regression analyses to explore reasons for this. If we are still unable to identify reasons for intransitivity or inconsistency, we will present direct and indirect estimates separately, since we do not expect mixed effects to be valid. We will provide risk of bias assessments for each. For direct evidence, we will use the study‐level RoB evaluations. We will assess indirect evidence using the contribution matrix in accordance with CINeMA (Confidence in Network Meta‐Analysis) approach [ , ]. We will perform analyses using R software with the netmeta package [ , ]. Investigation of heterogeneity and subgroup analysis We will conduct subgroup analyses stratified by trial inclusion criteria and design for the NMA: trials of children (< 18 years) versus adults (≥ 18 years), trials with different psoriasis severity criteria (mild versus moderate versus severe), and trials with different psoriasis location (scalp versus genital versus inverse). We will interpret subgroup analysis results with caution, and assess the credibility of any apparent subgroup effects using the Instrument to assess the Credibility of Effect Modification Analyses (ICEMAN) tool [ , , ]. We will conduct network meta‐regression using the following characteristics to determine the impact of potential effect modifiers on the results: mean age, proportion female/women, baseline PASI score, and year of publication. We will perform network meta‐regression when ≥ 10 studies are available on the underlying outcome. Equity‐related assessment We will not investigate health equity in this review because the included studies are

versus genital versus inverse). We will interpret subgroup analysis results with caution, and assess the credibility of any apparent subgroup effects using the Instrument to assess the Credibility of Effect Modification Analyses (ICEMAN) tool [ , , ]. We will conduct network meta‐regression using the following characteristics to determine the impact of potential effect modifiers on the results: mean age, proportion female/women, baseline PASI score, and year of publication. We will perform network meta‐regression when ≥ 10 studies are available on the underlying outcome. Equity‐related assessment We will not investigate health equity in this review because the included studies are likely to be primarily pharmaceutical company‐sponsored trials, which are not designed to assess the effects of the interventions in different socio‐demographic groups. Nevertheless, we will report on the age, sex, and ethnicity distribution in the included studies. Sensitivity analysis We will perform an alternative NMA using the WHO’s Anatomical Therapeutic Classification 4‐level potency system to create nodes for topical corticosteroids. This will allow us to evaluate the impact of the classification system on the network's construction and findings [ ]. This analysis will be conducted for the critical outcomes for which an NMA is feasible, and will be limited to the primary analysis. We will compare the resulting network geometry, treatment effect estimates, and treatment rankings with those from the primary analysis to assess the impact of the potency classification on the structure and findings of the network. We will conduct sensitivity analyses by restricting the analysis to studies with low risk of overall bias, and a complete case analysis, excluding participants with missing outcome data. To address the issue of studies reporting zero events in both groups, we will conduct a sensitivity analysis using alternative statistical approaches, notably, penalised likelihood regression, using R software [ , ]. In the main NMAs, we will exclude studies reporting zero events in both arms. In addition, to more comprehensively explore the potential impact of missing data, we will conduct sensitivity analyses using the Informative Missingness Odds Ratio approach for binary outcomes, and the Informative Missingness Difference of Means approach for continuous outcomes [ , ]. For sensitivity analyses, we will perform NMAs in a Bayesian setting, using different priors for the between‐study standard deviation (Tau). Specifically, we will apply a weakly informative prior distribution Tau ~ N(0,1), Tau > 0, as well as empirical prior distributions proposed by Turner and colleagues for dichotomous outcome data [ ], and Rhodes, and colleagues for continuous outcome data [ ]. Certainty of the evidence assessment We will assess the confidence in the findings of the NMA using the framework by Salanti and colleagues, applied using CINeMA, which is based on the contribution matrix and implemented through a web application [ , ]. This will be applied to the three critical outcomes. The six domains to be assessed are: within‐study risk of bias, across‐study risk of bias (publication or reporting bias), indirectness (relevance to the research question and transitivity), imprecision (comparing the range of treatment effects included in the 95% CI with the range of equivalence), heterogeneity (predictive intervals), and incoherence (if estimates from direct and indirect evidence disagree). Each domain will be rated as giving major concerns, some concerns, or no concerns. For the domain of reporting bias, CINeMA evaluates the risk using the categories low risk, some concerns, or high risk, rather than the grading applied to the other domains. The within‐study bias domain will be assessed using the weighted average risk of bias, calculated by the CINeMA framework. The equivalence range used to judge imprecision, heterogeneity, and incoherence corresponds to clinically unimportant differences between interventions. We will define relevant treatment effects that represent a minimal important difference (MID) using evidence from the literature (i.e. the MID for the DLQI will be set at 4 [ ]), and expert input. For each result of the NMA for each comparison, we will summarise the overall confidence as high, moderate, low, and very low. Summary of findings tables for the NMAs will be developed using the approach recommended by Cochrane and GRADE [ , ]. An NMA summary of findings table will be created for the critical outcomes for which an NMA is possible. Consumer involvement Our research team includes four consumers who have been involved with the study design since inception. These consumers have lived experience with chronic plaque psoriasis and have used, or are using topical therapies. We held a focus group with our consumer partners to help select and prioritise outcomes for this review. People with psoriasis have provided critical input on the protocol and will continue to be critical members of our team as we interpret results and disseminate findings. documents.title: NICE NG222 depression in adults treatment and management

chunks.content: Significance Statement Only around half of patients with depression respond to initial antidepressant treatment, and it can take multiple different treatment steps to find the right treatment for a particular patient. It is important to find the right treatment as early as possible to provide patients with symptom relief. One treatment option for patients with unresolved symptoms is to take brexpiprazole as well as an antidepressant. The aim of our study was to investigate whether adding brexpiprazole to antidepressant treatment improves symptoms in groups of patients who have been living with depression for a shorter time, and for a longer time. We found that adding brexpiprazole helped patients regardless of how long they had lived with depression. In general, the earlier that patients receive the right treatment, the longer they will benefit from it. INTRODUCTION Depressive disorders affect 332 million people worldwide, are a leading cause of disability, increase the risk of all-cause mortality, and exert a substantial economic burden. Guidelines recommend various psychological and pharmacological therapies for depression, of which antidepressant treatment is first-line pharmacotherapy (commonly a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor [SSRI] or serotonin–noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor [SNRI]). However, only around 50% of patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) respond to initial antidepressant treatment, and unresolved symptoms are common. Thus, for some patients, multiple steps may be required to optimize MDD treatment. Options for patients with unresolved symptoms of depression include switching antidepressants, combining antidepressants, or augmenting with another drug such as an atypical antipsychotic (among other options). However, repeated “trial-and-error” of different treatments can result in patients feeling frustrated and dissatisfied, increasing the risk of adherence issues. Optimized treatment should therefore be provided as early in the disease course as possible to increase the likelihood of achieving full symptomatic and functional recovery. The 3 main monoamine systems associated with the pathophysiology of depression are noradrenaline (norepinephrine), serotonin, and dopamine. , Brexpiprazole is an atypical antipsychotic with subnanomolar affinity for receptors across these 3 monoaminergic systems. Four phase 3 randomized controlled trials have demonstrated the efficacy and tolerability of adjunctive brexpiprazole in patients with MDD and unresolved symptoms on antidepressant treatment. Given that outcomes can be improved by shortening the time from diagnosis to optimized treatment, it is hypothesized that patients with unresolved symptoms on antidepressants may benefit from adjunctive brexpiprazole early in the disease course. The aim of this post hoc analysis was to investigate the efficacy and safety of adjunctive brexpiprazole in patients who were earlier and later in the disease course (based on the proxies of age, age at diagnosis, number of lifetime episodes, episode duration, and number of prior antidepressants), using pooled data from randomized controlled trials. METHODS Study Design and Patients Data were included from 3 phase 3 randomized controlled trials ( ClinicalTrials.gov identifiers: NCT01360645 , NCT01360632 , NCT02196506 ) conducted at multiple sites in North America, Europe, and Russia between June 2011 and May 2016. The fourth phase 3 trial was not included in this pooled analysis because it had a different design from the other 3 trials. Each of the trials was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, the International Conference on Harmonisation Good Clinical Practice guidelines, and local regulatory requirements. The trials were approved by relevant institutional review boards or independent ethics committees, and all patients provided written informed consent prior to enrollment. The 3 trials had similar eligibility criteria and designs, which have previously been published. In brief, the trials enrolled adult outpatients (18–65 years) with a Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fourth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-IV-TR) diagnosis of single or recurrent, nonpsychotic MDD and a current depressive episode of ≥ 8 weeks in duration. Patients were required to have a history of inadequate response (<50% improvement based on self-report) to an adequate trial of 1–3 prior antidepressants during the current episode. Patients were ineligible if they presented with suicidal ideation or behavior, substance abuse or dependence, or other protocol-specified psychiatric comorbidities. The trials had 2 distinct treatment periods. Initially, patients received an investigator-determined, open-label SSRI/SNRI antidepressant (escitalopram, fluoxetine, paroxetine controlled release, sertraline, duloxetine, or venlafaxine extended release) + single-blind placebo for 8 weeks. The purpose of this period was to identify patients with inadequate response to antidepressant treatment (ie, persistent symptoms without substantial improvement) under clinical trial conditions. Those patients who met protocol-specified criteria for inadequate response based on clinician-reported depression rating scale scores entered a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-arm treatment period. In this period, patients received the same antidepressant + either adjunctive brexpiprazole or adjunctive placebo for 6 weeks. Depending on the trials, brexpiprazole was dosed at 1, 2, or 3 mg/day (fixed doses) with titration over 1–2 weeks. Definition of Earlier and Later Disease Course In this post hoc analysis, patients were stratified into “earlier” versus “later” disease course subgroups according to baseline demographic

antidepressant treatment (ie, persistent symptoms without substantial improvement) under clinical trial conditions. Those patients who met protocol-specified criteria for inadequate response based on clinician-reported depression rating scale scores entered a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-arm treatment period. In this period, patients received the same antidepressant + either adjunctive brexpiprazole or adjunctive placebo for 6 weeks. Depending on the trials, brexpiprazole was dosed at 1, 2, or 3 mg/day (fixed doses) with titration over 1–2 weeks. Definition of Earlier and Later Disease Course In this post hoc analysis, patients were stratified into “earlier” versus “later” disease course subgroups according to baseline demographic and clinical characteristics. The following 5 characteristics were considered relevant, for a total of 10 subgroups. Age. Clinical trial data indicate that duration of illness (ie, time since diagnosis of MDD) increases with age, suggesting that older patients may be later in the disease course than younger patients. In the present analysis, the earlier disease subgroup was defined as patients with age < median, and the later disease subgroup as patients with age ≥ median. Age at diagnosis of MDD. In the US-nationwide STAR * D (Sequenced Treatment Alternatives to Relieve Depression) study, younger age at onset was associated with a longer duration of illness, before and after adjustment for current age, suggesting that patients with younger age at onset may be later in the disease course than patients with older age at onset. In the present analysis, the earlier disease subgroup was defined as patients with age at diagnosis ≥ median, and the later disease subgroup as patients with age at diagnosis < median. Number of lifetime depressive episodes. In the STAR * D study, a higher number of depressive episodes was associated with a longer duration of illness, before and after adjustment for age. In the present analysis, the earlier disease subgroup was defined as patients with < median number of depressive episodes, and the later disease subgroup as patients with ≥ median number of depressive episodes. Duration of current depressive episode. Longer episode duration has been linked with younger age at onset of depression, and with decreased likelihood of remission and recovery. , In the present analysis, the earlier disease subgroup was defined as patients with < median duration of current depressive episode, and the later disease subgroup as patients with ≥ median duration of current depressive episode. Number of prior antidepressants in the current episode. In the STAR * D study, patients with a current depressive episode were administered sequential treatments until they experienced an acceptable benefit, preferably achieving symptom remission. A greater number of treatment steps was associated with a longer duration of illness at baseline, suggesting that patients with a greater number of prior treatments in the current episode may be later in the disease course than patients with fewer prior treatments. In the brexpiprazole trials, patients with 1–3 prior antidepressants at screening were eligible to enroll, and approximately 80% of randomized patients had inadequate response to 1 prior antidepressant at screening. Thus, in the present analysis, the earlier disease subgroup was defined as patients with 1 prior antidepressant at screening, and the later disease subgroup as patients with 2–3 prior antidepressants at screening (As described in the “Study Design” section, to be eligible for randomization, patients were required to have inadequate response to an additional open-label antidepressant after screening). Outcome Measures The primary efficacy measure in each trial was the Montgomery–Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS), a clinician-rated measure of depressive symptom severity that is widely used in MDD trials. The MADRS comprises 10 items (apparent sadness, reported sadness, inner tension, reduced sleep, reduced appetite, concentration difficulties, lassitude, inability to feel, pessimistic thoughts, and suicidal thoughts), each of which is rated on a 7-point scale from 0 (least severe) to 6 (most severe). Thus, total scores range from 0 (least severe) to 60 (most severe). The Clinical Global Impressions—Severity of illness (CGI-S) scale was included as a secondary efficacy measure. The CGI-S is a clinician-rated, single-item measure of overall illness severity, rated from 1 (normal, not at all ill) to 7 (among the most extremely ill patients). In the brexpiprazole trials, safety was assessed by a variety of standard subjective and objective measures, including the incidence of patient-reported treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs). In addition to the overall incidence of TEAEs, the present analysis investigated the incidence of extrapyramidal-symptom-related TEAEs (including akathisia, dyskinesia, dystonia, and parkinsonism) and increased body weight as a TEAE, which are of particular interest in relation to antipsychotic treatment. Data Analysis The focus of this analysis was the 2–3 mg/day dose of brexpiprazole, which comprises the recommended dose (2 mg/day) and the maximum dose (3 mg/day, permitted in the United States) for the adjunctive treatment of MDD. , Data for patients randomized to brexpiprazole 2 or 3 mg were pooled from

the incidence of patient-reported treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs). In addition to the overall incidence of TEAEs, the present analysis investigated the incidence of extrapyramidal-symptom-related TEAEs (including akathisia, dyskinesia, dystonia, and parkinsonism) and increased body weight as a TEAE, which are of particular interest in relation to antipsychotic treatment. Data Analysis The focus of this analysis was the 2–3 mg/day dose of brexpiprazole, which comprises the recommended dose (2 mg/day) and the maximum dose (3 mg/day, permitted in the United States) for the adjunctive treatment of MDD. , Data for patients randomized to brexpiprazole 2 or 3 mg were pooled from all 3 trials. A corresponding pooled 2 or 3 mg-equivalent placebo group was created. As a supporting analysis, a pooled brexpiprazole 2 mg/day group was also investigated, representing the recommended dose for the adjunctive treatment of MDD, , with a corresponding 2 mg-equivalent placebo group. The 2 mg analysis included data from only the 2 trials that investigated the 2 mg dose, and therefore comprised fewer patients than the 2–3 mg analysis. All analyses were performed in the sample of patients randomized as per final protocols who received at least one dose of double-blind medication and who had a baseline and at least one post-baseline MADRS total score evaluation recorded in the randomized treatment period. Baseline values were defined as the last values obtained prior to randomization. Least-squares mean changes from baseline in MADRS total score and CGI-S score were calculated using a mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM) in an observed-cases dataset with no imputation for missing data. Treatment effect was calculated as the least-squares mean difference in score change between antidepressant + brexpiprazole and antidepressant + placebo at week 6. The MMRM had factors of treatment, visit, site nested in trial, baseline, and interaction of treatment with visit, as well as interaction of baseline with visit. An unstructured covariance was used by default. Between-group comparisons were tested at a nominal 0.05 level (2-sided), with no adjustment for multiplicity. Patient baseline demographic and clinical characteristics, and the incidence of TEAEs, were summarized using descriptive statistics. Analyses were performed using SAS Enterprise Guide 8.2 (SAS Institute Inc, Cary, NC, USA). RESULTS Patients In the 2–3 mg analysis, data were analyzed for 579 patients who received antidepressant + brexpiprazole 2–3 mg/day, and 583 who received antidepressant + placebo. Completion rates were 539/579 (93.1%) for antidepressant + brexpiprazole 2–3 mg/day and 557/583 (95.7%) for antidepressant + placebo. The most common reasons for discontinuation (>1% for antidepressant + brexpiprazole 2–3 mg/day or antidepressant + placebo, respectively) were patient withdrawal of consent (13 [2.2%], 13 [2.2%]) and adverse events (17 [2.9%], 3 [0.5%]). In the 2 mg analysis, data were analyzed for 366 patients who received antidepressant + brexpiprazole 2 mg/day, and 380 who received antidepressant + placebo. Completion rates were 341/366 (93.2%) for antidepressant + brexpiprazole 2 mg/day and 363/380 (95.5%) for antidepressant + placebo. The most common reasons for discontinuation (>1% for antidepressant + brexpiprazole 2 mg/day or antidepressant + placebo, respectively) were patient withdrawal of consent (10 [2.7%], 7 [1.8%]) and adverse events (9 [2.5%], 1 [0.3%]). Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics were similar between treatment groups (see for the 2–3 mg analysis, and for the 2 mg analysis). Characteristics used to stratify patients into earlier and later disease course subgroups were as follows: Median age at baseline: 46 years (2–3 mg analysis) or 44.5 years (2 mg analysis). Median age at MDD diagnosis: 44 years (2–3 mg analysis) or 43 years (2 mg analysis). Median number of lifetime depressive episodes: 3 (both analyses). Median duration of current episode: 8 months (both analyses). Number of prior antidepressants: the majority of patients (>80%) had 1 prior antidepressant at screening (both analyses), supporting the chosen subgroups (1 or 2–3). At baseline, MADRS total score was similar across treatment groups and disease course subgroups, except that the score was slightly higher among patients with longer duration of current episode (see for the 2–3 mg analysis and for the 2 mg analysis). Efficacy For the 2–3 mg analysis, change from baseline to week 6 in MADRS total score is presented in according to age at baseline, age at diagnosis, number of lifetime episodes, duration of current episode, and number of prior antidepressants at screening. Greater improvement ( P < .05) was observed with antidepressant + brexpiprazole 2–3 mg versus antidepressant + placebo in all subgroups, whether representing earlier disease course or later disease course. Treatment effects (least-squares mean differences in score change) at week 6 were −1.79 to −2.92 points across subgroups ( ). Changes from baseline by week are presented in . The CGI-S score changes from baseline to week 6 showed greater improvement ( P < .05) with antidepressant + brexpiprazole 2–3 mg versus antidepressant + placebo in most subgroups representing earlier disease

current episode, and number of prior antidepressants at screening. Greater improvement ( P < .05) was observed with antidepressant + brexpiprazole 2–3 mg versus antidepressant + placebo in all subgroups, whether representing earlier disease course or later disease course. Treatment effects (least-squares mean differences in score change) at week 6 were −1.79 to −2.92 points across subgroups ( ). Changes from baseline by week are presented in . The CGI-S score changes from baseline to week 6 showed greater improvement ( P < .05) with antidepressant + brexpiprazole 2–3 mg versus antidepressant + placebo in most subgroups representing earlier disease course and later disease course, with treatment effects at week 6 of −0.17 to −0.30 points (data not shown). The exception was the subgroup with < 3 lifetime depressive episodes (representing earlier disease course), which showed a numerical improvement with antidepressant + brexpiprazole (treatment effect, −0.13; P = .19). Similar results were observed in the 2 mg analyses. The MADRS total score change is presented in and . Safety Across subgroups, the proportion of patients with at least one TEAE ranged from 53.1%–67.2% for antidepressant + brexpiprazole 2–3 mg/day, and 43.0%–51.8% for antidepressant + placebo ( ). The incidence of TEAEs was not consistently higher or lower in patients who were earlier or later in the disease course. Similarly, the proportions of patients with at least one extrapyramidal-symptom-related TEAE and with increased body weight as a TEAE were greater for antidepressant + brexpiprazole 2–3 mg/day than antidepressant + placebo, and the incidence was not consistently higher or lower in patients who were earlier or later in the disease course ( ). Similar results were observed in the 2 mg analyses ( ). DISCUSSION In MDD, a patient’s treatment should be optimized as early as possible to provide symptom relief, maximize their opportunity for full functional recovery, and help prevent the cumulative damage and neuroplastic changes that may occur with repeated episodes of depression. , In this post hoc analysis, adjunctive brexpiprazole 2–3 mg/day was associated with greater improvements in depressive symptoms than adjunctive placebo in patients with unresolved symptoms on antidepressants who were early in the disease course (based on the proxies of age, age at diagnosis, number of lifetime episodes, duration of current episode, and number of prior antidepressants). Similar improvements were observed in the brexpiprazole 2 mg/day analysis. These results suggest that adjunctive brexpiprazole may be a valuable treatment option when administered early in the disease course. Furthermore, this analysis showed that there was no advantage for patients in delaying adjunctive brexpiprazole treatment, since adjunctive brexpiprazole was efficacious to a similar degree in patients who were later in the disease course. Thus, patients with unresolved symptoms on antidepressants may obtain the maximum benefit from adjunctive brexpiprazole when it is initiated early in the disease course. , Real-world evidence supports the early initiation of adjunctive antipsychotic treatment in patients with MDD to reduce healthcare resource use and costs. , Specifically, initiation of adjunctive brexpiprazole within the first 2 months of antidepressant treatment (versus after 1 year) is estimated to reduce the annual cost of MDD-specific outpatient/inpatient visits and pharmacy by approximately 4000 USD per patient. Safety was assessed by the incidence of TEAEs, extrapyramidal symptoms (including akathisia, dyskinesia, dystonia, and parkinsonism), and weight increase. Given that MDD is a risk factor for the development and worsening of a range of comorbidities, it might be expected that patients later in the disease course will experience more medication side effects; however, this was only consistently observed for patients with a longer duration of current episode. With regard to treatment, adjunctive brexpiprazole was associated with a greater incidence of extrapyramidal symptoms and weight increase than adjunctive placebo, as previously noted in a pooled analysis of phase 3 trials. Prior studies indicate that adjunctive brexpiprazole is neither among the most activating (akathisia, restlessness, anxiety, and insomnia) nor the most sedating atypical antipsychotics and is associated with small changes in metabolic parameters and moderate weight gain during short- and long-term treatment. , Strengths of this analysis are the large dataset that included over a thousand patients, and the use of 5 different approaches to identify patients early in the disease course. Limitations are the post hoc nature of the analysis with no correction for multiple comparisons, meaning that the results should be considered hypothesis-generating. With regard to the proxies for disease course, investigators may not accurately record number of lifetime episodes or duration of current episode when enrolling patients. There was no adjunctive active comparator in this analysis, and to the authors’ knowledge no other adjunctive antipsychotics have been investigated in these disease course subgroups, which means that comparisons with other agents cannot be made. Finally, as with all analyses of clinical trial data, patient selection criteria and other protocol-specified restrictions limit the generalizability

With regard to the proxies for disease course, investigators may not accurately record number of lifetime episodes or duration of current episode when enrolling patients. There was no adjunctive active comparator in this analysis, and to the authors’ knowledge no other adjunctive antipsychotics have been investigated in these disease course subgroups, which means that comparisons with other agents cannot be made. Finally, as with all analyses of clinical trial data, patient selection criteria and other protocol-specified restrictions limit the generalizability of these results to a broader patient population. CONCLUSION In patients with MDD and unresolved symptoms of depression on antidepressant treatment, therapeutic doses of adjunctive brexpiprazole improved depressive symptoms in patients who were earlier in the disease course, as well as those who were later in the disease course. Adjunctive brexpiprazole is generally well tolerated in MDD, and there were no consistent differences in adverse events in patients who were earlier or later in the disease course. These results suggest that eligible patients will benefit from adjunctive brexpiprazole regardless of their stage of MDD. However, treatment should be optimized as early as possible in the disease course to minimize patient suffering and maximize clinical benefits, as well as to reduce healthcare resource use and costs. Given that there was no advantage of delaying brexpiprazole treatment, adjunctive brexpiprazole may be of maximum benefit to patients and healthcare systems when taken early in the disease course.
